#5571. Housing Starts Pull Back, but Top Markets Hold Their Ground

Zonda’s third quarter 2026 data shows housing starts over the past four quarters declined 10% from the same period a year ago. More specifically, 22 of the top 25 housing production markets posted year-over-year declines, pointing to a broad-based slowdown. However, the national slowdown can translate into very different competitive conditions depending on geography.

Sarasota was the clear outlier, with starts rising 20% year over year to 9,691 during the four quarters through Q3 2026. Chicago also managed growth, increasing 1% year over year to 7,680 starts, while Boise was effectively flat at 7,303.

At the other end of the spectrum, Las Vegas and Provo posted the largest declines among the top 25 markets, with starts falling 22% year over year in each. Riverside/San Bernardino followed closely with a 21% decline. Washington, D.C., Nashville, Raleigh, and Jacksonville were also among the markets recording double-digit contractions.

Despite declining activity, Dallas and Houston continue to operate on a different scale from the rest of the country.

Dallas ranked first with 37,497 starts over the past four quarters, down 10% year over year. Houston followed with 34,996, down 8% year over year. The two metros operate in a league of their own, each producing more than twice as many starts as any individual market elsewhere in the top 25.

Phoenix and San Antonio were the only other markets to top 15,000 starts, at 16,770 and 15,531, respectively. The rankings also point to relative stability at the top. Every market in the top 10 retained its position from the previous quarter, even as housing production softened nationally.

For industry professionals planning for 2027, the numbers reinforce the importance of looking beyond national trends. The size and direction of the housing adjustment vary substantially by market. Production is still highly concentrated in the Sun Belt metros, but growth in markets like Sarasota and Chicago shows that opportunities remain even against a weaker national backdrop.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Sean Fergus, Vice President of economic research at Zonda, leads the published research team. Fergus has 20 years of expertise in economic research, market studies, and financial analysis.

#5570. Alix Earle Opens the Doors to Family’s $4.1 Million New Jersey Mansion in Season 2 of Drama-Filled Netflix Series

Social media sensation Alix Earle is preparing to once again welcome fans into her family's sprawling New Jersey mansion, this time in the second season of her hit Netflix series "Earle Meets World."

Earle, 25, initially rose to stardom on TikTok, where she amassed a legion of followers with her candid "get ready with me videos," which were filmed inside her student housing at the University of Miami.

After graduating, her career continued to go from strength to strength—while the bubbly blonde expanded her work from short-form video to podcasts, drinks brands, and numerous ad campaigns.

Then, she took her success to "next phase" by partnering with Netflix to showcase all of the most "vulnerable," "hard," and "fun" moments in her life, many of which she experiences with her family by her side in the series, which hit the streaming giant on Sept. 4.

Now, the internet star has revealed that fans will get an even closer into her life away from the camera's during the second season of the show, which Earle announced in a joint Instagram video with Netflix.

In the clip, Earle can be seen strutting into the Netflix office while on the phone with her dad.

"Okay dad, when I said, 'What's the worst that could happen?' I didn't think it would be that bad. I know they aren't talking. I'm telling you, we have to just show it all, it will be fine," she said on the call before dumping a box of football-themed items onto the floor.

"Earle Meets World is coming back for season two, I'm just making myself at home," she added while lounging in the office.

In a press release shared by Netflix, Earle revealed, “Since Season 1 aired, some s— has hit the fan. But hey, that makes for a good Season 2. I couldn't be more excited to be back and get the cameras rolling. Lots to catch up on and share with our Netflix family!”

Meanwhile, Vice President of nonfiction series, Brandon Riegg, added, “Our goal with Earle Meets World was authenticity and going deeper than social media ever could. We’re thrilled that viewers connected with that and grateful to Alix for trusting us to tell her story. We’re excited to welcome her and her family back for Season 2!”

The influencer is once again handing over control of the cameras to Netflix producers, who will continue to focus their lenses on Earle and her family, including her TikTok star sister Ashtin, her mom, Alisa, her father, Thomas "TJ," her stepmother, Ashley Dupré, and her younger half-siblings, Izabel, Penelope, and Thomas.

Those who follow Earle's content will no doubt already be familiar with many of these characters, who regularly feature in the TikTok star's videos, particularly when she returns home to Red Bank, NJ, to spend time with her loved ones.

While the online starlet has continued to reside in Miami since graduating, while also taking on a property in Los Angeles, where she regularly travels for work, her family is largely located in and around New Jersey, where TJ and Ashley live in a sprawling mansion that they share with their three youngest children.

Records show that the couple, who wed in 2013, purchased the enormous property in 2013 for $2.25 million, scoring quite the deal on the home, which had previously been listed for $3.35 million. It is currently estimated to be worth $4.1 million, according to Realtor.com®.

However, the family appears to have made numerous upgrades to the dwelling in the six years since they bought it, with Earle's videos showcasing a much more modern and elegant interior than featured in the original listing images.

Meanwhile, records show that Earle's mother, Alisa, resides in a newly-built dwelling in nearby Point Pleasant.

When they are in New Jersey, the TikTok star and her sister, Ashtin, who resides in New York City, split their time between the two dwellings and it is understood that both parents will feature heavily in the Netflix series.

Earle announced the news of the first season of the show via a joint Instagram post with Netflix, in which she was filmed on the phone with her dad—who serves as her manager—outside of the Netflix offices.

In the clip, she tells her dad that things will be "fine," adding, "Dad, it's gonna be fun! It's gonna be fine. What's the worst that can happen?"

The video was captioned, "From your FYP to your TV: Alix Earle, her family, and friends will star in an unscripted series dropping later this year on Netflix."

In a press release shared by the streaming giant, the TikTok star confessed that partnering with Netflix felt "unreal," adding that she was excited to show fans her life behind the scenes.

"It honestly feels unreal to be partnering with Netflix, and I’m so excited to be creating this show with them," she shared. "I’ve shared my life for years through my own camera, but this felt like the next phase because it’s a chance to go deeper.

"Not just the highlights, but the real moments, too. The vulnerable ones, the hard ones, and the fun, chaotic ones in between. It’s the same authenticity people know me for, but now with a different lens."

The social media mogul revealed that she was most "excited" for her fans to see her "fun" and "modern family."

"People either think we’re insane or they’re like, wait, this is exactly like my life. And honestly, both are true. I’m excited for fans to experience the full picture as it happens. The chaos, the emotional moments, the stressful parts, and all the little things in between that you don’t always see online," she added.

She admitted that the process was a "little scary," adding, "I’m so used to being in control of what I share and what I keep private, so having cameras around in moments I normally wouldn’t post is definitely an adjustment.

"But the real, human moments are what connected me to my audience in the first place. If letting people in even more makes someone feel less alone, or even just makes them laugh, then it’s worth it."

Although she is hesitant to give up power over he content, Earle noted that she finds comfort in the relationship she has with her followers.

"My relationship with my followers has always felt really personal because I’ve been sharing my life the same way I would with my best friends. With this show, I want it to feel like you’re even more in it with me, in a way that’s real and not curated.

"The goal is not to be someone different on camera. It’s to show more of who I already am, and who my family really is. The fun, the messy, the growth, while capturing the way we help each other through it all," Earle added.

The news of her family's reality TV show comes a mere month after her and Houston Texans player Braxton Berrios called it quits after two years of dating.

Earle and Berrios, 30, began dating in February 2023 but kept their romance coy on social media, with the TikTok tycoon referring to her now-ex beau simply as "NFL man," when she started discussing their relationship with her followers.

They then took things to the next level in April, when Earle revealed to her followers that she had moved out of her rented Florida condo and into her boyfriend's $2.7 million Miami home, just as former Miami Dolphins star Berrios relocated to Texas, where he now plays for the Houston Texans.

Meanwhile, Earle moved to Los Angeles temporarily earlier this year, when she landed a role on "Dancing With the Stars," ultimately finishing in second place alongside professional dance partner, Val Chmerkovskiy.

Throughout her time on the competition, Berrios failed to make a single in-person appearance in the ballroom—however, Earle insisted to fans that his absence was the result of his intense football schedule.

In December, Earle admitted to fans that they had indeed split, insisting that there was no bad blood between them.

#5569. 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle

The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.

For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.

“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”

Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:

Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.

At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.

Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.

At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.

Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.

Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

#5568. Legal Funds, Legislation and ORE: Amid Unprecedented Challenges, Are MLSs On the Same Page?

The Council of Multiple Listing Services (CMLS) claims around 230 members—MLSs ranging in size from a couple hundred to over 100,000 members. As many in real estate are quick to point out, each serves a unique geography, and often has different structures, resources and goals—both a unique boon and a huge pitfall in the face of threats.

As MLSs face an existential—or at least foundational—challenge from Compass, and bigger questions about their role in the real estate ecosystem, can the fractured and notoriously entrenched community rally to protect the structures that have undergirded real estate for decades?

“This industry has been insulated,” says Brian Donnellan, CEO of Bright MLS, the nation’s largest. “Folks have been able to ignore what’s going on and not necessarily help…(but) the tide’s going out, and we’re going to see who has a bathing suit on. Because I think you can’t hide anymore if you’re not helping.”

Donnellan, who has led significant changes at Bright, focuses on what he has described as the necessity of evolution and scaling MLS, while also saying unequivocally that he believes MLSs are broadly coming together, led by CMLS CEO Jessie Edgerton.

Richard Haggerty, CEO of OneKey® MLS in New York, says he is also optimistic about MLSs coming together, and supports the “very important” role of CMLS, particularly around advocacy. He argues that people who question the “relevance” of the MLS industry aren’t “looking at the consequences of what would happen if the MLS were to disappear tomorrow.”

“I think that is a rallying cry, quite frankly,” he says.

Not every MLS leader is so confident. One MLS executive, who spoke to RISMedia on the condition of anonymity, said they were considering leaving CMLS in the near future, pointing to how some MLSs are on vastly different paths in relation to their legislative, legal and infrastructure priorities.

“I just want to be sure that (my MLS’s) dollars, that’s money from brokers—I have to make sure that it’s not going to come back to bite me,” the executive says.

Compass has not shied away from characterizing the MLS industry as an illegal monopoly—sometimes affirming its positive impact on real estate while arguing that MLSs should essentially cease any rulemaking or oversight over brokers.

The mega-brokearage has repeatedly pointed to what it characterizes as a significant portion of the MLS market that has dropped restrictions on off-MLS listing practices. Other MLSs (and brokers) have claimed that these rules prevent “free-riding” by brokerages that want to access other company’s listings without providing their own (at least initially), and repealing them would spell the end of cooperation and the “open marketplace.”

CRMLS, which has led pushback against Compass’s attacks on the MLS, is currently embroiled in a court battle with the mega-brokerage, joined by (at press time) eight other MLSs, including OneKey.

Notably, CRMLS announced it was launching an “MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund,” intending to cover legal costs for MLSs targeted for policies that CRMLS argues support cooperation. CMLS kicked off the process to create a similar fund only weeks later.

CRMLS declined to speak to RISMedia for this story.

Edgerton tells RISMedia that both funds will continue to operate separately “at this stage.”

“We support both efforts and encourage those who want to contribute to the MLS community’s efforts in current litigation to consider supporting both funds,” she says.

Edgerton, a lawyer herself, says she is confident that the legal fund is grounded in good practice and precedent, while acknowledging that every initiative at this scale has risk and “anyone can sue for anything.”

“The function of a legal action fund is one of those fundamental offerings made by trade organizations regularly,” Edgerton says. “Is there the possibility that we will get sued? Sure. Am I ready for that? Absolutely. That’s the world that we’re living in right now.”

It is one thing for the industry to confront these external legal challenges together. But what happens when MLSs are litigating essentially opposite positions on policies—and theoretically drawing from the same resources?

Most notably right now, MRED in Chicago is tied up in court-ordered mediation with Zillow as it stands by policies ostensibly meant to prevent the portal from restricting “private” listings—with Compass as a co-defendant.

In New York, CRMLS and the other eight MLSs are fighting Compass while essentially taking the opposite position from MRED, defending their ability to restrict off-MLS transactions.

Other MLSs have taken very different approaches to these questions, which are now being mulled by at least one federal judge.

Asked if CMLS’s fund can function in this type of environment, Edgerton says the organization is being “very strategic” and setting up a process with “deep objectivity,” planning to anonymize grant applications and ensure decision-makers bring “as much outside voice…as possible,” along with legal expertise.

“Everyone has been deeply, deeply in support of the Legal Action Fund,” Edgerton says. “But the other half of it is, this is not a standalone effort in terms of the voice the MLS needs right now.”

The MLS executive who was granted anonymity said they wanted to see evidence that CMLS’s fund—and the organization more broadly—was actually functioning in this objective way.

The executive also expresses skepticism about CMLS’s ongoing lobbying push, based on the same conflict—specifically, that “template legislation” (theoretical, at this point) that could be used as a roadmap by multiple states to advance MLS priorities might not be what some MLSs want enacted in their markets.

“We’ve spent years investing in our government affairs,” the executive says. “And now, is it going to split the message if a regulator has a decision to make one phone call or another phone call? That just diluted the messaging that we’re trying to put forward.”

As many MLSs prepare for a drawn-out legal battle, in the meantime, the real estate industry continues to move relentlessly toward control and consolidation. Regardless of any decision by judge or jury, the role of the MLS as either broker cooperatives or listing platform is likely to face challenges.

Open Real Estate (ORE), which has promised to launch its own listing platform with “sole discretion” over where data is syndicated, remains somewhat of an enigma, with many MLS leaders expressing support while still looking for answers on specifics.

“Open Real Estate isn’t the MLS,” Donnellan says. “The MLS offers a transparency that individual brokers can’t.”

Donnellan says he believes that ORE is really just about brokers having more control over listings, while adding he believes that the brokers involved “believe that an MLS does a really good job for them…in terms of an open and fair marketplace.”

“I know Bright has worked hard to work with a variety of brokers to have a clear and transparent marketplace,” he says. “So no, I don’t see this as competition with us. Our jobs may be a little bit different. We may have different aspects or focuses, but we’re here to have rules for what a listing is and how that listing is going to be used within a professional environment.”

As far as how MLSs need to evolve, Donnellan emphasizes scale, and notes that around 30% of agents aren’t affiliated with any of the big national companies like Compass or those behind ORE. He also says that 99.3% of listings end up in the MLS before they are sold, even after Bright tweaked its rules to allow more off-MLS “pre-marketing.”

“That leads me to believe that we’ve been doing the right policies and going the right way for transparency,” he says.

Could a big court decision or new legislation—potentially driven by a landslide election that shifted power at both state and federal level—change how MLSs operate? Donnellan says he isn’t expecting any surprises, noting that the industry has always had to monitor legal changes as well.

“It’s more about states, not about federal,” he says. “I suppose the good news in all of this, and I say this somewhat tongue in cheek, is that it doesn’t move fast. And usually the signs are on the wall before something happens.”

Haggerty, for his part, says that he believes MLSs need to start at a much more basic level in terms of advocacy and lobbying, something that (hopefully) they are more united on. He notes that CMLS’s early meetings with lawmakers have really just been explaining to lawmakers what an MLS is.

“We have to educate, first off, our local, state and federal legislators why an MLS is so vital to a vibrant, open, pro-competitive marketplace,” Haggerty says.

MLSs are “that key building block,” he adds.

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5567. Mortgage Rates Fall for Fourth Straight Week Despite Looming Fed Hike

Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.24% one year ago.

"Mortgage rates dropped to their lowest level in seven weeks, a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility as they navigate the current housing market," says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

A month of falling mortgage rates comes as welcome news for homebuyers, though Realtor.com® senior economist Jiayi Xu warns that a reversal could come as soon as next week.

The stronger-than-forecast October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Federal Reserve's next federal funds rate hike as part of its mandate to curb inflation.

Fed Gov. Christopher Waller warned this week that a larger 50-basis-point increase should be considered in December’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting if inflation remains hot.

Shortly after Waller's warning, the October consumer price index report exceeded economists' expectations, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%.

A December hike is now essentially priced in, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase topping 93%, according to CME FedWatch. The odds of another quarter-percentage-point hike in January 2027 currently stand at 67%.

"The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast," says Xu.

Today's homebuyers find themselves squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, and Xu contends that inflation is the bigger long-term problem.

"High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are," notes the economist. "But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated."

Crucially, inflation also erodes households' purchasing power, especially when wages lag consumer prices.

In October, existing-home sales dropped to their lowest level since August 2010, according to the latest data  from the National Association of Realtors®.

In this economic environment, first-time buyers are hit the hardest because they have no existing equity to use as a cushion, forcing them to save toward a down payment from already stretched budgets.

"Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years," says Xu.

Sellers have responded to cooling buyer demand by pulling back. This week, new listing activity fell 10.3% year over year after six weeks of more incremental declines, according to the latest weekly Realtor.com housing trends report.

"Sellers are discouraged because of how disengaged buyers are," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones. "The prices buyers are open to are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower."

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. #5566. Telegram Doesn’t Need to Convert Crypto Users: 1M Wallets in 48 Hours Reveal Its Massive Distribution Advantage

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Telegram is gaining crypto users without having to convince them to download another app. More than 1 million self-custodial wallets appeared on the messaging platform within 48 hours. Founder Pavel Durov says the growth reflects a simple feature: wallets activate automatically when users receive Grams. The milestone shows Telegram’s biggest advantage in crypto: distribution.

Unlike traditional crypto wallets, Telegram’s native wallet operates inside an application millions already use daily. Crypto traders, project founders, airdrop hunters, and blockchain communities have long relied on Telegram. That existing audience gives its wallet a distribution advantage that standalone crypto applications must spend years building.

The latest growth also raises an interesting question about blockchain adoption. Does crypto really need another wave of new users, or does it need easier access for people already participating? Telegram could provide exactly that bridge, provided wallet registrations translate into meaningful economic activity.

Durov reported more than 1million new self-custodial wallets over 48 hours in an X post. The dashboard accompanying his announcement showed more than 1 million registrations across the period.

1M+ self-custodial Gram wallets activated on Telegram in just 48 hours. $GRAM is up 10% in 24h, the #1 gainer in the CMC top 100. pic.twitter.com/VGVTT5AZQk

According to Durov, users do not need to manually create a wallet before receiving crypto. Their wallets activate when someone sends them Grams.

This creates a potentially powerful viral distribution mechanism. One user sends tokens to another, introducing the recipient to an on-chain wallet. The recipient can then hold or transfer assets without leaving Telegram.

This approach removes several familiar barriers to crypto adoption. New users do not necessarily need to understand seed phrases, download separate applications, or navigate an exchange. Telegram already provides the social environment where these transactions can begin.

The platform also has more than one billion monthly users, giving its crypto ambitions an enormous potential audience. Even a small conversion rate could produce substantial wallet growth.

The latest wallet milestone is not the only sign of expanding activity across The Open Network (TON), the blockchain powering Telegram’s wallet. TON averaged 4.06 million daily transactions during October. The network also added approximately 2.73 million wallets throughout the month, its strongest monthly addition since October 2024.

Stablecoin activity offers another indication of growing utility. TON averaged 37,693 daily stablecoin users in October, representing a 23.44% increase from September.

The stablecoin figures are particularly interesting because they point toward activity beyond token speculation. Payments and transfers could give Telegram crypto a more practical role in everyday digital interactions.

TON’s stablecoin supply stood at $585 million today. Its decentralized finance total value locked, however, remained comparatively modest at approximately $44 million.

Payments, stablecoin transfers, digital collectibles, and Telegram’s mini-app ecosystem could provide reasons to return. These services could gradually make blockchain transactions feel like another ordinary messaging feature.

#5565. Jenny McCarthy Reveals She and Donnie Wahlberg Have Disposed of ’30 Years of Clothes’ and ‘All’ of Their Furniture After Mold Poisoning Diagnosis

Jenny McCarthy is still dealing with the fallout from her mold and mycotoxin poisoning diagnosis.

The actress had recently shared that she’s been living in a tent in her yard as she continues to “detox,” and during the Nov. 10 episode of her podcast, “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed some of the additional steps she’s taken to work toward a solution.

McCarthy, 54, explained that she recently had to persuade her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, to say “bye-bye” to his clothing “and also furniture” after the couple went through the costly experience of remediating their home.

“We left all of our furniture behind,” she said, adding that she believes her mold poisoning came from the makeup and dressing room at her workplace. “I didn’t want to risk anything.”

The “Masked Singer” judge went on to explain that she “wound up throwing everything away” and has been purchasing inexpensive items from TikTok shop to replace her wardrobe.

McCarthy and her podcast guest, functional medicine physician Amy Myers—who has also dealt with a mold poisoning diagnosis—commiserated on how challenging it can be to spend money on clothing and household items after going through the costly process of remediating a home.

“I’m afraid to spend money on clothes anymore because I had to give everything away. And I’m like, that’s 30 years of clothes, of red carpet events, and memories,” said McCarthy.

Myers said that following her own treatment, she spent four years working with an architect, builders, and engineers to construct a “forever home” where she would “never get sick.”

The Santa Fe, NM, home was constructed using pumice-crete, steel, and glass, but after just six months, Myers discovered that it had also developed mold spores after an incorrectly installed dryer vent was affected by water condensation.

The doctor was then advised to enter another remediation process.

McCarthy has previously opened up about the “mold protocol” she embarked on in January 2025, which involved a routine of vitamins and various treatments.

“Remediation costs are so high because it takes a specialist to be able to move the mold without ruining your entire house,” she said on the Oct. 28 episode of her podcast. Following remediation, she hired contractors to “come in and rebuild” the home.

“We remediated and because I am paranoid now about basically sleeping anywhere, I live in a tent. And I’m not even joking,” she said.

Adding that she feels “a little bit crazy sometimes” and has a “paranoid” state of mind, McCarthy said the situation has been “really, really hard.” Wahlberg, 57, has not been living in the tent with her.

“Donnie is working in Canada, and he is safe inside of a building,” she said. “Does he think I’m crazy? Yes. But he completely understands it.”

After nearly two years of work to move past the diagnosis, McCarthy and Wahlberg have considered relocating.

“I am so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donnie about moving out of the Midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” she said.

While it appears that the tent McCarthy is residing in is located in California, it’s unclear whether the home she had remediated is the St. Charles, IL, residence she and Wahlberg listed for $2,799,000 in September of this year.

In a recent Instagram comment, McCarthy indicated that the couple were “going to Vegas. Not Cali.” following the listing of their longtime home.

The couple have owned the property for over a decade, purchasing it for $1.1 million in 2015.

“This isn’t an extravagant home, but there’s no greater symbol of our love for each other than this house and how much love has gone into it,” Wahlberg told People magazine of the dwelling in 2019.

The four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home was built in 1996. Spanning 7,236 square feet, the abode sits on 1.26 acres. Based on the contingent status on the property’s listing, it appears the couple have found a buyer.

#5564. October Existing-Home Sales Sink to 16-Year Low; Rates Only Partly to Blame

The National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) Existing-Home Sales report for October came in on a somewhat dismal note: Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month to a rate of 3.75 million.

That marks the lowest level since August 2010’s 3.68 million, according to Realtor.com®  Chief Economist Danielle Hale.

Year-over-year home sales were down 8.8% compared to October 2025, which recorded a sales pace of 4.11 million.

Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West, but held steady in the relatively “inventory-constrained” and “competitive” Northeast market, Hale noted. Year-over-year sales, however, declined for all four regions.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun blamed mortgage rates. “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” he said.

As the housing market enters its slowest season, rates that have held above 7%—a huge leap from before the Iran War, when they touched 6%—have depressed demand and discouraged many buyers, who already face longer-term issues with housing affordability.

Hale concurred with Yun’s diagnosis. According to her, climbing mortgage rates in September (the time when many October closed sales would have been in contract) “were the highest rates of 2026 at the time…and they likely derailed some homebuying plans.”

If mortgage rates “derailed” home-buying plans in October, could the recent ease in mortgage rates signal a gentler turn in the market in the coming months?

Hale thinks the story is not so simple. In her words, the October market “reflect(ed) a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

She added that “several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go, including a strong economy and jobs market, persistent inflation, and an expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments.”

Overall, Hale said she “expect(s) to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Sean Fergus, VP of Economic Research at builder-focused data and analytics firms NewHomeSource and Zonda, largely came to the same conclusion as Hale.

“Rates have since eased,” he said, “but buyers need to trust that relief will last before they come back in force.”

Yun had a more positive outlook, predicated on whether mortgage rates continue to decline. In NAR’s press release, he said that “(b)ased on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.”

Yun also commented on the relatively good financial position of homeowners currently, saying that they “are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation.”

As evidence for this claim, he pointed to the “historically low” number of distressed property sales, which “remains…at only 2% of all transactions.”

As a final sort of snapshot on the real estate ecosystem, total unsold inventory ticked up 1.3% to 1.59 million units, or the equivalent of 5.1 months’ supply. September 2026 recorded 4.7 months’ worth of unsold inventory, still higher than 4.4 months’ unsold inventory in October 2025, from which 1.59 million units represents a 4.6% yearly  increase.

Median existing-home sale prices increased more modestly, only crawling up 0.4% year-over-year to $416,700. The same median price was $414,900 last October. Even so, this is the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5562. What to expect during SC26: Join theCUBE Nov. 17–19

High-performance computing and artificial intelligence are converging, driven by advances in exascale computing, accelerated systems, data storage and high-speed networking.

The convergence of these technologies is a prime topic for discussion during SC26 in Chicago this month. Major industry players, such as Dell Technologies Inc., Google LLC and Nvidia Corp., have pursued a set of initiatives in the HPC arena, and SC26 will be an occasion to learn more about how AI and HPC workloads are evolving to write supercomputing’s next chapter.

“SC26 provides an important opportunity to examine how the convergence of AI, high-performance computing and application development are reshaping enterprise infrastructure priorities,” said theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty. “Organizations must connect high-performance infrastructure, accessible data and modern application development to move beyond experimentation and accelerate production-ready AI deployments. For Dell and the broader HPC ecosystem, SC26 offers a platform to demonstrate how integrated compute, storage and AI infrastructure can address these challenges.”

TheCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will be covering the latest HPC news and announcements from SC26 in Chicago, Nov. 17–19. Coverage will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with industry leaders and analysts as theCUBE explores how supercomputing’s future is being shaped at the intersection of exascale systems and AI infrastructure. Discussion will focus on ways that accelerated computing is transforming research environments, while quantum-HPC integration and agentic AI push scientific discovery toward greater autonomy. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s ongoing collaboration with Nvidia and other organizations has yielded several new developments in the HPC arena over the past year, particularly in the area of quantum computing.

The two companies have been working with the U.S. Department of Energy to build and deliver the Doudna supercomputer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The system will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platform and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking inside Dell’s integrated rack systems and PowerEdge servers to support large-scale scientific computing and data-intensive research.

In September, Dell announced a collaboration with silicon-spin qubit developer Diraq to integrate quantum processing units with HPC and AI server infrastructure. The joint effort is designed to integrate quantum processors with classical computing infrastructure in commercial data centers.

Moves such as these point toward a convergence of AI and quantum technologies, which will likely propel both forward as new platforms are built and deployed.

“The market for high-performance computing is meeting the AI factory at the point of innovation,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “HPC has always led the most challenging data problems, so this trend makes perfect sense. Quantum will be the next big inflection point and we’re seeing that new technologies are often complementary to existing infrastructure. We expect that to be the case between accelerated computing and quantum, particularly in the area of error correction.”

Hyperscaler Google Cloud is also building systems to support HPC demands for industries like manufacturing, health care and life sciences, weather forecasting and electronic design automation.

At the forefront of Google’s HPC initiative is the H4D VM, the company’s high-performance computing virtual machine. Introduced last year, the H4D VM is powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and offers whole-node VM performance of more than 12,000 GFLOPS and memory bandwidth exceeding 950 GB/s.

An example of how HPC is making inroads in daily life can be seen in the use of H4D VMs by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. In July, Google Cloud announced that it had been selected as the primary provider of high-performance computing infrastructure for the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System.

The adoption of HPC to enable meteorologists and researchers to develop future forecasting models is an example of how systems technology will play a critical role in both supercomputing and AI infrastructure moving forward.

“Systems are the key in supercomputing advances,” said theCUBE Research’s John Furrier. “Different architectures. Different bets. Same underlying problem: How do you keep the multiplication engines doing useful work instead of waiting for data? That’s why I think the next era of AI infrastructure won’t be defined by the ‘best chip.’ It will be defined by the best system architecture.”

While the field of HPC is being defined by major players such as Dell and Google, other firms are making contributions as well in areas such as cloud infrastructure and analytics.

Vultr Inc. is building high-performance cloud computing infrastructure for AI, risk management, compliance and fraud prevention. The company is developing its platform across 33 global regions by leveraging CPUs, GPUs and open, composable architectures to position itself as a cloud infrastructure specialist in the agentic AI era.

High-performance computing is also generating a need for consistent data sharing and access across platforms. Omni Analytics Inc. is building a data collaboration solution that can connect directly to cloud data warehouses without needing to preload or duplicate data.

SC26 will offer an opportunity to not only assess the progress of HPC in the enterprise but also examine how AI is continuing to transform the compute stack to generate meaningful business results.

“As organizations invest in increasingly sophisticated AI environments, the competitive differentiator will be the ability to optimize the entire technology stack from data movement and storage performance to application development and deployment,” Nashawaty said. “The central SC26 narrative is that the future of AI supercomputing will be defined not simply by how much compute organizations deploy, but by how effectively they translate that investment into measurable business and scientific outcomes.”

Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of SC26, Nov. 17–19. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.

SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.

SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.

#5561. Social Security Could Have Paid Full Benefits Until 2059. What Went Wrong?

Social Security could have paid full benefits until 2059—25 years longer than currently projected—if the share of the U.S. economy subject to payroll taxes had remained at its 1983 level, according to a new analysis.

Under that scenario, the program would have collected an additional $10.8 trillion in payroll tax revenue and interest between 1984 and 2034.

The findings, from AARP's Public Policy Institute, come as Social Security's combined trust funds are projected to run dry in 2034. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only about 83% of scheduled benefits that year.

And while much of the debate over Social Security's financial troubles has centered on declining birthrates and a growing number of retirees supported by fewer workers, the new analysis points to another major factor.

As more of the nation's income flows to high earners and investors, a shrinking share of the economy is subject to the payroll taxes that finance Social Security.

In 1983, wages subject to those taxes accounted for 41% of the nation's gross domestic product. By 2025, that share had fallen to just 34%.

To understand what changed for the trust fund, it helps to take a trip back to 1984: when "Ghostbusters" dominated the box office, Madonna broke out with "Like a Virgin," and the median household income was $61,910, compared with an average of $75,850, according to U.S. Census Bureau data adjusted to 2025 dollars.

Today, those figures have climbed to $87,460 and $126,700, respectively.

That's a 41% increase in median household income, compared with a 67% increase in the average—evidence of how income growth has become more concentrated toward the upper end of the distribution.

And that's where Social Security runs into trouble.

The program collects payroll taxes on wages, but only up to an annual limit. In 2026, workers and employers each pay 6.2% on the first $184,500 of wages. So someone earning $2 million pays the same amount in Social Security payroll taxes as someone earning $184,500.

As more wage income accumulates above that ceiling, Social Security collects nothing from those additional earnings, even as they contribute to the growth of the economy.

But the problem extends beyond how wages are distributed.

Between 1970 and 2023, labor compensation's share of GDP fell from 65% to 57%, as a larger portion of national income flowed to business owners and investors through profits and investment returns.

Unlike wages, most of that income isn't subject to Social Security payroll taxes. So as economic growth generates more profits and investment returns, Social Security doesn't necessarily collect additional revenue.

And those earnings are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans.

Taxpayers earning $1 million or more represented just 1% of filers in 2023 but received 48% of all investment income, according to AARP's analysis of Internal Revenue Service data.

AARP also points to the growth of businesses whose owners can receive some of their compensation as profits rather than salaries, further reducing the amount subject to payroll taxes.

Together, these changes have allowed the U.S. economy to generate substantially more income without a corresponding increase in the share subject to Social Security taxes. As a result, the program has captured a shrinking portion of the nation's economic growth, leaving less revenue available to pay future benefits.

Millions of older Americans are already struggling to afford their homes, leaving them particularly vulnerable to any potential reductions in benefits.

In 2023, more than 12.4 million households headed by adults 65 or older spent over 30% of their income on housing, according to Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies. More than half of those households—6.7 million—spent over 50% of their income on housing alone.

"Even without any insolvency-driven benefit cuts, millions of seniors already struggle to pay for food, basic healthcare, and even housing," Shannon Benton, executive director of The Senior Citizens League, said in a Nov. 10 statement.

And retirees could face those cuts sooner than the combined trust fund projection suggests.

The separate trust fund responsible for retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, two years before the hypothetical combined funds. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.

Based on the average retired worker monthly benefit of $2,089 in September 2026, a 22% reduction would amount to roughly $460 a month.

Now, advocates warn that decisions over Social Security's financing can no longer be deferred.

"The incoming class of senators face an enormous responsibility," Benton said, noting that their six-year terms will run through January 2033—past the point when Social Security's retirement and survivors trust fund is projected to exhaust its reserves.

Richard W. Johnson, vice president of financial security at AARP’s Public Policy Institute and author of the analysis, argues that strengthening Social Security requires bringing its financing into line with the modern economy.

"Strengthening Social Security does not require re-creating the economy of 1983," he said. "It just means updating Social Security's financing to reflect how Americans receive income today."

And it was a popular idea on the 2026 midterm campaign trail, too.

In October, Sherrod Brown, who won Ohio's Senate race, called for higher earners to contribute more "by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program."

Troy Jackson, Maine's senator-elect, went further, calling for eliminating the cap altogether.

"Making sure that wealthier people pay the same rate that working class people do would definitely strengthen the Social Security system overall," Jackson said in a September TV interview.

The idea has also drawn bipartisan interest, with Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) jointly proposing the elimination of the cap in June.

Based on Social Security actuaries' 2025 assumptions, eliminating the cap could close about 67% of the program's 75-year financing gap if higher contributions didn't generate additional future benefits—or roughly half if they did.

Other proposals would tax certain business and investment income that currently falls outside Social Security's revenue base.

#5560. Construction Site Next to Deadly Brooklyn Building Collapse Had History of Safety Issues

As authorities continue to search through the rubble of a deadly building collapse in Flatbush, Brooklyn, that killed eight, troubling details have emerged about safety concerns at a neighboring construction site.

On Wednesday afternoon, the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed, taking the shared wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. with it, leaving the bedrooms and closets of residents in that building exposed.

The deadly tragedy occurred next to an active construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., where an existing structure had been demolished and excavation was underway to build a new residential building.

In a press conference at the scene of the tragedy, Mayor Zohran Mamdani vowed a full investigation into what preceded and caused the collapse, including whether the construction work underway at 2625 Bedford Ave. played any role.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

The construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. was purchased for $3.99 million by a pair of LLCs registered to Judith Swimer and Faigy Fischman in June 2024, just days after the duo purchased another property at 600 Utica Ave. in East Flatbush for $5 million, according to public records.

Public records show they initially planned to develop a three-story apartment building on the lot, but the project had been plagued with stops and starts over amendments to the building plan and safety concerns from city inspectors.

In March of this year, the Department of Buildings halted the demolition of a one-story building on the site after an inspector reported that demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

According to signs posted on the site, the construction and development management firm Promont is overseeing the project. Realtor.com has reached out to Promont for comment.

The alleged deviation from filed plans may have been related to a new permitting request submitted by Robert Fischman of WG Facility X LLC, amending the proposed project to a nine-story structure on the site with a ground-floor grocery store. That amended permit request has not yet been approved.

Fischman has a troubled history. In 1999, Fischman was charged in a real estate kickback scheme involving his company, M.S. Berkoff Co. Earlier this year, Berkoff Supply sent tenants of 1321 Flatbush Ave. a letter alerting them to the excavation work.

In March of this year, as a part of its survey of the property in advance of submitting the request for the revised nine-story build, Promont commissioned a pre-construction report from structural and geotechnical monitoring company Quiver Monitoring.

The report focused on the buildings surrounding 2625 Bedford Ave. and assessed the masonry on the north facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. as being in poor condition, "with a wide range of deficiencies noted" according to the report.

Jessie Kramer is a licensed professional engineer in Colorado. She has deep experience in forensic engineering, including uncovering the causes of building collapses.

Kramer tells Realtor.com® that an older brick building adjacent to an active excavation site immediately raises red flags.

“Tons of thoughts pop up when I see something like that,” she says. "My day-to-day is looking at collapsed buildings, looking at failed buildings, and saying, 'Why did this happen? How widespread is the damage?' And often, the answer involves multiple issues."

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced that the city would sweep 100 other properties associated with five entities tied to the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. The mayor and the city’s Department of Buildings commissioner declined to name those entities.

Isolag Realty Corp. purchased 1321 Flatbush Ave. in 2024, and Olufemi Falade signed the deed. The property consisted of four residential units and a ground-floor commercial space. A three-bedroom unit in the building rented for $3,550.

The 96-year-old building had 98 recorded violations dating to 1972, according to the city's Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development. Eleven of those violations were from this past year, including a violation for "unsafe electrical wiring" and a notice to "provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe."

Falade has a tumultuous history of building ownership. In 2006, he spent 12 days in jail for failing to repair issues in numerous properties he owned. “In just 12 buildings he owns, there are more than 1,800 violations of the city’s housing and maintenance codes,” Housing Preservation and Development Commissioner Shaun Donovan told the New York Post at the time.

"I can't speak to what potential deficiencies might have been there before this happened," Kramer says. "But I can say on a building of this age, our modern codes differ a ton from what were the standards back then. So it's imperative to keep up with maintenance in these old buildings. And that's an active process. Owners have to be super on top of it.

“People obviously are wanting answers immediately, and that’s not going to happen,” Kramer adds. “This is going to be a yearslong investigation process to decide who’s at fault and what happened.”

Andrea Cavallier contributed to this report.

#5559. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

#5558. Rates Come Down Again but Remain Over 7%

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates eased again for the fourth-straight week but remain almost a full percentage point over last year at this time, a key reason buyers continue to hold back and why the market remains sluggish.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.11%, down seven bases points from  7.18% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.24% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.45%, down from 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.

At presstime, the average rate was back up to 7.42% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said that while rates are at their lowest level since late September, borrowing costs are still nearly a full percentage point higher than they were last year at this time.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines,” she said. “In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets. Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly even if rates move higher.”

Sturtevant noted that data on pending home sales suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the fourth quarter. “It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jiayi Xu added that the recent downtrend trend with rates could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%.

“The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike,” Xu said in a statement. “On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast.”

Xu also said today’s homebuyers are being squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, with inflation being the bigger long-term problem.

“High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.”

San Francisco 49ers star Christian McCaffrey has showed off his unusual skill while also giving fans a glimpse of his and Olivia Culpo's $14.5 million property.

The pro athlete, 30, took to social media to showcase his skills off the football field while holding his 5-week-old son, Roman.

In the clip shared online, he played the harmonica to Billy Joel's hit "Piano Man," while his brother-in-law Gus Culpo worked the keyboard.

“Ear training with Uncle Gus,” McCaffrey penned alongside the video.

In the clip, baby Roman is nestled asleep on McCaffrey’s chest as the NFL star holds him in his left hand while he plays the harmonica with his right.The glimpse of his musical talent came mere days after his wife, Olivia Culpo, 34, took to Instagram to share a picture of the family on game day. It showed her, Roman, and daughter Colette, 1, stepping out to watch McCaffrey take on the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium.

One of the snaps showed off their game-day attire, which included a 49ers shirt with "Daddy" on the back.

Another image showed Roman in his stroller and was captioned, "Roman's first game."

The beauty mogul also shared a photo of her and her daughter, which she captioned, “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom.”

Culpo also shared a video of her taking their children to embrace their dad after the game.

“We’re back with one more little fan in the stands this season," she added. "A little more love coming along for the game this season."

The model revealed that she welcomed their second baby on Sept. 29.

Months before, she revealed that she had transformed their guest room into a nursery. She shared that she overhauled the room her sister Aurora Culpo's kids Remi, 7, and Soleil, 5, use when they visit.

The room featured a neutral aesthetic with an animal theme.

Honestly, newborns don’t really sleep in their room in the beginning anyway because they’re eating around the clock. That same month, Culpo revealed she and McCaffrey were in the process of overhauling their $14.5 million property to ensure it would look its best by the time their newest family member arrived.

Culpo and McCaffrey purchased the Fryman Canyon, CA, dwelling from actor George Clooney in 2025, but they are now removing all traces of the "Ocean's Eleven" star from the home as they turn it into their dream family abode.

Revealing a sneak peek at the changes, Culpo pointed to one particular area of irritation that she has since transformed: dual bathrooms that sat next to each other with their own doors.

"Remember the two bathrooms next to each other that made no sense? All gone! I moved the door to the kitchen and now it will be a scullery,” Culpo wrote alongside an image of her hallway with the offending bathrooms on full display.

The model did not stop there, moving on to other spaces in the house, all of which have been given a stunning face-lift with new wallpaper, paint, and upgraded floors.

#5555. As AI agents take control, Nvidia rethinks the security playbook

Nvidia Corp. recently added a new pillar to its AI networking infrastructure with the unveiling of Scale-In.

Scale-In brings purpose-built acceleration to secure, manage and operate agentic AI factories. It is designed to deliver secure access, high-performance data movement, tenant isolation, simpler operations and more predictable performance as agents assume increasingly larger roles within AI factories.

“In agentic AI, it’s a completely different use case because now we’re dealing with many agents that need to run on the infrastructure,” said Gilad Shainer (pictured), senior vice president of networking at Nvidia. “You need to increase security because you need to make sure that those agents are contained in their sandbox and are not doing the wrong things. You need to build an infrastructure that needs to ensure security all around…what happens in the memory, what happens on storage. This is why we needed to bring an infrastructure which actually enabled the security across everything. And that’s what Scale-In is.”

Shainer spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Nvidia’s Scale-In architecture is designed to help transform scaled compute into a secure and operational AI factory platform.

Since the August introduction, Nvidia has expanded its agent security strategy. In September, the company introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform, combining OpenShell with Nvidia Sentry for out-of-band monitoring and hardware-based security enforcement. An October announcement added the OpenShell Reference Architecture, integrating Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 to support secure agent execution across enterprise systems. Nvidia’s announcement outlines the expanded architecture.

Scale-In is powered by Nvidia BlueField-4 and Nvidia DOCA and connected over Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet. BlueField-4 is Nvidia’s fourth-generation data processing unit, a networking platform built for agentic AI factories and large-scale infrastructure needs. BlueField is essential to the management of agentic AI security, according to Shainer.

“You can think about BlueField or Blue-Field-4 as a device that has in-silicon security engines that are working out of band and collecting telemetry from everything, from memory, from storage, from GPUs, from CPUs,” Shainer told theCUBE. “That’s why that infrastructure connects to all other infrastructures and ensures security all around. That out-of-band monitoring enables BlueField to actually understand exactly what agents are doing.”

Along with BlueField-4, Nvidia DOCA also powers Scale-In deployment. This software platform enables the rapid creation of apps and services that offload, accelerate and isolate data center workloads.

Using DOCA, developers can create software-defined, cloud-native, DPU- and SuperNIC-accelerated solutions. Like Nvidia CUDA, which provides a programming platform for GPU workloads, DOCA gives developers access to DPU acceleration capabilities.

“DPU brings the in-silicon engines security engines, storage accelerations,” Shainer explained. “DOCA is the framework, the software, the APIs that enable you to access all of those engines that BlueField-4 provides.”

Nvidia has further reinforced agentic AI security with its open-source runtime offering called OpenShell. The tool is designed to govern agent execution, access and inference routing. Nvidia combined OpenShell with BlueField-4 because it wanted a device that could collect information outside the GPU and monitor an environment that no agent could influence.

“I want to also have another device which is completely separated, completely isolated from the agents, that can monitor everything out-of-band,” Shainer said. “That’s what we’re doing with BlueField-4, bringing all the security elements together with OpenShell, and now you have a secure infrastructure for agents. This is how the combination of OpenShell and BlueField-4 brings all the security elements that we need for gen AI.”

The more recent OpenShell Reference Architecture builds on that approach with Nvidia Sentry, which runs on BlueField-4 using DOCA software. According to Nvidia, Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior and can quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their defined software boundaries. The combination extends OpenShell’s runtime controls with an independent enforcement layer.

#5554. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.
