#5553. Realty Executives Associates Appoints New Executive Vice President of Agent Development

Realty Executives Associates (REA) has announced the appointment of J Lewis as executive vice president of Agent Development, a newly established leadership role focused on strengthening the success, productivity and long-term relationships of REA’s agents.

According to a release, prior to joining REA, Lewis served as CEO of Keller Williams for 13 years, bringing extensive experience in brokerage leadership, agent development and organizational growth.

In this new role, the company says Lewis will focus on helping existing agents increase productivity and profitability, strengthening agent relationships and retention and creating meaningful opportunities for professional development and business growth. He will work to provide agents with the resources, guidance and support they need to build sustainable businesses.

“One of the things I enjoy most is sitting down with an agent or a team, understanding what they’re trying to accomplish, and helping them figure out how to get there. That might mean looking at their production data, analyzing their financials, identifying opportunities they’re not seeing, or simply fine-tuning the way they run their business,” he says. “Every agent has different goals, and I enjoy helping them develop a plan to reach those goals and build a business that supports the life they want.”

“I’m incredibly excited to join the number one brokerage in East Tennessee,” Lewis added. “What really attracted me to REA is the opportunity to work with a company that understands the value of investing in its people. I’ve always enjoyed working alongside agents, understanding what they want to accomplish, and helping them find ways to get there. REA has created an environment where that kind of work is valued, and I’m excited to be part of it.”

“At REA, we believe our agents are our customers. Our responsibility is to create an environment where they can build successful, sustainable businesses and feel supported along the way. This position is an extension of that commitment,” said Justin Bailey, CEO and partner of Realty Executives Associates.

Bailey added: “Success isn’t simply measured by how many agents we have. It’s measured by the success of the agents who choose to call REA home. We want to be intentional about helping them become more productive, more profitable, and better positioned for the future. We have always believed that taking care of our people is what makes a great brokerage, and this is another way we are putting that belief into action.”

#5552. Joanna Gaines Reveals How Her Approach to Holiday Decorating Has Evolved as She’s Gotten Older

Joanna Gaines keeps a beautifully decorated home year-round, so it’s no surprise that she pulls out all the stops for the holidays.

The “Fixer Upper” star recently shared her best holiday hosting tips as she prepares to celebrate the season with her family. She also noted the surprising way her approach has changed over time.

“The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” Gaines, 48, told USA Today. “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.”

While the Magnolia co-founder encouraged aspiring decorators to feel empowered to go big with their festive displays, she left room for those who prefer to take a more subdued route.

“There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.”

Gaines also noted that she’s committed to upholding food traditions, using recipes she’s been working on since she and Chip Gaines wed in 2003.

“Food is really at the center of our holidays,” she said. “Thanksgiving especially is this day I feel like I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.”

Gaines also detailed her approach to Christmas in the editor’s note she published in the Nov. 10 issue of Magnolia Journal.

“Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.”

She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory.

“Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.”

Explaining that she’s choosing to prioritize holding space for both the major moments and the much more relatable ones, Gaines also reflected on being the “gatekeeper” of her family’s yearly traditions as she aims to “do the same things” they always have, “if not bigger and better” this year.

She wrote about the “dressing up” that is encouraged toward the end of the year and romanticized the “fresh delight” of decorating the home, hosting loved ones, and “trying to create standout experiences” that her “kids will remember and tell their kids about someday.”

The Gaineses certainly have their hands full with their five children: Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8. But during a recent conversation on the “Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce” podcast, the proud mom revealed that they’d recently been discussing the idea of expanding the family once again.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

“He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” Gaines quipped, adding that her husband had even told their “grown kids” that she was expecting, and their eldest daughter said that she’s “not coming home” if the news is true.

The HGTV personality went on to encourage Kelce, a mom of four, to add another little one to her family.

“Five is a good number,” Gaines said, noting that she would “have more babies” if she “could.”

#5551. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5550. DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues

A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners’ association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium as part of a shooting spree on Thursday, according to police.

The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area.

Dr. Matt Wade Lambert, a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was publicly identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life.

Lambert is suspected of going down to the luxury fitness center VIDA housed inside the building, locating the building manager next to the treadmills, and shooting him from a point blank range, D.C. Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, per WUSA9.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gym goer James Spellman told the Associated Press. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout inside the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and a shelter in place order in the area.

While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect.

Lambert then ran out of the gym and shot four other people in the vicinity, among them three construction workers who were across the street. Interim D.C. Police Chief Jeffery Carroll said one of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he turned the gun on himself, committing suicide.

D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence."

Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025, alleging that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage.

Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment.

According to the filing, Lambert has incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the homeowners association's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027.

#5548. Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model said to outscore Argon

Google LLC today released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model in its Gemini 4 artificial intelligence family that it says outscores its frontier Gemini 4 Argon model on an independent intelligence ranking.

Measured on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, Hydrogen scored 51 to Argon’s 50, according to Google. A fourth thinking level called xhigh, new with Hydrogen, takes the score to 54.

The rollout is different, too. Argon spent nearly two weeks with members of Google’s Fairwind Program, a group of vetted cybersecurity defenders, before paying developers could get at it on Oct. 13. Hydrogen skipped that stage. Anyone can use it from today, including people on the free version of the Gemini app.

Koray Kavukcuoglu, who became head of Google DeepMind in August when Demis Hassabis moved into a chairman role, wrote in the announcement that Hydrogen is “built for rapid execution.”

Orchestrator, which Google added to its Antigravity coding tool today, picks between Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon as a session goes along. Google’s runs of the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test found Orchestrator getting close to Carbon’s success rate on an average of 24% less quota.

Gemini 3.8 Flash, which came out in September, is the yardstick for most of the other numbers in the announcement. Against it, Hydrogen finished tasks 2.5 times faster at the default setting. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, which tests work done at a command line, Hydrogen more than tripled the older model’s 18.2% with a score of 57%.

Among the early testers Google quoted, Andrew Carr, a former OpenAI scientist who is now chief scientist at 3D animation startup Cartwheel Inc., said the model caught two problems with an approach his team had been stuck on for 10 days. Discovery Loop Inc., the startup former Google Chief Scientist Jeff Dean co-founded after leaving in August, was another.

#5546. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

#5545. Inside Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio as the Nvidia CEO Resigns After Affair with Suspected Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned after having extramarital affairs with a business executive—Alice Huang, who the U.S. government has determined to be working with Chinese intelligence—and a Nvidia employee.

Finance chief Colette Kress will work as the interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent replacement, Nvidia said Thursday.

External and internal candidates will be considered as the company searches for a Jensen's successor.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world," the statement read. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

The news follows a Nov. 8 statement from Huang, who admitted to the affairs.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang stated in a previous message to the company. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

While the board of Nvidia claimed it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” an external counsel will be selected to investigate

The revelation, first reported by the New York Times, is expected to have an economic impact not only on Nvidia—whose stock price has already taken a hit—but on the artificial intelligence industry as a whole, given the chipmaker’s influence.

The company was the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence bom.

According to the New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent to ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Larry Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

However, he has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan in 1963, spent his early childhood in Thailand. He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to America to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school.

While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

As the future of Nvidia's stock remains unclear, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech tycoon's expansive property portfolio.

In 2017, the tech tycoon splashed over $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is tied to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell, of Marble Management, previously told the Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Of course, Huang is also neighbors with Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech mogul owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters, which is in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

#5544. Fed Governor Outlines Inflation Progress as ‘Disappointing,’ Sees Path to 2% Goal in the Next Year

Inflation seemed to be making good progress at the end of 2025 and start of 2026, with the Federal Reserve actually starting to cut interest rates. The start of the conflict in the Middle East in February, however, threw a wrench in that progress, as inflation turned course and began to elevate once again.

Now, after the Fed chose to raise rates at its September meeting, inflation has reached a “disappointing” state, as outlined by Federal Reserve Governor and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman.

In a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations focusing on the current economic outlook, Bowman said that the Fed’s “progress on lowering inflation has disappointed,” but bringing down inflation does remain a “priority” for the organization.

As inflation has elevated, housing has felt the strain. Mortgage rates have been on the rise, recently returning to the 7% range. Affordability has been constrained for buyers, not just due to rate, but also due to inflation affecting their purchasing power and ability to save up for down payments.

Bowman said she remains vigilant on “monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices” and their influence on risks to lowering inflation, and she continues to “focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.”

“While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated,” she continued. “It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.”

Bowman said what is currently holding back progress on inflation is a “confluence of shocks,” stemming from Middle Eastern conflict, tariffs imposed from the Trump Administration and “AI-related price pressures.”

“It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations,” she said. “But today’s consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer.”

Bowman, appointed by President Donald Trump in his first term and elevated to vice chair in 2025, said the U.S.’s conflict in the Middle East continues to exert downward pressure on the economy, but pressure is also sourcing from the AI boom and “buildout,” as she characterized it.

As for how these two issues could affect inflation in the future, Bowman said that she can see “sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist.”

However, she also said she could “envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly,” in which case core PCE inflation (meaning price increases excluding volatile energy fluctuations) would return toward the Fed’s 2% target in a “timelier” fashion.

In terms of the Middle East, Bowman said that as the conflict persists, energy prices could remain elevated, keeping inflation on the rise “because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.” Additionally, if conflict were to escalate, she said it could have “more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.”

On the potential of a “quick resolution” to the conflict, Bowman noted that it “may take some time for energy prices to normalize” even in the aftermath.

As for AI, Bowman said she “expect(s) the AI shock to play out over some time” as plans for new data centers continue to “surge.” However, she noted that as AI investment is “increasingly being financed with external funds,” there are other potential risks it presents to the economy.

One such risk is the potential of workers being displaced. Bowman said that even though any monetary policy can’t “address that transition directly,” it can still “support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.”

Another risk is the financing of AI, as Bowman said that “AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers.” As such, she also noted that “AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year.”

The rapid expansion of AI has also put some “upward pressure on a number of price categories,” as Bowman noted, specifically to the prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers and more. However, she said that she expects “production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.”

Bowman did point out that the risks from AI “seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services.”

Overall, Bowman said that if “AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit.”

“This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation,” she concluded.

Bowman said that looking ahead, her expectation is that “policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence.” Such policies include “pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses.”

Bowman went on to say that she does expect the labor market, which has performed resiliently through most of 2026, to “remain stable.” She also expects for inflation to “slow” as “special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year.”

“Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices,” she continued.

Bowman said as these “shocks” to the economy and inflation fall back, her forecast is for “core PCE inflation to move closer to 2% next year.”

Right now, she said that the pressures persist, indicating that “there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5542. CNCF data shows cloud native is the on-ramp to AI, and maintainers are paying the price

The global population of cloud-native developers has topped 21 million, but the headcount tells only part of the story. Artificial intelligence is changing what those developers build and how open-source projects absorb their work.

Fresh research is putting numbers on that shift. The latest State of Cloud Native Development report from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData Ltd. counts more than 21 million practitioners, or 41% of developers worldwide. Yet that figure likely misses many people who rely on cloud-native infrastructure without knowing it, according to Bob Killen (pictured, right), director of technical program management at CNCF.

“The big thing is it actually might be undercounting a significant amount of them,” Killen said. “Because there’s a very large amount of people that are essentially consuming cloud-native applications without even realizing it.”

Killen and Liam Bollmann-Dodd (left), principal market research consultant at SlashData, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the latest State of Cloud Native Development findings, AI adoption, the strain on open-source maintainers and the shift toward cost discipline. (* Disclosure below.)

The report’s most striking finding concerns AI. About 75% of cloud-native developers use AI in some form, compared with only about 55% of other developers, Bollmann-Dodd noted. The gap mirrors a broader trend of agentic AI pushing Kubernetes into a second act.

“It’s a massive difference,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “So somehow being cloud native enables you and your organization and your personal stack to do AI in all its forms.”

The same AI wave is straining the people who keep the ecosystem running. Sustainability dominated the Maintainer Summit ahead of KubeCon, as maintainers face a flood of pull requests frequently generated by agents, Killen explained.

“How do we as maintainers keep up with the flooding of PRs and issues and things like that?” Killen said. “Especially when many of them are frankly just slop. And the real frustrating part is they’ll be just good enough.”

Cost discipline is the next shift. Just as financial operations practices followed rising cloud bills, cloud-native developers will soon manage model and token spending closely, according to Bollmann-Dodd.

“I think token maxing is dead and it’s going to stay dead forever,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “And I think it’s going to become much more focused on how you spend your money and how you spend your tokens.”

#5541. Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

#5540. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5539. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5538. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5537. Did Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Just Expose Real Bitcoin Bottom in January 2027?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin’s cycle bottom is likely already in or very close, as a Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Bitcoin bottom prediction highlights a final low expected in the $60,000–$68,000 zone by late December 2026 or early January 2027 at the latest. As of November 11, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $73,700–$73,900, roughly 41% below its October 2025 all-time high around $126,000.

The market has been grinding lower after a failed recovery attempt into the low $80,000s, with recent sessions testing the psychologically important $73,000 level. While the short-term trend remains soft, longer-term structure and historical cycle patterns suggest the deepest part of the correction is largely complete.

Bitcoin is consolidating in a tight range after a multi-week decline. Immediate support sits at the $73,000 round number, which coincides with recent daily lows, the approximate 200-day moving average, and prior structural levels from earlier in the year.

A daily close below $73,000 would open the door to the next support cluster near $71,500 (prior swing area) and then the 50-day moving average zone around $68,500. Deeper support resides in the $62,000–$65,000 region, with the July 2026 low near $57,700–$58,000 acting as the major cycle floor.

On the upside, resistance is layered at $75,000, followed by the more significant $80,000 area. Momentum indicators such as the RSI have cooled into neutral-to-oversold territory on daily timeframes, leaving room for either a relief bounce or one final liquidity sweep lower before a more durable base forms.

Volume has been elevated on down days, consistent with distribution by short-term holders, but longer-term holder metrics and the 200-week moving average (historically a strong demand zone) continue to provide a structural floor.

Bitcoin | Net shorts just hit an ATH.The last 4 times we saw these levels, they marked a major bottom. pic.twitter.com/n9DkeYEYqy

My base-case view is that the primary cycle low was printed in July 2026 near $58,000. That level marked a roughly 54% drawdown from the prior peak, shallower than the 70–80%+ declines of previous bear markets, reflecting Bitcoin’s growing institutional base and ETF demand.

The current pullback into the low $70,000s looks more like a higher-low retest or secondary correction within a broader bottoming process rather than the start of a new leg down. If $73,000 fails, a final flush into the $62,000–$68,000 zone remains the most probable destination.

This area aligns with Fibonacci retracements of the 2025–2026 rally, prior demand zones, and the upper end of the July low region. I expect any such move to occur relatively quickly, within the next four to eight weeks, driven by residual profit-taking, macro uncertainty, or year-end positioning.

By late December 2026 or the first half of January 2027 at the latest, this process should be complete. A sustained defense of the $68,000–$70,000 area (or a higher low above $70,000) would strongly support the thesis that the bottom is in.

Conversely, a decisive break below the July low near $58,000 would invalidate the constructive view and open a path toward $50,000–$55,000, though that outcome currently carries lower probability given the maturity of the correction and the strength of long-term holder support.

In short, Bitcoin appears to be in the late stages of its post-2025 correction. The most likely final low sits in the $60,000–$68,000 range, timed for the remainder of Q4 2026 into very early 2027. Once that floor is confirmed with a higher low and a reclaim of $80,000, the stage would be set for a more meaningful recovery phase.

#5536. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.

#5535. Nearly Half of Gen Z Admit Skipping Rent or Mortgages Just To Fund Holiday Spending

The holiday season is an exciting time, but it can also be very expensive.

If you’re careless, festive gatherings, gifts, and travel may leave you in debt well into the new year.

A new survey by Accredited Debt Relief found that 67% of Gen Z have taken on or expect to take on holiday debt this year. And nearly 15% of Americans are still paying off last year’s holiday debt.

Furthermore, 46% of Gen Z respondents have delayed or skipped rent or mortgage payments to afford holiday spending, compared with 28% of millennials, 14% of Gen X, and 3% of baby boomers.

“Holiday spending should never come at the expense of someone's financial stability, but these findings show just how difficult it can be to balance financial responsibilities with the social expectations and pressure to create a memorable holiday," said Bobbi Rebell, chief financial education adviser at Accredited Debt Relief in San Diego.

"Making tough choices around spending may feel like you’re disappointing those you care about, but protecting your financial future needs to be non-negotiable."

If you’re worried about holiday debt or keeping up with housing expenses, a bit of planning, dedication, and creativity can help you enjoy the season without putting your finances on the line.

Experts agree that your rent or mortgage and related bills should always come first, before you spend money on holiday extras.

“I’ve spent a lot of time helping people who have struggled to keep their homes. And I’ve seen how hard it can be to recover once things get out of control and they start falling behind on mortgage payments,” says Casey Yontz, bankruptcy attorney at Yontz Law, PLLC in Phoenix.

One missed mortgage payment probably isn’t going to get you into foreclosure, but it can be the beginning of a snowball of serious delinquency.

And depending on the terms of your loan, you can incur late fees on your missed payment.

Once that payment is 30 days late, it could get reported to credit bureaus and take a serious toll on your credit score. If you continue to fall behind, foreclosure is a possibility.

“It’s true that under federal mortgage-servicing rules, foreclosure generally cannot begin until you are 120 days behind. But this doesn’t mean you should treat these 120 days as extra time to spend money on something else, like holiday gifts or travel,” Yontz explains.

According to Yontz, there’s no holiday present that’s worth putting your family's home at risk.

Howard Dvorkin, chairman at Debt.com in Fort Lauderdale, FL, shares those thoughts.

“What’s worse: Someone thinking you cheaped out on their holiday gift? Or sleeping outside? Financially speaking, housing must be your top priority. I’ve yet to meet a client’s friends and family who would want you to jeopardize your housing,” says Dvorkin.

If you're still paying for the 2025 holidays, putting 2026 holiday expenses on another credit card is not the solution.

“Holiday debt is an indicator that your holiday spending is beyond your budget, and might be a little bit out of control,” says Yontz.

Stop adding to it, and be honest with yourself about the math.

Look at your actual income versus expenses and debt numbers.

Ask yourself these questions: How much do I still owe? What’s the interest rate? How much can I afford to pay each month after paying my living expenses?

“Try to prioritize higher-interest card debt first. Pay more than the minimum payments, because making minimum payments on credit cards is like throwing buckets of water on a five-alarm fire,” say Yontz.

Dvorkin also recommends seeking professional help.

“Call a certified credit counselor and receive a free, in-depth debt analysis. With that in hand, you can consider all your options and make an informed choice,” explains Dvorkin.

Depending on your situation, a debt management program may make sense. It can reduce your total credit card payments by up to half without any long-term damage to your credit score.

“It can also lower your interest rate to 10% or less—sometimes even zero. You pay a fee for a professional to set this up, but those fees are dwarfed by how much you save,” Dvorkin adds.

Holiday spending should come out of whatever disposable income you have left after paying for your necessities like housing, gas, and groceries.

These tips can help you enjoy the holiday season while still keeping your finances in check:

You'll save more if you focus on what to buy than how you buy it. That’s why a holiday budget is so important.

“Nothing evokes images of Scrooge more than sitting down with pen and paper and listing everything you'll buy. But we don't live in 'A Christmas Carol.' We have the technology to make holiday budgeting a breeze. There’s no shortage of apps that act as busy little elves and do the work for you,” say Dvorkin.

Inviting family members over for a no-cost game night will be far more memorable than buying each of them a shiny, new gadget.

“I just lost my mom this spring, and I can guarantee you that no present could ever be better than more time with her. Presents don’t matter, people do, in my opinion," Yontz explains.

You’ll notice a lot of companies that will let you buy something for the holidays and pay for it over time, especially if you’re shopping online.

Unfortunately, they’re not making your purchase any cheaper. In fact, you will probably end up paying more with interest and fees.

“They tempt you, and you pay for it. Don’t fall down the buy now, pay later chimney of misfit payments,” says Yontz.

Train your brain to dislike overspending.

Do some research on how much you’re actually paying for credit card debt if you have it. Notice how much you’re paying in interest when you buy something.

“When I started doing this, I felt like I was being taken advantage of and that was enough for me to not want to use credit cards,” Yontz explains.

At the end of the day, the holidays should be something your family remembers fondly, not something you're still paying for next Christmas.
