#5523. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5522. Compass pushes back on antitrust claims, says it owes StreetEasy nothing

Compass filed a motion to dismiss an amended antitrust complaint in SDNY tied to pulling rental listings from StreetEasy. Compass argues the suit conflates sales and rentals, lacks causation, and cites the FARE Act as a driver of inventory visibility.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings is seeking to dismiss an antitrust lawsuit alleging that it created a monopoly through its acquisitions, which it used to harm consumers as well as competitors like Zillow when it decided to pull its rental listings from StreetEasy in early August.

Filed in late August, the lawsuit claims that Compass’s removal of listings from StreetEasy reduced consumer choice, while also driving up rents and brokerage fees.

In a filing on Tuesday, Compass told the court it was seeking to dismiss the amended complaint with prejudice, which would prevent the plaintiff from refilling the lawsuit.

In the filing, Compass claims that the plaintiffs have confused the residential sales market with the rental market, noting that the information cited in the complaint pertains to for-sale homes and not rental listings. The filing also notes that Compass does not own rental properties or set rental prices, claiming instead that Zillow and StreetEasy dominate the online listing-search market. The defendant also claims that the plaintiff cannot demonstrate that Compass’s alleged conduct caused his higher rent.

The filing also notes that rental inventory in New York City began to decline seven months prior to its acquisition of Anywhere and more than a year before Compass began instructing agents to pull rental listings from Street Easy. Instead, Compass points to the June 2025 implementation of New York City’s Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses (FARE) Act, which prohibits brokers hired by landlords from charging broker fees to tenants and requires landlords to disclose applicable fees before a lease is signed, as the reason behind the drop in visible inventory.

Compass also claims that it does not have monopoly power in the rental listings market and that it has no legal obligation to share its listings with platforms like Street Easy.

According to a notice on the court docket, the plaintiff has until December 8, 2026, to respond to Compass’s motion to dismiss the suit. While the parties wait for the court to rule on the motion, Compass is also asking the court to stay discovery. The court has not yet ruled on that motion.

#5519. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5518. Kubernetes now runs containers and VMs side by side

KubeVirt’s graduation from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) marks a turning point in a debate that once pitted containers against virtual machines. A decade on, Kubernetes is becoming one platform for legacy VMs, cloud-native apps and AI.

Enterprises still run much of their IT on VMs, even as AI pushes them toward new infrastructure. Red Hat Inc. is betting they won’t have to choose, with OpenShift 5 managing containers, VMs and AI workloads in one environment. Running two separate systems was never the goal, according to Fabian Deutsch (pictured), director of engineering for OpenShift Virtualization and Modernization and a KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat.

“But you’ve also got VMs, right, where you’re running applications in the old way that we did for decades before. And do you really want to maintain these two systems?” Deutsch said. “So our vision was, how can we unite those worlds to eventually make it easier to have one paradigm to run both, all these compute workloads on one platform.”

Deutsch spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed KubeVirt’s graduation, running VMs and containers on one Kubernetes platform, AI’s influence on virtualization and what comes next for the project. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has drawn open-source projects and commercial providers onto a common platform, and AI’s hunger for compute has deepened that pull. Much of KubeVirt’s recent innovation now comes from the AI side, Deutsch explained.

“You don’t want to repave your data center just because you’ve got a new workload that you need to address,” Deutsch said. “So you’re having that flexibility to run it in the way that you need it.”

The CNCF announced the graduation at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, seven years after accepting the project into its sandbox. Next on the list is passing GPUs, CPUs and memory into VMs, while AI is changing how the community values virtualization itself, Deutsch noted.

“There’s a lot of influx of features due to AI, by the way,” Deutsch said. “The isolation model, we didn’t get to it in the beginning, but the isolation of virtualization is helping, right, in the AI age as well.”

The project already runs on edge devices and in the cloud because it offers a consistent API across those footprints, according to Deutsch. Nvidia Corp. was an early adopter, and Microsoft Corp. is now stepping up, he noted.

“I think it’s about getting the right and next generation infrastructure into your house,” Deutsch said. “KubeVirt allows you to carry forward what you’ve got, what you invested in over the past decades, and not to leave it alone because you have to carry it forward.”

United Wholesale Mortgage introduced “40 to the Finish,” a year-end pricing incentive that adds 40 basis points to all products for loans with 700+ FICO scores when brokers use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools through Dec. 31. At the same time, UWM expanded its partnership with Bilt to integrate Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing platform.   AI Summary

United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) this week announced the launch of a year-end pricing incentive for broker loans and an expansion of its partnership with Bilt.

Effective immediately through Dec. 31, brokers who use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools will receive 40 basis points on all agency and nonagency products when the borrower has a credit score of at least 700, UWM said.

The incentive is intended to give brokers more pricing flexibility in the final weeks of 2026 while encouraging use of the lender’s underwriting and closing technology. Year-end pricing specials are common in the wholesale channel as lenders seek to pull volume into the current year, clean up pipelines and help partners hit production goals.

UWM – which was more aggressive on pricing in the past but is seeking to deleverage its balance sheet amid a deal with Oaktree Capital Management and the Ishbia family – saw its gain-on-sale margins decline to 124 basis points in the third quarter, down from 133 basis points in the second quarter.

UWM chairman, CEO and president Mat Ishbia told analysts he expects margins to be steady, adding that “people don’t use UWM because we’re the lowest rates” and arguing that competitors offering lower rates are not good partners.

Separately, UWM said it’s expanding its partnership with Bilt, a neighborhood commerce and rewards platform, to bring Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing ecosystem.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is designed to help businesses reach customers and build loyalty through neighborhood-level experiences. Through UWM, it links mortgage servicing with homeownership tasks and local commerce, while keeping independent brokers visible to borrowers after closing.

“The broker who helps you buy your home should be your first call when you’re ready to take the next step, whether that’s refinancing, accessing equity or buying again,” Ishbia said in a statement. “With Bilt Neighborhood OS, we’re making the servicing experience more valuable to homeowners and creating more reasons for them to stay connected to their broker between those major decisions.”

UWM already services hundreds of thousands of loans through Bilt, giving these homeowners a single place to manage their mortgage and access rewards. With Neighborhood OS added, UWM said the experience will extend into more day-to-day homeownership activities, from finding a local contractor to exploring neighborhood offers, or reconnecting with a broker about a home equity or refinance opportunity.

Bilt said it has delivered more than $1 billion in value to its 8 million members, who redeem rewards toward travel, housing payments, student loans, dining and other categories. The company also says it powers one in four U.S. rental homes, primarily through the Bilt Alliance of large owners and operators.

#5515. Newrez partners with Upgrade to add personal loans for servicing customers

Newrez is adding unsecured personal loans for eligible servicing customers through a partnership with fintech firm Upgrade, which will originate and service the loans via issuer Cross River Bank. The product gives existing Newrez borrowers a way to access cash without using their home as collateral or changing their mortgage, with no prepayment fees and soft-credit prequalification.  AI Summary

Multichannel lender Newrez partnered with financial technology firm Upgrade to offer unsecured personal loans to eligible mortgage servicing customers, giving homeowners another option to access cash without tapping home equity or refinancing.

The loans, originated and serviced by Upgrade and issued by its partner Cross River Bank, do not change the existing Newrez mortgage. Newrez funded $12.9 billion in mortgages in the third quarter and reached $878.9 billion in unpaid principal balance across its mortgage servicing rights (MSR) portfolio at the end of September.

According to the company, the loans can be funded in as little as one business day for qualified borrowers, have no prepayment fees and allow customers to see prequalified offers through a soft credit inquiry.

Newrez framed the launch as an extension of its relationships with homeowners beyond the mortgage, with loans designed for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Leslie Gillin, Newrez’s chief commercial officer, said in a statement. “Homeowners’ financial needs often extend beyond their monthly mortgage payment, and we’re proud to broaden the ways we can support them, including helping identify opportunities for savings as they navigate important financial decisions.”

The launch comes as many homeowners are struggling with revolving debt. In a June 2026 survey conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of Newrez, 51% of homeowners reported carrying credit card balances, with 59% saying the debt is negatively affecting their finances. The online survey of 2,203 U.S. adults was conducted in June 2026.

“The findings show that many homeowners are looking for ways to improve their financial position but may not know where to start,” Gillin said. “By combining education with access to responsible financing options, we can help customers make informed decisions that support their long-term financial goals.”This article was generated using HousingWire Automation and reviewed by a HousingWire editor before publication. #5513. Gates Introduces Compact ThermalCool™ 2100SS Pump to Expand Data Center Portfolio

4U-Compatible Design Delivers High Performance for AI and High-Density Computing Applications

DENVER, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Gates Industrial Corporation Ltd. (NYSE: GTES), a global manufacturer of highly engineered power transmission and fluid power solutions, today introduced Gates ThermalCoolâ¢ 2100SS Pump, expanding the company's portfolio of liquid-cooling solutions for AI and high-density data center applications. The new stainless steel pump expands Gates participation across the data center cooling loop, adding a new, purpose-built active coolant circulation solution alongside its fluid conveyance and connection technologies.

Higher rack densities are changing where data center cooling equipment is located and how much space it can occupy. Rack-mounted coolant distribution units (CDUs) integrate coolant circulation within the IT rack, which puts tight size and integration demands on every component. Gates developed the ThermalCool 2100SS Pump to meet those demands, combining substantial output with a 4U-compatible design while combining substantial coolant flow with integrated active cooling for the motor. Delivered in a platform configurable for different CDU architectures, these capabilities position Gates to serve a wider range of data center coolant circulation applications including those with high ambient temperature operating conditions.

"As data centers pack more computing power into every rack, CDU manufacturers are facing infrastructure challenges that existing pumps weren't designed for," said Rebekah Headley, general manager of data centers at Gates. "We developed the ThermalCool 2100SS Pump in response to requirements from a leading CDU manufacturer, working as an engineering partner to address an emerging system need. That application-driven approach resulted in a configurable platform that takes the solution beyond the original application and into the broader data center cooling market."

Key features of Gates ThermalCool 2100SS Pump:

The ThermalCool 2100SS Pump expands Gates' capabilities across the data center cooling loop, complementing its portfolio of hoses, UQDs, fittings and engineered assemblies. Together, these technologies strengthen Gates' ability to help customers engineer the fluid path from coolant circulation through rack-level connection and conveyance. The Gates ThermalCool 2100SS Pump is expected to be available globally in early 2027. For more information, to connect with a Gates engineer, or to request a sample, visit the Data Center Pumps Innovations page.

#5512. Reverse mortgage executives read the tea leaves to decipher the industry’s next chapter

At NRMLA Annual, executives said reverse mortgage growth hinges on distribution through forward lenders and better LO education, supported by new prospecting and qualification tools. They also pointed to rising proprietary loan share and a 2027 pivot as traditional purchase and refi volumes remain pressured.  AI Summary

At this week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio, executives offered their thoughts on the evolving product landscape and efforts to expand the sales force while cautioning that hurdles around consumer misperceptions remain.

In a panel discussion held Tuesday and moderated by former NRMLA board member and current Texas Mortgage Bankers Association CEO Scott Norman, executives covered a wide range of topics including proprietary reverse mortgages, distribution efforts with traditional forward lenders and the potential for a broad marketing push to consumers.

“I think one of the things that’s held us back is our lack of distribution,” said Jim Cory, managing director of Guild Mortgage‘s reverse division. “It’s such a sea change in our business to suddenly have to go from this beloved group that we have here and begin adding to it. And literally thousands of loan originators now have access to this product.”

At a time when federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) have dropped to their lowest levels in about 10 years, private-label loans have stepped up to fill the void. Data compiled by New View Advisors showed that proprietary products accounted for 60% of all reverse mortgage volume in September 2026 — a share that is expected to continue growing.

Melissa Macerato, the newly appointed president and chief commercial officer at Longbridge Financial, said that these products have changed business for the better and that the industry would “be in a very different place” without them. Longbridge has been among the lenders to introduce private-label solutions in recent years through its Platinum suite and HELOC for Seniors.

Macerato said she expects to see more hybrid reverse mortgage products developed soon, with a focus on giving borrowers higher proceeds alongside mandatory but flexible payments.

“In order to get that broader distribution, in order to have more exposure for our products, we’re going to have to start speaking the language and developing products that more mainstream mortgage entities and loan officers really understand,” she said.

Jonathan Scarpati, chief production officer at Finance of America, told NRMLA attendees that the products “from 10 years ago are not reverse mortgages that everyone is selling today.” His company has also been at the forefront of product innovation with its HomeSafe suite — including a second-lien option that allows borrowers to tap into their home equity without touching their low-rate first mortgage.

But Scarpati believes that new products are meant to “cast a wider net” rather than replace the traditional HECM that’s been the industry’s cornerstone since the program was authorized in 1987. Mike Kent, senior vice president of corporate development and industry relations at Onity Mortgage, agreed.

“The reason we have proprietary products is that [the HECM] set the baseline, it set the standards, it ushered in the appropriate regulation and safeguards for the product, and it kind of cleared the way for us to begin to innovate,” Kent said.

Scarpati also pushed back against the notion that more competition in reverse mortgages is a bad thing.

“I think 2027 is a very pivotal moment for the industry in general,” he said. “I think as the products continue to evolve, some of them are looking closer to the forward industry. … The closer we have our products look to what the forward industry is used to, the more growth and the more adoption we’re going to get.”

Cory said that lack of distribution has been a longstanding obstacle for the industry. But many of the large independent mortgage banks (IMBs) — including Guild, Rate, Fairway Home Mortgage and CrossCountry Mortgage — now have a visible presence in the space. According to Cory, the six largest IMBs have about 17,000 originators today, and business would expand significantly if this group alone put more resources into reverse.

Jesse Allen, president of the 55+ lending division at Rate, said that while the largest IMBs have reverse mortgage options to offer borrowers, the ongoing hurdle is to get more engagement from loan officers. That work falls to reverse specialists, who must do a better job of sharing their knowledge and building relationships.

“If you want other people to trust you, you have to really know your craft,” Allen said. “Language matters. And so, as a reverse industry, I would encourage all of you to think about the language you use when you walk in with a traditional mortgage loan officer and a real estate agent. Use language that feels familiar to them and that will start to build trust.”

Some companies are introducing technology solutions to engage LOs who are unfamiliar with reverse products.

Earlier this month, Nationwide Equities Corp. launched ReverseReach, a tool to help uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in existing customer databases and referral networks. And in July, Reverse Market Insight expanded its loan qualification tool to include Smartfi Home Loans‘ proprietary products, part of Smartfi’s push to get more traditional LOs involved.

Scarpati said many lenders are looking for new opportunities as traditional purchase and refinance is expected to decline in 2027. Home equity lending, including reverse mortgages, presents a massive opportunity as U.S. homeowners hold roughly $35 trillion in equity, including $15 trillion among those 62 and older.

Lenders that don’t diversify beyond traditional products may find tough sledding if liquidity issues and consolidation continue over the next 12 to 18 months, he added.

“Originators are starving to find new opportunities to continue to succeed in mortgages in general. I think it just makes so much sense for a forward originator to start looking back at their client base,” Scarpati said. “We just have to continue to double down on education and technology to sort of help bridge that gap and make it easier for them to originate our loans.”

Audience member Melinda Hipp, a San Antonio-based Certified Reverse Mortgage Professional at Reverse Mortgage Authority, relayed some relevant information to the panelists on stage.

She said she recently recorded seven hours of conversations at two senior expos near San Antonio. People who passed by her booth frequently said they have no need for a reverse mortgage because their home is paid off, or that they “would never do that.” These comments feed into the laundry list of misunderstandings about the products.

While reverse mortgages often serve needs-based clients who want to access their home equity for repairs, healthcare expenses and other costs of living, their use cases also involve affluent clients who want better retirement tax strategies and cash-flow solutions.

The industry also continues to push for greater awareness of reverse for purchase transactions, which give seniors with large amounts of home equity a path to buy their next home without the burden of a monthly payment.

Hipp also suggested that the industry might look to do a broader advertising push, a reference to past efforts through celebrity spokespeople like Tom Selleck, Robert Wagner and others.

Allen offered his thoughts, saying that “marketing and messaging” is one of the industry’s “three big rocks” alongside product development and distribution. He said that any efforts through digital media or social media need to be different than what was done 10 years ago, since the addressable market has changed significantly.

“What’s the saying? ‘Many hands make light work.’ Well, many hands and it still won’t be light work,” Allen remarked. “We have to really figure out how to speak in a different way to the marketplace. … I think it has to be at an enterprise or an institutional level.”

#5510. University of Phoenix launches Bachelor of Science in Business Analytics focused on data-driven business decisions

New online degree combines business analytics, responsible AI use and skills-based digital badges with predictable pricing for working adults.

PHOENIX, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix has launched a new online Bachelor of Science in Business Analytics (BSBAN) degree program designed to help working adults develop skills to translate data into insights that support business decisions, improve processes and solve organizational problems. The new program combines data analytics with business strategy, decision-making, project management and communication skills, offering students a career-relevant education supported by the University's commitment to affordable, predictable pricing.

For nearly a decade, University of Phoenix has supported price certainty through its Tuition Guarantee, which held students' per-credit tuition rates steady from enrollment through graduation. Building on that commitment, the University's new Locked-In Pricing Guarantee provides one predictable per-course price covering both tuition and resource fees, fixed through the completion deadline of a student's enrolled program. Together with clear, upfront pricing and opportunities to save, this approach helps working adults plan their education with greater confidence.

Housed in the College of Business and Information Technology, the program reflects the importance of professionals who can do more than analyze data â they must also interpret findings, communicate insights and apply analytical thinking to business challenges. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, employment of management analysts is projected to grow 10% from 2025 to 2035, faster than the 3% average for all occupations. Management analyst is among the occupations aligned with the new program's curriculum.

"Business analytics is about more than identifying patterns in data. It is about understanding what those patterns mean, communicating insights and guiding organizations to make informed decisions," said Jim Bruno, MBA, associate dean of the College of Business and Information Technology at University of Phoenix. "We developed this program to connect analytical skills with the business judgment, problem-solving and communication skills professionals use to address real organizational challenges. Students learn not only how to work with data, but how to turn that information into recommendations stakeholders can act on."

Business analytics curriculum emphasizes applied skills and decision-making

The Bachelor of Science in Business Analytics focuses on the intersection of business operations and analytical methods. Students develop skills in data analysis, visualization, business intelligence and decision modeling while learning to apply those capabilities to organizational challenges.

The curriculum emphasizes career-relevant skills, including:

Students develop applied analytics skills through coursework that integrates data visualization, business communication and responsible AI use. In BSA/250, students will use Copilot to assist in creating data visualizations that communicate analytical findings. In BIS/340, students will learn advanced Excel functions and use Copilot to support the development of dashboards that translate data into insights for business stakeholders. These skills also connect to the program's Business Analytics Capstone, with learning outcomes focused on analyzing complex datasets, identifying actionable business insights and presenting data-driven recommendations aligned with organizational objectives.

Responsible AI integration and opportunities to earn digital badges

Students will have opportunities to earn skills-based digital badges that recognize a set of demonstrated competencies:

The new program expands the University's business and technology degree offerings alongside its existing Bachelor of Science in Data Science. While data science places greater emphasis on programming, statistical methods and technical analytical processes, the Bachelor of Science in Business Analytics focuses on applying analytics to business operations, decision-making and stakeholder communication.

Designed for working adults balancing education with professional and personal responsibilities, the 120-credit Bachelor of Science in Business Analytics is offered 100% online, with students typically focusing on one five-week course at a time.

The degree requires a minimum of 30 upper-division credits within the 120-credit total. University of Phoenix has a generous transfer credit policy; students may be able to transfer up to 87 eligible credits toward the degree and can explore additional opportunities to reduce the time and cost of their education through scholarships and credit for prior learning.

#5509. Why QXO sees homebuilders as its mainstay of future growth

QXO wants to become a broader supplier to production and custom homebuilders, using cross-selling across building materials and installation. The company cited improved pricing, daily sales growth, and plans for procurement consolidation, private label expansion, and AI-enabled systems.  AI Summary

QXO, which aims to have $50 billion in annual revenue within the next several years, is counting on homebuilders as a launchpad for growth.

Chairman and CEO Brad Jacobs said Monday on a conference call that the company wants to supply builders with far more than lumber and trusses. QXO, which reports full Q3 2026 earnings after the market closes Thursday, has overhauled sales incentives, technology and pricing to become a primary supplier to production and custom builders.

The push follows its acquisitions of TopBuild and Kodiak Building Partners this year and Beacon Roofing Supply in 2025. Collectively, these acquisitions gave QXO exposure to a wide range of building products, including residential and commercial insulation, roofing materials, waterproofing, lumber and building materials, siding and exteriors, drywall and interior finishes, installation services, and tools and equipment such as fasteners, compressors and safety gear.

That broader footprint comes as the company’s core business is showing momentum. With $4.9 billion in combined revenue last quarter, the firm is well on its way to achieving Jacobs’ lofty annual revenue goal.

QXO, which generates roughly 50% of its revenue from residential construction, reported preliminary Q3 2026 results earlier this week showing organic revenue per day improved for the second consecutive quarter. Companywide pricing rose 2.2% year over year, with nine of 11 business areas posting positive pricing, and daily sales were up 5.4% year over year by the end of October.

Roofing and Waterproofing, QXO’s longest-held business after its April 2025 acquisition of Beacon Roofing Supply, grew daily sales 9.1%. Jacobs credited better on-time deliveries, invoice accuracy and inventory management for Beacon’s performance. Insulation was another strong performer, largely because of data center demand.

Beyond those gains, Jacobs said during the conference call that homebuilders represent a big growth opportunity. He outlined how QXO plans to capture more of their business, along with several ways QXO plans to grow in 2027.

During the call, Jacobs made it clear that QXO plans to cross-sell more to homebuilders, an important and growing customer segment.

“Our strong relationships with production homebuilders are typically rooted in our truss and wall panel capabilities, as well as insulation, where we solve some of their greatest needs. At the same time, it creates an opportunity for us to expand share of wallet by becoming their primary supplier for a wider range of building materials, with the added value of scale to support their growth,” Jacobs explained.

The company’s $17 billion acquisition of TopBuild, announced earlier this year, gave QXO an installation business with a presence at roughly 22,000 job sites every day. QXO, with an established distribution business, plans to leverage TopBuild’s installation services to supply more building materials, coordinate additional trades and manage more work and installations on individual job sites.

QXO’s $2.25 billion acquisition of Kodiak Building Partners, announced in February, additionally gave the firm exposure to building materials like lumber, engineered wood, doors, windows, trusses and gypsum products. These materials are essential to the company’s plans to sell more to Kodiak’s many existing homebuilder customers.

To incentivize cross-selling, Jacobs explained that QXO is changing its sales compensation structure to reward employees for selling customers a broader range of products across its businesses. Salespeople will have a financial incentive to introduce existing customers to other parts of QXO’s portfolio, including building materials and installation services.

“Homebuilders are a big opportunity,” Jacobs said. “One of the main reasons we bought Kodiak is that they brought phenomenal relationships with the big production homebuilders and the custom builders. And they were mainly selling them lumber or trusses or engineered products. So, we’re building on those great relationships, and we’re going to sell them much more. We’ve already started talking to many of these customers about this. There’s a lot of appetite for this.”

Cross-selling to homebuilders comprises just one focus area among QXO’s growth plans. Jacobs named five other areas where the company expects to improve margins and market share, including stronger supplier relationships, additional acquisitions, pricing improvements, smarter use of private-label products and technological improvements.

As QXO continues to integrate and improve its Beacon, Kodiak and TopBuild acquisitions, the combined company intends to leverage its larger scale in negotiations with suppliers.

The business has about $12 billion in combined spending, including about $11 billion in direct spending on products and materials. About $7.6 billion of that spending is with suppliers that serve at least two of QXO’s legacy businesses, including about $5 billion to suppliers serving all three.

QXO plans to consolidate its supplier base to capture that overlap, which could allow the company to push for better pricing and rebates and standardize purchasing agreements across the businesses.

“We want deep relationships with a smaller number of strategic supplier partners,” Jacobs said. “We want to be important partners with them and preferably their most important partner. And there’s quite a lot of overlap among the key suppliers across the three acquisitions we’ve recently done.”

If QXO strengthens its supplier relationships, its homebuilder clients could see better product availability and service, making the company a more appealing primary supplier for builders, particularly as it expands its offerings through additional acquisitions.

Jacobs sees additional acquisitions as a key way to expand its product portfolio, customer base and geographic reach. Following its blockbuster acquisition of TopBuild, QXO is now eyeing smaller, highly accretive acquisitions, but Jacobs did not identify specific acquisition targets or product categories.

Any future acquisitions could add complementary building-material categories, installation capabilities or regional relationships, all of which could support QXO’s push to become a primary homebuilding supplier and deepen QXO’s reach with builders.

QXO’s leadership changes also signal that it continues to eye acquisitions. On Thursday, the company named Dev Ahuja its next CFO, effective in January, succeeding Ihsan Essaid, who will become Vice Chairman. Essaid brings M&A experience from Novelis, where he helped complete and integrate the $2.8 billion Aleris acquisition.

During the call, Jacobs described pricing as one of QXO’s largest company-specific levers for expanding profitability. The company is moving to data-driven pricing based on demand, elasticity, inventory, fulfillment and customer profitability. Better service and availability, he said, can give QXO room to charge more, but the goal is value-based pricing, not blanket price increases.

“I’m not just talking about raising prices; it’s optimizing prices. I think we’re on a good trajectory to getting price where it needs to be, and I think we have an excellent pricing team,” Jacobs explained.

For homebuilders, a broader product and services offering could make QXO a more valuable supplier. However, the company also signaled that it is eyeing strategic price increases, and its expanding offerings, market share and value could give it the leverage to do just that.

QXO launched its private-label brand TRI-BUILT in 2024 and is now actively trying to grow the brand’s sales. Because it’s an original brand, it has stronger gross profit margins – about 2,000 basis points higher – than comparable branded products.

TRI-BUILT accounted for a record 10.6% of Roofing and Waterproofing sales in the third quarter, all from Beacon. QXO wants to expand the brand into more product categories and grow sales to more than $2 billion over the next three years, while also extending private-label offerings across Kodiak and TopBuild.

To support the push, QXO is redesigning sales incentives to encourage employees to sell more private-label products, and the company’s new compensation structure will also reward salespeople for selling private-label products.

QXO is integrating its acquired businesses into a connected technology platform that includes a new ERP, point-of-sale system, warehouse management system and AI-enabled CRM. The systems are meant to make it easier for customers to check inventory, receive quotes, place orders and track deliveries.

“When this is fully rolled out, our employees will be able to get their work done in one connected, AI-enabled environment. They’ll spend less time entering the same information into different systems or tracking down information that will be readily available. The new ecosystem will give our people more capacity to serve customers and run the business,” Jacobs explained.

The public can get a fuller look at whether these strategies are already translating into results when QXO reports full third-quarter earnings after the market closes Thursday.

#5508. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5507. Quantum sensor and software maker Q-CTRL raises $290M in funding

Q-CTRL Pty Ltd., a provider of quantum sensors and software for managing qubits, today announced that it has raised $290 million in funding.

Q-CTRL sells a series of quantum navigation systems called Ironstone Opal. The company positions the product family as a more reliable alternative to GPS. Q-CTRL says that the devices can withstand jamming attempts, adverse weather and other challenging conditions that interfere with GPS signals.

Ironstone Opal tracks the host vehicle’s position with the help of sensors known as quantum magnetometers and quantum gravimeters. The sensors use variations in the Earth’s magnetic field and gravity as navigation cues.

Gravity is weaker at the top of a mountain than at sea level because the peak is farther away from the Earth’s core. The Earth’s magnetic field, in turn, exhibits perturbations at regions that have mineral deposits. Such gravitational and magnetic anomalies act as a unique fingerprint of the location where they occur. When a quantum sensor detects the fingerprint, it can deduce its location with relative ease.

Q-CTRL’s quantum magnetometers collect navigation data using tiny glass structures filled with clouds of atoms. The atoms change in specific ways when they encounter an anomaly in the Earth’s magnetic field. According to the company, its sensors detect those changes with the help of laser beams. Quantum gravimeters operate on a similar principle.

Ironstone Opal includes not only sensors but also software that processes the data they generate. It filters erroneous measurements, combines the remaining data with logs from other sensors and compares the information against pre-loaded maps.

C-QTRL offers Ironstone Opal alongside a pair of software tools designed to make quantum computers easier to use. The first tool, Boulder Opal, helps researchers calibrate qubits in a manner that optimizes their performance. It’s complemented by Fire Opal, which makes quantum algorithms less prone to errors.

“The hard problem in quantum is not building the machine, it is getting useful output from it,” said Salesforce Ventures partner Robert Keith. “Q-CTRL solves that with AI-powered control software, and the proof is already public: a materials simulation on IBM hardware that any developer can now call directly from the IBM Quantum Platform, and the first quantum navigation system qualified for safety of flight.”

Q-CTRL will use the proceeds from the funding round to enhance its software and grow its international presence.

SYDNEY, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nuix (ASX: NXL), a leading provider of investigative analytics and intelligence software, today announced the appointment of Lori Cornmesser as Global Vice President, Partner Ecosystems. Cornmesser will lead the strategic evolution of Nuix's partner network, scaling strategic alliances across global systems integrators (GSIs), service providers, cloud marketplaces, channel partners, resellers, and technology ecosystems.

Cornmesser brings over 25 years' experience building and leading partner ecosystems globally. Reporting directly to Oliver Harvey, Chief Customer Officer, Cornmesser will oversee partner engagement, enablement, and joint go-to-market execution. The appointment underscores Nuix's expanded commitment to its partner strategy, prioritizing co-innovation and services opportunities that deliver transformative solutions to mutual customers.

"Lori has a rare track record of turning partner programs into primary growth engines," said Oliver Harvey, Chief Customer Officer, Nuix. "Organizations facing the highest scrutiny increasingly rely on trusted advisors to help them turn complex data into defensible insight, and our partners are central to how we reach and serve them. Lori's experience building repeatable, partner-led motions will accelerate that strategy globally."

Nuix's partner ecosystem offers an opportunity to integrate its unstructured data intelligence platform, Nuix Neo, more deeply into the technology stacks of large enterprises, government agencies, and law enforcement organizations.

"Nuix sits at the intersection of two things partners value most: hard problems and high-stakes customers," said Cornmesser. "Investigations, compliance, and legal review demand forensic-grade data intelligence, and there is a significant opportunity to put that capability in the hands of partners who already advise the world's most scrutinized organizations. I look forward to building an ecosystem that grows alongside them."

Prior to joining Nuix, Cornmesser was at Juniper, managing more than 5,000 global alliance partners and developing go-to-market strategies with major service providers including AT&T, Verizon, BT, Orange Business, TelefÃ³nica, Optus, and Telstra, before leading channel growth for Juniper's newly formed Enterprise business. More recently, Cornmesser expanded 1Password's channel, distribution, MSP, marketplace, and strategic alliances footprint across Europe and Asia and built global partner ecosystems at Infoblox, Ixia/Agilent, Deepwatch, and CyCognito.

Cornmesser holds an MBA and a Bachelor of Business Administration from Columbus University, and is based in San Jose, California, USA.

#5505. Builders are looking for a bottom. 2027 plans can’t wait that long

Builders are balancing incentives, margins, and cash recovery as resale inventory rises and rental options improve. Key signals include a 5.5% drop in existing-home sales, 5.1 months of supply, and widespread builder discounting.  AI Summary

We’re at that agonizing moment in a housing market downturn when finding “the bottom” becomes the first next thing to hope for.

The trouble is, market bottoms tend to reveal themselves only in the 20/20 clarity of hindsight, not in any set of measures we can confidently decipher in the present.

For America’s homebuilders, residential developers and investors, this creates an uncomfortable predicament. They’re not just competing with the clock. They’re competing with other parts of the residential continuum –rentals and resales – that are also competing with the clock. They must make decisions that will determine their performance in 2027 before they know whether the worst is behind them.

Decisions, for instance, like how much to build, where to commit capital, what prices will move homes, and what sales pace will sustain profitability.

The evidence accumulating as 2026 nears year-end offers little or no assurance that the housing market has found solid footing. Weakening household demand, rising competition in the resale market, increasingly attractive rental alternatives, and persistent uncertainty about employment, incomes, and home values are making it harder to balance pricing and sales pace sustainably.

The question for builders is not whether they can predict the precise moment the market turns. It is whether they can adapt their businesses to current conditions, preserve financial and operating flexibility to withstand further weakness, and position themselves to benefit when household demand eventually stabilizes.

The latest evidence points to a market that is still losing momentum

Thursday’s report from the National Association of Realtors offered another indication of the challenges facing the housing market. Existing-home sales fell 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, down 8.8% from a year earlier and the weakest reading since August 2010.

The number of existing homes for sale increased to 1.59 million, up 4.6% from October 2025. At the current sales pace, that represented 5.1 months of supply, compared with 4.4 months a year earlier and the highest level since November 2015.

The national median existing-home price, meanwhile, rose just 0.4% from a year earlier to $416,700. That combination of declining transactions, rising months’ supply and relatively stable reported prices illustrates a housing market in which buyers and sellers have yet to agree on home values under prevailing financing and economic conditions.

Telling data points came through in this analysis, breaking out trends that speak to a softening market:

The numbers reveal a critical point of distinction. A rising months’ supply does not necessarily mean homeowners are flooding the market with listings. It can result from sales falling faster than inventory is being absorbed. Both dynamics are relevant to builders, whose homes compete with an increasing selection of existing properties for buyers.

The latest data offer little encouragement to builders expecting a quick rebound in household demand. The National Association of Home Builders reported that September new-home sales fell to a 676,000-unit annual pace, 5.3% below the year-earlier level, while the supply of new homes for sale remained elevated at 8.4 months.

The October NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell to 29, its lowest level since June 2012. Forty-three percent of builders reported cutting prices, while 65% continued to offer sales incentives.

Those findings point to a persistent problem for homebuilding companies: Builders continue to make meaningful concessions to stimulate sales, but households’ response remains insufficient to establish confidence in a sustained recovery.

Mortgage rates remain an important constraint, but the industry’s demand problem is increasingly difficult to explain through financing costs alone.

Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp points to the cumulative financial pressures facing prospective buyers. Elevated mortgage payments, tariff-related construction costs, insurance premiums, property taxes, utilities, and everyday household expenses are affecting households’ ability and willingness to take on the obligations of ownership.

“For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market,” Hepp says.

Her observation highlights a sharp difference between qualifying for a mortgage and deciding that buying a home makes financial sense.

A household may technically qualify for a mortgage yet still find that the monthly payment, down payment, and ongoing ownership costs leave too little room for savings, unexpected expenses, or other financial commitments. For households concerned about job security or declining home values, waiting may seem increasingly prudent.

The broader economy complicates that calculation. Higher-income households with substantial savings, accumulated home equity, or financial assets may be able to absorb elevated housing costs, whereas entry-level and middle-income households have far less flexibility.

That unevenness helps explain why a national decline in mortgage rates might boost sales only modestly. Some prospective buyers need lower monthly payments. Others need greater confidence that their incomes will remain secure, that their other living expenses will stabilize, and that the home they purchase will retain its value. These concerns are not necessarily resolved by a builder’s offer of a temporary mortgage-rate buydown.

The Federal Reserve’s latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey underscores the demand problem. Banks reported weaker demand across all residential mortgage categories in the third quarter, even as lending standards remained largely unchanged for most mortgage products. Banks also reported weaker demand and tighter lending standards for construction and land development loans.

The implications extend beyond individual homebuyers. When expected sales absorption weakens, the financial justification for developing additional lots, opening communities, and committing construction capital becomes more difficult.

One of the most important changes in homebuilding’s competitive environment has been the reversal of several conditions that supported new-home demand during the pandemic and its aftermath.

During that period, builders benefited from an unusually tight existing-home market. Homeowners who had secured historically low mortgage rates had little incentive to sell, limiting resale inventory and directing prospective buyers toward new construction.

At the same time, elevated rents in many markets made homeownership relatively more attractive. Builders with available lots, construction capacity, and mortgage financing relationships were positioned to capture buyers with fewer alternatives.

The appeal of renting is not limited to households that cannot afford to buy. For some households, renting lets them keep their savings, preserve geographic flexibility, and avoid the risk of buying a home before local prices have stabilized.

Existing homes are also becoming more formidable competitors. In markets where resale listings have increased and homes are taking longer to sell, prospective buyers can compare new construction with a wider selection of existing properties. Sellers who need to relocate, settle estates, or complete other transactions may be increasingly willing to negotiate.

Builders therefore face a three-way competitive challenge that was less pronounced during the pandemic-era housing boom. They must compete against other builders, existing-home sellers and rental operators, each offering a different mix of price, location, amenities, monthly cost and financial commitment.

This competition is especially intense in markets where builders have substantial inventories of completed homes and developed lots. A resale seller may have the financial flexibility to postpone a transaction, whereas a builder must continue to carry land, construction, financing and overhead costs until inventory converts to cash.

This pressure can prompt builders to adjust their effective prices sooner than many existing-home sellers. Yet lower new-home prices can also influence resale sellers’ expectations, triggering another round of competitive adjustments. The process may continue for some time before either market reaches a sustainable balance.

For builders, the most immediate challenge is determining how much pricing flexibility is needed to maintain sales velocity without sacrificing the profitability required to sustain their businesses. Reducing prices and offering incentives may increase orders, but those measures can also erode gross margins and reduce returns on capital already committed to land and construction. Maintaining prices may protect reported margins on individual transactions, but it can leave completed homes on the market longer, increase carrying costs, and delay the recovery of invested capital.

Neither approach necessarily produces a better outcome without understanding the relationships among sales pace, effective pricing, inventory costs and cash generation.

The problem becomes more difficult when household demand continues to weaken. Pricing decisions that seem sufficient to generate sales in one month may need to be reconsidered the next as competing builders adjust incentives, resale sellers lower expectations, or rental operators offer more attractive terms.

The industry’s challenge is therefore to find a lower price at which buyers will purchase homes and to determine whether homes can be produced, marketed, and sold at that price while still generating acceptable returns. Not one or the other, both. That distinction directly impacts 2027 budgets.

A community that achieves an acceptable gross margin with three sales per month may generate inadequate returns if absorption drops to one or two sales. Conversely, a lower-margin community that turns inventory quickly and requires less capital may outperform one with stronger nominal margins but slower cash recovery.

These tradeoffs will vary by market, product type, land basis, construction costs, and financing structure. A single national assumption about mortgage rates or home-price appreciation cannot resolve them.

The industry’s search for a bottom should not become a reason to postpone decisions about how businesses will operate if demand remains weak. Instead, the uncertainty should drive builders to test their 2027 plans against a broader range of outcomes, including scenarios in which conditions deteriorate further before improving.

The first priority is a more precise understanding of household purchasing power and competing housing alternatives in each community’s trade area.

Builders need to know not only which prospective customers qualify to purchase, but also what they are willing to pay when comparing a new home with available resales and rental properties. That analysis should include the full monthly cost of ownership, the incentives required to attract buyers, and the potential impact of additional competing supply.

The second priority is reassessing land commitments, community-opening schedules, and construction starts.

Projects approved under stronger demand assumptions may no longer meet their original return requirements. Builders should evaluate whether development schedules can be phased, whether lot deliveries can be adjusted, and whether to defer capital commitments until sales absorption justifies additional investment.

The third priority is to maintain the financial and operational flexibility to respond when conditions change.

That means closely monitoring completed-home inventory, construction cycle times, cancellation rates, financing costs, and cash recovery. It also means identifying opportunities to reduce product and construction costs rather than relying indefinitely on incentives to bridge the gap between household purchasing power and home prices.

These are practical operational decisions, not substitutes for a stronger housing market. They can, however, determine how much financial strain a builder faces while waiting for demand to stabilize. They may also determine which companies are positioned to invest as better opportunities emerge.

Hepp identifies the upcoming spring selling season as an important test of whether housing activity can begin to recover.

“Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner,” she says.

Homebuilders cannot control when household demand stabilizes. They can control how quickly they recognize market changes, how effectively they adjust their cost structures and capital commitments, and how well they prepare their businesses for conditions that may remain difficult longer than expected.

The bottom will become clear in hindsight. The work of getting through it – and of emerging stronger – waits for no one.
