#5504. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

Any traction in real payments or on-chain activity with DogeOS could bolster the perception of DOGE evolving beyond a mere meme.

#5501. Exclusive: ARA forms AI Task Force to back licensee-in-the-loop laws

The American Real Estate Association launched an AI Task Force, chaired by Dmitriy Kruglyak, to advocate licensee-in-the-loop rules. The group plans white papers and state-by-state outreach to require licensed supervision of AI actions in real estate transactions.  AI Summary

The American Real Estate Association (ARA) has launched an AI Task Force focused on advocating for and advancing “Licensee-in-the-Loop” legislation in all 50 states.

Jason Haber, a co-founder of ARA along with The Agency’s Mauricio Umansky, said the legislative effort was inspired by a contributor article published on HousingWire by Dmitriy Kruglyak, a self-described software engineer turned real estate broker. In the piece, Kruglyak argues that the growing use of agentic AI in real estate could put consumers at risk by allowing unlicensed automated systems to perform tasks traditionally handled by licensed agents, including negotiating contracts and guiding transactions.

“I think this could be the defining issue for our industry in 2027,” Haber told HousingWire. “I read Dmitry’s oped and I was glued. I immediately understood the implications of what he was writing about. It struck me as a gigantic red flag in our industry and no one was talking about it.”

Haber said Kruglyak is now chairing ARA’s AI Task Force, which will be meeting for the first time in the coming weeks. The group will work on white papers focused on the issue, along with AI policy analysis and advocacy, with “licensee-in-the-loop” being the first issue the group will focus on.

“AI has no fiduciary, it holds no license, it has no errors and omission insurance and when something goes wrong, there is no real estate board to file an ethics complaint with,” Haber said. “So what happens is you have a consumer that has no idea how the AI model has been trained. For example, maybe it has been trained to benefit the seller and not the buyer so it convinces a buyer to make a higher offer.”

However, if a real estate licensee is involved, the whole situation changes, Haber said. ARA views “licensee-in-the-loop legislation as a guarantee that anyone who buys, sells or rents a home has a licensed, accountable real estate professional standing behind the transaction.

“We’re saying, if you have an act performed by an automated system on behalf of the consumer for a real estate transaction, it has to be supervised by a responsible licensee that’s identifiable to the consumer with a name and license. And, before any offer goes in or counter offers are transmitted, it’s really reviewed by someone who holds a license and that the autonomous system is backed by the licensees fiduciary responsibilities to a client,” Haber said.

He said ARA views this as the responsible way to embrace AI technology, as it enables consumers to hold someone accountable if something goes wrong in their transaction. Although the share of consumers buying or selling their home solely with the help of an AI model or an AI real estate agent product is still the minority, Haber said he believes the industry will see more of these AI real estate agent platforms popping up in the next year, which is why he feels it is important for ARA to get ahead of the issue.

“We are looking to future proof for the consumer in the industry,” he said. “We see this coming and we want to have regulatory and statutory framework in place so that we don’t have to react after the consumer has been harmed. So, we think by moving now we are in a better position.”

Haber also noted that these efforts take time, especially because there are no federal real estate licensing laws. Due to this, Haber said ARA is going state-by-state talking to legislators regarding this issue in hopes that they will be willing to introduce this legislation in their state.

“We are tapping our state association chairs and working with our federal lobbyist to connect us with elected officials around the country,” Haber said. “It is going to take some time and just getting one bill through one state is Herculean enough, but now we are trying to take this already very challenging thing and do it 50 times.”

While Haber acknowledges that this will be a tall order, he believes it is a great opportunity for ARA to show what it is doing to help agents and American consumers at a national level.

“I think it is going to be interesting to see how it plays out, it is a long process, but we think we will have legislation introduced as early as the end of the year or early January in some states,” Haber said.

#5500. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5498. Cisco beats expectations, lifts guidance and forecasts AI infrastructure revenue to double in fiscal 2027

Shares of Cisco Systems Inc. were flat in late trading today after the networking infrastructure giant reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s expectations.

The company also raised its guidance for fiscal 2027, citing strong demand for artificial intelligence network infrastructure.

Cisco reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.40 per share, comfortably beating the Street’s target of $1.33 per share. Revenue for the quarter jumped 24% from the same period one year earlier, to $18.5 billion, ahead of the $18.1 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, Cisco’s net income rose to $4.6 billion, up from just $2.9 billion a year ago.

Although the stock was flat in extended trading, it’s still up 32% in the year to date, way ahead of the broader Nasdaq index, which has gained just 9% over the same stretch.

Cisco has been pushing to gain a foothold in the AI infrastructure buildout that’s dominating the technology industry these days after failing to capitalize on the generative AI boom in the early days. However, its push has come at a critical juncture, as investors have become increasingly concerned over the prospects of a slowdown in data center building following the Democratic party’s sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, there are growing fears about the impact rising borrowing costs will have on debt-fueled data center construction projects.

Still, Cisco Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) expressed confidence in the company’s ability to maintain its momentum. He told analysts on a conference call that we’re still in the “very early stages of a multiyear network supercycle.” He said he’s confident Cisco’s AI networking technology is strong enough to continue to capture a portion of the multibillion-dollar opportunity that presents.

“Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” Robbins added.

Cisco is also building out its software portfolio with new tools that can help businesses to build armies of autonomous AI agents that can perform work on behalf of humans. It also sells the security software necessary to protect those agents and their underlying infrastructure against cyberattacks.

The company said it’s increasing its AI infrastructure revenue forecast for the fiscal year to $9 billion, which would be more than double what it earned in fiscal 2026. According to Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson, the company is “unlocking significant operating leverage,” and this is what’s enabling it to grow its earnings “much faster” than its revenue.

Investors may still be worried about Cisco’s gross margins, though. This has been a concern for many companies, as the global shortage of memory chips has steadily increased the cost of the components that hardware makers need to build their data center infrastructure products.  Cisco’s gross margin of 65.6% in the quarter was in-line with the Street’s estimates, but down from 68.1% in the year-ago period.

TECHnalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the decline was unlikely to worry too many people, though. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” he said. He added that the company’s raised forecast and strong earnings and revenue was the main thing the market wanted to see.

For the current quarter, Cisco said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.34 and $1.36 per share on sales of $18 billion to $18.2 billion. That’s a strong forecast, with the Street looking for earnings of just $1.23 per share on revenue of $17.88 billion.

#5497. California cities get firm notice: follow new housing laws, or else

California housing fights are increasingly happening before a vote, with nonprofits sending letters that cite HAA, density bonus law, and CEQA reforms. The goal is to warn officials and create a record that can be used if a city rejects or reduces a project.  AI Summary

A 135-townhome project cleared the Rancho Cucamonga Planning Commission on Tuesday on the planning department’s recommendation.

That is the outcome state reforms are meant to produce: more housing, including affordable units. Warmington Residential Homes’ project includes seven for very-low-income households. Still, the meeting showed how these disputes now run. Before a decision, a pro-housing nonprofit reminds the city to follow the law, creating a record it can cite if officials ignore the warning.

In Rancho Cucamonga, the California Housing Defense Fund sent a three-page letter citing the Housing Accountability Act, the state Density Bonus Law and last year’s California Environmental Quality Act reform. Rejecting the project or cutting its size, it warned, would require written findings of a specific health or safety hazard.

The Rancho Cucamonga letter was one of at least five CalHDF sent that day, along with letters to Santa Clarita, Whittier, Escondido and Twentynine Palms. Four concerned projects of 17 to 146 units. One addressed an ADU ordinance.

Those letters are a fraction of the total. James Lloyd, the organization’s director of planning and investigations, told HousingWire the number reaches about 100 a year.

They serve as a first step toward making sure cities implement state housing reforms properly, according to the organization.

Broadly, the letters pair legal warnings with a pitch to local officials: new housing helps a city’s finances and existing residents while meeting the state’s need for more homes.

“While no one project will solve the statewide housing crisis, the proposed development is a step in the right direction,” the organization writes.

Lawmakers have spent years trying to speed housing construction to improve affordability. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 to reform CEQA and SB 131 in 2025, exempting qualifying infill housing from environmental review and narrowing review for projects that nearly qualify. Legislators also tightened the Housing Accountability Act, which limits when cities can deny or shrink projects that meet zoning.

Neighbor suits have not disappeared. They have shifted to different arguments. Attorneys at the legal publisher CEB expect litigation to focus on whether a project qualifies for a CEQA exemption at all, rather than on the adequacy of an environmental report.

Builders and advocates pose a growing risk for cities that resist state law. Cities frequently lose when they test the rules in court, and the losses can be costly. Under Senate Bill 1037, penalties can reach $50,000 per unit for willful Housing Accountability Act violations.

La Cañada Flintridge refused to process a builder’s remedy project. A judge ruled against the city in March 2024, and the city dropped its appeal a year later rather than post a $14 million bond. It paid CalHDF $1,262,500 in fees and costs last year.

A small project in Pacifica shows the stakes. Neighbors sued over an eight-townhome project, arguing it needed a full environmental impact report instead of the lighter review the city used.

A trial court sided with them, rescinded the approvals and awarded nearly $1.3 million in attorney’s fees. In December 2025, an appeals court vacated the fee award, saying the judge had wrongly discounted the project’s housing value. It sent the question back to the trial court.

But when it came to a recommendation, staff tracked the laws CalHDF cited. They wrote in their staff report that the project qualified for waivers under the state density bonus law, which limits when a city can deny them. Staff also noted the project was exempt from environmental review under CEQA guidelines.

#5496. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5494. Compass sues 15 MLSs over office exclusive rules

Compass filed 15 lawsuits against MLSs alleging they punish agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings at a seller’s request. The claims track Compass’ earlier CRMLS suit and focus on rules requiring MLS submission for cooperation.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings is taking its fight with MLSs over their cooperation and listing submission rules to the next level. On Thursday evening, the real estate brokerage conglomerate fielded 15 lawsuits against 15 MLS.

The lawsuits all claim that these MLSs fine and punish agents who publicly market office exclusive listings at the request of the home seller.

Defendant in these lawsuits include bridgeMLS, Bay East MLS, Contra Costa MLS, MLSListings, The MLS-CLAW, San Diego MLS, Canopy MLS, Hive MLS, Doorify MLS, Arizona Regional MLS, Recolorado, NorthstarMLS, Houston Association of Realtors, Stellar MLS and OneKey MLS.

Compass also contends that MLS boards consist of Compass’s competitors who are dictating how Compass and its agents can and cannot compete in the marketplace. Compass has recently announced that it is banning all employees from serving in Realtor association leadership roles. The firm has not clarified if this also extends to non-Realtor affiliated MLSs or if it pertains to brokers and agents affiliated with Compass, as many Compass International Holdings agents and brokers serve on MLS and Realtor association boards.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner. Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer,” a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire. “It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true. For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

These lawsuits come after Compass International Holdings sent letters to MLSs in early September demanding that they stop enforcing rules governing when publicly marketed listings must be submitted to the MLS for cooperation. On stage at the Council of MLSs (CMLS) Open House conference in late September, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin  threatened to sue any MLS that refused to change their rules in response to his firm’s demands.

In response to these threats, CRMLS, ARMLS, OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS have filed two separate lawsuits against Compass International Holdings in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeking a declaratory judgement from the court allowing them to continue enforcing their cooperation rules and policies without violating antitrust law.

The MLS defendants have not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

The Compass brokerage brand has recently announced a new broker-to-broker cooperation policy, which requires all Compass agents to cooperate with other brokers and agents, including for listings in Private Exclusive or Coming Soon marketing phases, unless otherwise instructed by the client in writing.

TORONTO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DeFi Technologies Inc. (the "Company" or "DeFi Technologies") (Nasdaq: DEFT) (CBOE CA: DEFI) (GR: R9B) (B3: DEFT31), a regulated capital markets platform for digital assets, today announced its financial results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. Valour â AUM, Net Inflows, Management Fees, Staking and Lending Income

Cash, Treasury, Venture, and Working Capital Position

Together, total cash, USDT/USDC, STRC/RWUSD, digital asset treasury, Smart Crypto Fund and venture portfolio value stood at approximately $159 million as of September 30, 2026. Comment from Johan WattenstrÃ¶m, Chief Executive Officer of DeFi Technologies

"The third quarter demonstrated how our business can respond to improving digital asset markets. We reported $18.3 million in revenue, $7.0 million in operating income, and $22.3 million in net income, with trading gains and investment revaluations contributing materially to those results.

Valour's AUM increased approximately 62%, from $397.2 million at the end of June to $643.7 million at September 30. We generated $26.1 million in positive net inflows during the quarter, bringing net inflows for the first nine months to $48.9 million. During September, we also launched Valour Funds SPC and its Smart Crypto Fund SP, extending our offering into actively managed strategies for professional and qualified investors, with additional institutional offerings in development.

Stillman demonstrates the contribution our broader platform can make. It generated $7.6 million in trading commissions through the first nine months, up approximately 22% year over year. We are building on that foundation by expanding its institutional reach and client relationships.

Looking ahead, we are optimistic that the lows of this bear market may now be behind us. If that proves to be the case, we believe DeFi Technologies is entering the recovery with a broader revenue opportunity than in previous cycles. Higher AUM can increase management fees and staking income on eligible assets, while greater trading activity supports our institutional business. With much of our supporting infrastructure already in place, revenue growth can translate into meaningful operating leverage and margin expansion.

Our financial position supports our ability to pursue that opportunity. At September 30, we reported $165.8 million in total shareholders' equity and approximately $159.1 million in balance sheet holdings and investments, compared with a recent market capitalization of approximately $130 million. Considering those resources alongside Valour's asset management platform, Stillman's profitable trading business, and the new offerings we are developing, we believe our valuation materially understates the value and earnings potential of the company.

I see considerable potential in the business we have built. With a wider product range, continued investor inflows, and more ways to generate revenue, I believe we can deliver substantially stronger results in a sustained recovery than in previous bull market cycles.

Our focus now is on attracting capital, expanding distribution, and bringing our new offerings to market. I am confident in our direction and excited about what we can achieve from this position. Our responsibility is to turn that opportunity into stronger earnings and long-term value for shareholders."

#5492. Paytient-Greenwald Study Finds 61% of Insured Workers Have Paid for Healthcare Entirely in Cash Without Filing a Claim

In a new study of over 2,000 employer-insured workers, 68% said they would prefer predictably paying cash for a major healthcare expense through small paycheck deductions. These findings put payment experience alongside plan design as a cost and experience lever for employers and benefits advisors.

COLUMBIA, Mo., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Employers are projecting healthcare cost increases of 11% or more without plan changes. Against that backdrop, a new national study commissioned by Paytient and conducted by Greenwald Research points to a plan design tenet that can lower premiums year over year and improve the employee experience: payability, or a person's ability to self-pay or cash-pay for care. The data shows that when employers build payability directly into plan design, they create patient-centered health plans. Those plans allow employers and employees to move to lower-cost plan designs with confidence, in a way that improves, rather than impairs, the employee experience.

Payability, Measured is the second in Paytient's Payability Papers, a four-part series examining how the out-of-pocket payment experience shapes health plan performance and the employee experience. Surveying 2,024 full-time, employer-insured workers, the study finds that two-thirds of employees prefer a $2,000 cost spread over six months to a $1,000 copay paid in full upfront to receive care. Greenwald's research is the first of its kind to reveal this behavioral preference in how consumers pay for healthcare, and it highlights real opportunities for employers and insurers to design health plans around how people prefer to pay for care.

These findings that have direct implications for employers stand out:

"Insurance was built to protect people from the financial risk of rare, catastrophically expensive care. Over time, we've stretched it to cover nearly everything, which drives up premiums and makes the system harder to navigate. This research shows that people want to pay for healthcare the way they pay for almost everything else in their lives: upfront, in-full with a clear cash price or predictably, over time to fit their household budget. A smarter plan design pairs lower-cost coverage for rare, high-cost care with the payment tools "Paytients" have told us they want for everything else. Employers already use payroll to collect premiums (and smooth the payment of taxes) over the life of employment. Using payroll to smooth out-of-pocket costs is the plan design opportunity hiding in plain sight, and it can help employers save substantially on plan costs," says Joe Gabler, Chief Operating Officer of Paytient.

The findings support that when employees have a reliable, structured way to pay for out-of-pocket costs over time, plan design can become more efficient without becoming less supportive â and that changes the calculus on deductible architecture, total cost of care, and the actual value delivered by healthcare benefit.

"What stands out in this data is how universal the preference for payability in healthcare is. It holds across income levels, from workers earning under $50,000 to those earning over $100,000.

"This isn't a low-income affordability story. It's a structural preference that cuts across the entire workforce, and can be a universal strategic advantage for employers," says Lisa Weber, Chief Research Officer and Head of Healthcare Insights at Greenwald Research.

Payability, Measured is available for download here. For more information, visit www.paytient.com. If you're attending HLTH 2026, stop by Paytient's booth (#2824).

About PaytientPaytient is the leader in innovative healthcare payment solutions. Our Healthcare Payability Platform has put over $50 billion of purchasing power into the hands of 26 million individuals across employer, ACA and Medicare plans. In doing so, Paytient is helping shape more accessible, equitable, and lower-cost health plans across commercial, individual, and regulated healthcare markets. To learn more, visit www.paytient.com and join us on LinkedIn.

#5491. Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5490. Applied Materials posts impressive 53% jump in revenue as it beats expectations again

Semiconductor industry giant Applied Materials Inc. chalked up another strong quarter as it continued to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom, delivering fourth-quarter results that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations on earnings and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share on revenue of $10.41 billion, up by an impressive 53% from a year earlier. The results were impressive, with analysts modeling earnings of just $4.06 per share on sales of $10.3 billion. Net income rose to $2.71 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same period one year ago.

Applied Materials is the world’s biggest supplier of the equipment used by semiconductor manufacturers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc., so its results are widely seen as a bellwether for the broader chipmaking industry. If Applied is growing, it means chipmakers are investing in their factories and presumably expecting to churn out more chips, driving growth in the industry. The company manufactures all sorts of machines to support different semiconductor manufacturing processes, catering to the most advanced silicon for AI workloads.

Chief Executive Gary Dickerson (pictured) said the company delivered record-breaking results in fiscal 2026, with full-year sales rising 21% from the prior year, to $34.31 billion. He also said the semiconductor systems business unit is on track to grow more than 40% in calendar 2026. “AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors and Applied has the most-enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing roadmap, putting us in a great position for multiyear revenue and profit growth,” he added.

Applied’s stock was under pressure earlier in the day following the news of Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which came after he admitted to having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working for China’s intelligence services. Some investors worry that instability at Nvidia, which is the world’s most dominant AI chip supplier, could have a knock-on effect on the broader chipmaking industry.

However, the strong results brought Applied’s daytime slide to a halt, and the stock gained more than 2.5% in late trading. In the year to date, its stock is up 48%.

Applied’s main business, the semiconductor systems unit, saw revenue jump from $4.88 billion in the year-ago period to $7.99 billion. Meanwhile, sales from the smaller applied global services segment rose from $1.5 billion a year earlier, to $1.89 billion.

For the current quarter, Applied said it’s looking for earnings of $4.35 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue coming to $11.1 billion. Those numbers were better than expected too, with the Street modeling first quarter earnings of just $4.24 per share on sales of $10.85 billion.

During the quarter, Applied made a big splash when it said it’s going to invest $5 billion in a new chip research and development facility located in Silicon Valley. It’s called the EPIC Center, and it will act as a shared R&D center for chipmakers to collaborate on new process manufacturing technologies.

Initial partners include Intel Corp., which is working with Applied and other companies on the development of next-generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging technologies. Other founding partners include Kioxia Corp., BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. and the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.

#5489. LCH2 Awarded Additional $1 Million to Advance Lewis County Clean Energy Campus

Total grant support reaches $1.4 million as the "From Wood to AI" project advances site, engineering, permitting, commercial and financing work.Supported in part by a grant from TransAlta Centralia Generation LLC.

CENTRALIA, Wash., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Lewis County Hydrogen Alliance, Inc. (LCH2) has been awarded an additional $1 million from TransAlta Centralia Board Funding, LLC, acting through its Energy Technology Board under the Centralia Coal Transition Grants program, to advance development of the Lewis County Clean Energy Campus. Total grant support now reaches $1.4 million.

The new funding supports site control, engineering, permitting, feedstock-supply and product-offtake agreements, and project-financing work. The initial assessment examined feedstock and logistics, the site-selection pathway, concept-level process engineering and permitting, supporting a recommendation to advance.

The full-campus vision would use regional forestry residuals to produce hydrogen, clean carbon coproducts and dispatchable electricity, with a next-generation AI Advanced Compute Complex alongside the energy infrastructure.

At full buildout, the current planning case targets approximately 1,000 wet metric tonnes per day of forestry residuals and a 50-megawatt advanced-compute IT load. LCH2's management target of more than 220 family-wage jobs is a project target, not an independently completed economic-impact forecast.

"Centralia's Coal Transition Grant program was created to help communities build durable economic and energy opportunities through change. LCH2's next stage brings together Lewis County's forestry strengths, emerging clean-energy technology and new industrial demand in a way that is aligned with that long-term purpose. We are pleased to see locally grounded projects continue moving from concept toward execution, supporting the region's next industrial chapter," said Chris Fralick, Executive Vice President, Generation and Chief Operating Officer of TransAlta.

"This $1 million award does more than extend a study â it funds the next substantive development stage. We have completed the first round of feedstock, site, engineering and permitting work, and now our job is execution: secure site control, advance the engineering and permits, formalize supply and offtake, and build a financeable commercial project," said Ken Cavallon, Executive Director of LCH2.

Near-term work is development workânot full-campus constructionâand future buildout remains dependent on site control, engineering validation, permits, commercial agreements and project financing.

#5488. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5487. LIVE – Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. She is reportedly suspected of facilitating Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies. The investigation has raised concerns about potential Chinese intelligence involvement and whether Nvidia’s technology reached restricted customers.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

A second relationship emerged through a New York Times report identifying Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell reportedly worked directly under Huang, creating additional corporate governance questions.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. Directors previously expressed confidence in Huang, but Bloomberg subsequently reported that Nvidia had engaged an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. Losing Huang would remove the founder most closely associated with its AI dominance, potentially forcing investors to reassess the company’s leadership and long-term strategy.

The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.
