#5454. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5453. Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang

Whether she was a spy, a fixer, or just a paramour of Jensen Huang, the name Alice Huang (no relation) has roiled the business world this week following reports that the two were having an affair. The revelation snowballed into Jensen’s shocking resignation Wednesday.

Now come reports that officials are looking into other companies Alice was working with. Bloomberg reported, based on an anonymous source, that the Department of Justice is running multiple probes into Nvidia. One is focused on antitrust issues and two others are focused on Megaspeed—where Alice Huang was a former top executive—and Super Micro Computer. Separately, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in alleged efforts to smuggle Supermicro hardware laced with Nvidia’s red-hot GPUs into China. It is unclear whether that probe is tied to smuggling cases already brought in the U.S. or Asia. Neither Jensen Huang, Nvidia, nor Supermicro have been formally charged with any wrongdoing.

Supermicro stock tumbled 12% after U.S. markets opened this morning. The company did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Thus far, much of the speculation about Jensen Huang’s catastrophic downfall as the leader of Nvidia has centered on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that reportedly became one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Southeast Asia. But Supermicro, the San Jose server maker run by Charles Liang, Jensen Huang’s friend of three decades and an important partner to Nvidia, has been in under the microscope regarding export-control compliance and is being pulled along with Nvidia.

Fortune has reported on the Supermicro case since before federal agents arrested its co-founder in March, and that reporting shows a company with a documented track record of governance and compliance failures. Despite its history, Supermicro has remained in lockstep with Nvidia. Liang and Jensen have shared the stage together at Computex in Taiwan, where Jensen was photographed in 2024 with Alice at a cocktail bar.

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with allegedly routing about $2.5 billion in servers laced with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China through a Southeast Asian front company. Bloomberg later reported the front company is OBON, a Bangkok-based AI infrastructure firm, which has not been charged. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme.

Liaw, who immediately resigned his executive and board roles at Supermicro following his arrest, has pleaded not guilty. His trial was pushed to March 2027 after Liaw’s lawyers told the judge in his case that subpoenas issued to Supermicro could be material to Liaw’s defense. Nelson Boxer, Liaw’s attorney, declined to comment.

One of Liaw’s co-defendants in the smuggling case, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October, including to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app from his phone on the day of the arrests. Sun’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment, and it’s unclear if Sun has a cooperation agreement with the government.

There is no public evidence so far that the Supermicro and Megaspeed cases are directly connected but there are mounting threads. Thursday, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a statement noting that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had initiated investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang and in doing so sought information from Supermicro. Supermicro only offered “limited cooperation,” Singaporean authorities said.

In a July 2025 meeting, Singapore officials raised this with U.S. authorities and asked for their assistance in getting Supermicro’s cooperation and have repeated the request “on several occasions” to the Department of Justice and the FBI.

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement reads. Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Supermicro’s export-control problems did not start with Liaw’s arrest, Fortune’s reporting has found. In 2006, the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai, mirroring the basic scheme prosecutors alleged in the Liaw case.

Liaw himself has been through the crisis wringer before. He left Supermicro in 2018 amid a board-led investigation tied to Supermicro’s Nasdaq delisting and an SEC probe of its accounting, which ended with a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned as a consultant in May 2021, became a full-time employee, and rejoined the board in December 2023.

In 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research accused Supermicro of accounting manipulation and export-control failures and the company denied the allegations. Ernst & Young then resigned as auditor mid-audit, saying it could no longer rely on management’s representations. A special committee recommended in December 2024 that Supermicro replace CFO David Weigand and the company agreed to do so “immediately.” The company didn’t name a successor until October.

As Fortune has reported, the Liaw indictment describes thousands of nonworking dummy servers staged in warehouses to fool auditors, contractors using hair dryers to peel off serial-number labels, and a compliance auditor who was off-site allegedly enjoying “entertainment” paid for by another company during an inspection. It also shows how the alleged scheme fed directly into Nvidia’s supply pipeline. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly told the front company that “the only way” to get Nvidia to commit B200 chip allocations was to create monthly forecasts. Nvidia is not accused of wrongdoing in the Liaw indictment.

After Liaw’s arrest, Supermicro’s board opened its own investigation, overseen by independent director Scott Angel and former audit committee chair Tally Liu (no relation to Liang’s wife and co-founder Sara Liu). In August, Supermicro said that probe found no evidence that current senior management knew about the alleged scheme to diver the chips. The investigation resulted in an unspecified number of terminations in sales, business development, and technical support, Supermicro said at the time, for failure to follow policies or the code of conduct.

Supermicro has also disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls, along with subpoenas or inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.

Through all that has beleaguered Supermicro, the company’s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast. This will all become a test for Supermicro’s new CFO, Mark Long, a former Western Digital finance chief who took over from Weigand last month and reports to Liang. The two tag-teamed the company’s most recent earnings call, when it reported record fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.9 billion, well ahead of Wall Street consensus estimates. Supermicro also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $72 billion to $82 billion.

But now, Supermicro—and its CEO Liang—is losing an important champion in Nvidia’s Huang. Liang built much of Supermicro’s AI-era business through the close relationship with Nvidia combined with Supermicro’s almost supernatural ability to get the newest GPUs to market quickly. Liang has also maintained a public friendship with Huang that included joint keynotes in Taipei before adoring crowds.

Nvidia will now be led in the interim by Kress while an outside investigation into the foreign intelligence operation will be run by former acting SDNY U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and powerhouse law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

Nvidia is slated to report third-quarter results on November 17, with Kress in place of Huang. House lawmakers have requested a closed-door grilling with Huang the following day. In January, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is likely to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and she’ll have subpoena powers. Warren has already sought answers from Nvidia about Supermicro and chip smuggling in June and she re-upped her request this week.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5452. 10 flash flood checklist steps for your home, car and household

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Knowing how to prepare for a flash flood starts long before the rain, with 10 practical steps covering alerts, emergency kits, insurance, evacuation routes and safer driving

A flash flood leaves almost no room for improvisation. The National Weather Service defines it as rapid flooding of low-lying areas, usually within six hours of heavy rain or a similar cause. That short window means the useful decisions happen well before the storm. Once water is rising in a street or a basement, the time for gathering supplies, reading insurance terms or choosing a route has passed.

That is the core of how to prepare for a flash flood: move as much of the work as possible to a calm, dry day. A household that already knows its risk, its alerts and its exit routes can act on a warning quickly instead of scrambling under pressure.

Risk also extends beyond the obvious places. Official flood maps are a useful starting point, but flash flooding does not stay inside mapped high-risk zones. Dry creek beds and land scarred by wildfire can turn dangerous during heavy rain.

The 10 steps that follow are a practical selection of preparations, grouped into three broad stages. The first steps cover knowing your exposure and making sure an alert actually reaches you. The next ones turn to supplies and paperwork: an emergency kit and protected documents. The rest address plans that are hard to make in the moment. Those include evacuation routes, flood insurance, readying the home, driving near water and caring for relatives and pets with extra needs.

Each step stands on its own. A reader can start anywhere and work through one item at a time.

Most of the resources named here are U.S. agencies and programs. They include the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the National Weather Service, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the National Flood Insurance Program and Ready.gov, the federal government's preparedness site. Readers outside the U.S. can apply the same principles through their own national weather service and local emergency authorities. Alert systems and insurance options differ by country.

The aim is not to predict the next storm. It is to make sure that when a warning arrives, the household's next moves are already settled.

U.S. residents can look up the flood risk for a specific address through FEMA's Flood Map Service Center at msc.fema.gov. That result is a first reading, not a guarantee. Flash floods also strike places outside mapped high-risk zones.

The Flood Map Service Center is run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. A user enters a street address, and the site shows the flood map information on file for that location. The same lookup works for a current home, a rental or a property a household is considering buying.

A map is one layer of information. A home can sit outside a zone labeled high risk and still lie in the path of a flash flood. Three kinds of terrain show how that can happen.

Dry creek beds are the first. A channel that holds no water for most of the year can fill quickly during heavy rain. A house beside a dry wash or arroyo carries flash flood exposure, even when no stream is visible from the yard.

Low-water crossings are the second. These are spots where a road dips through a creek or drainage channel instead of crossing it on a raised bridge. A home reached only by such a crossing can be cut off even if the building itself stays dry.

Burn scars are the third. Land stripped of vegetation by wildfire is one of the places where flash floods can occur outside mapped zones. Residents near recently burned hillsides should count that as part of their risk.

Knowing the risk at an address shapes the rest of a household's flood planning. It helps decide where an emergency kit and important papers are stored. It also helps determine which routes out of the neighborhood make sense when water starts to rise.

FEMA's maps cover U.S. addresses only. Readers in other countries can check with their national weather service or local authorities for comparable flood risk information.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding. A flash flood warning means flash flooding is occurring or imminent, and anyone in the warned area should move to higher ground immediately.

The National Weather Service issues both alerts. The two names differ by a single word. The similarity makes them easy to mix up when a notice arrives late at night or in the middle of a heavy storm. In practice, one signals a time to get ready and the other signals a time to leave low ground.

A watch describes the setup, not the event. It tells people that the conditions for a flash flood are in place across the covered area. It does not mean water is rising yet, and it does not mean a flood will definitely happen.

That makes a watch the point to finish any preparation that would be hard to do later. Charging phones, confirming the emergency kit is where it should be and reviewing the household's route to higher ground each take minutes under a watch. The same tasks become much harder once water is moving.

A warning describes the event itself. It means flash flooding is already happening or is about to start in the warned area. The guidance at that stage is direct: move to higher ground right away. Waiting to see whether the water reaches the house uses up time that may not be available.

The two alerts also call for different questions. Under a watch, the useful question is whether the household is ready to leave quickly. Under a warning, the question is how to reach higher ground by the safest route available.

Readers outside the U.S. should check how their own national weather service labels flood alerts. Other agencies may use different terms, and those terms may not line up with the NWS watch and warning system.

A flash flood alert only helps if it reaches you. Keep Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on, keep a NOAA Weather Radio with battery backup at home and join your local government's alert system if it runs one.

Wireless Emergency Alerts are messages that authorities such as the National Weather Service send to compatible phones in an affected area. Delivery is based on where a phone is, not on a home address. A household member at work, at school or on the road can receive a warning for wherever they are at that moment. The same applies to a visitor passing through an unfamiliar town, who may have no idea which local roads tend to flood. Every phone user in the household should confirm that emergency alerts are switched on in the device settings.

Phone alerts have a weak point. They depend on cell service, and the phone depends on a charged battery. A severe storm can knock out power, cell service or both.

A NOAA Weather Radio covers that gap. A model with battery backup keeps working when the power goes out or the cell network fails. Place it where people in the household will hear it, including overnight, when phones may be silenced or out of reach. It also reaches anyone at home who does not carry a phone, such as young children or some older relatives. Check its batteries on a regular schedule so the backup is ready when it is needed.

Many local governments also run their own alert systems. These are opt-in, which means residents have to sign up to receive them. A city or county website or emergency management office is the place to find out whether one exists and how to enroll. Enrolling before storm season avoids hunting for the sign-up page while a storm is already underway.

Each channel protects against a different failure. Using all three makes it less likely that one outage leaves a household without warning.

A flood emergency kit built to Ready.gov guidance starts with water: one gallon per person per day, enough for several days. Store the finished kit above the level floodwater is likely to reach. That keeps the supplies dry and within reach.

Water takes up more space than anything else in the kit. The amount adds up quickly. A household of four needs four gallons for each day the kit is meant to cover. Plan the storage space around the water first, then fit everything else in.

Nonperishable food is the next layer. These items keep for long stretches without refrigeration. That matters if a flood knocks out power. Pick foods the household already eats and that need little or no cooking. Unfamiliar or hard-to-prepare items are harder to use when a household is under pressure.

Light and information come next. Ready.gov lists a flashlight, extra batteries and a battery-powered or hand-crank radio. A hand-crank model makes its own power when the handle is turned. It keeps working after the spare batteries run out. A radio lets a household follow updates when phones are dead or networks are down.

Health supplies belong in the same container. A first aid kit covers minor cuts and scrapes. Medications are on the Ready.gov list as well. Anyone in the household who takes a daily prescription should have a supply packed with the kit, not left in a bathroom cabinet.

Ready.gov also lists a whistle. It is small and light, and it gives someone a way to signal for help if they are stranded or trapped.

Copies of important documents round out the list. Packing a set in the kit means proof of identity and insurance leave the house with everyone else.

Where the kit sits matters as much as what is in it. A shelf on an upper floor or a high closet shelf works better than a basement or garage floor, where water tends to collect first. Keeping everything in one container that a single person can carry makes it easy to grab when it is time to leave.

A kit also needs regular upkeep. Swap in fresh batteries, rotate food and water before they go stale, and replace medications before they expire.

Seal passports, insurance policies, birth certificates and property deeds in waterproof containers, and keep digital copies somewhere you can reach from anywhere. Doing both gives a household a backup if the originals are soaked, lost or left behind.

A flash flood can leave very little time to gather paperwork. Documents sorted into one sealed container ahead of time can be picked up in seconds on the way out the door.

The papers worth protecting first are the ones that prove identity, citizenship and ownership. Passports and birth certificates establish who each household member is. Deeds document who owns a property. Insurance policies record the coverage a household has in place.

Where the container sits also matters. Floodwater rises from the ground up. An upper floor is a safer spot for a document box than a basement or a ground-level closet.

A copy of the insurance policy is useful after the water recedes. It keeps the policy number and the insurer's contact details on hand, which a household needs to start a claim.

Digital copies add a second layer of protection. Scanning or photographing each document and saving the files to a secure cloud account makes them retrievable from a phone or another computer. That access holds even if the house cannot be reached. Losing the physical box does not mean losing the record.

A portable drive is the other option for digital backups. A drive left behind in the house offers no backup if the house floods. Packed in its own waterproof container alongside the paper originals, it can leave with the household during an evacuation.

The stored set needs to stay current. When an insurance policy renews or a passport is replaced, the copy in the container and the file in the cloud should be swapped for the new version.

Keeping the document container near the household's flood emergency kit, above likely water levels, lets both be carried out in a single trip.

Choose at least two routes from your home to higher ground, and plan both so they avoid low-lying roads, underpasses and bridges over creeks. Then agree on a household meeting place and name a contact person who lives outside your area.

The second route exists for the moment the first one is cut off. Floodwater collects in the lowest ground first. The roads most likely to become impassable are the ones that dip below their surroundings, run beneath rail lines or highways, or cross a stream. A route that avoids all three gives a household a better chance of getting out before water closes the way.

Start by tracing each route on a map. Follow it from the front door to the destination and mark every point where the road drops, passes under something or crosses water. Each marked point is a spot to plan around. Two routes that share the same weak point are really one route.

A meeting place matters because a flash flood can arrive while a household is spread out, with people at work, at school or on the road. Pick a single spot on higher ground that every member can reach by at least one of the planned routes. Everyone then has the same destination, even if they cannot reach home or contact one another.

The out-of-area contact serves a different purpose. A person living outside the flooded area is less likely to be dealing with the same emergency. Each household member can check in with that one person, who can pass updates along to the others. Write the contact's number on paper as well as saving it in a phone. A paper copy still works if a phone is lost or its battery dies.

Share the routes, the meeting place and the contact with everyone in the household, including children old enough to follow the plan. Revisit the plan after a move or a change in the roads nearby.

Standard homeowners insurance policies generally do not cover flood damage. Flood coverage is a separate purchase, and a National Flood Insurance Program policy typically takes 30 days to take effect.

That waiting period is the reason to buy early. Coverage needs to be in place well before rain shows up in a forecast. Unlike an emergency kit or an evacuation route, a flood policy cannot be pulled together at the last minute. The calendar, not the weather, decides when it starts.

The first move is to read the current homeowners policy. Its terms, or a direct question to the insurer, will show whether flood damage is excluded.

The National Flood Insurance Program, known as the NFIP, is run by FEMA, the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency. It is not the only source of flood coverage. Private insurers also sell flood policies. A homeowner can compare both routes before choosing. A useful comparison looks at when each policy begins and what each one covers, not only at the price.

A flash flood can develop within hours of heavy rain. The typical NFIP wait is 30 days. A household that starts shopping for coverage after a flash flood watch is issued has already missed the window. Under the typical rule, an NFIP policy bought at that point would not cover the flood that follows.

A limited number of exceptions to the wait exist. An insurance agent or the NFIP can confirm whether any of them applies to a particular purchase.

A home's flood map designation does not change what a standard policy covers. A homeowners policy generally excludes flood damage wherever the home sits. An owner outside a high-risk zone faces the same exclusion as one inside it.

Private flood policies set their own terms, which can differ from the NFIP's. The start date printed on any flood policy shows when protection actually begins. Comparing that date with the purchase date shows whether a waiting period applies.

Find your home's main electrical panel, main water valve and gas shutoff before storm season, and move valuables and electronics to an upper floor ahead of heavy rain. Both tasks are simple on a dry day and much harder once water is coming in.

Start with the utilities. Walk through the house and note where each shutoff sits, whether that is a basement wall, a garage, a utility closet or an outside meter. Every adult in the household should know these locations. Each of them should also know how to operate every valve and switch, not just where it is. A flash flood can arrive when the person who usually handles home repairs is away.

The most important rule involves electricity. Never touch electrical equipment, including the breaker panel, appliances and extension cords, while standing in water. If the floor around the panel is already wet, leave it alone. Shutting off power is a step to take while conditions are still dry. It is not a reason to wade back inside.

Then move the things you can least afford to lose. Computers, televisions, game consoles and external drives belong on an upper floor rather than in a basement or on the ground floor. Family photographs, heirlooms, jewelry and other valuables belong there too. In a single-story home, high shelves and upper cabinets are the closest substitute. Unplug electronics before carrying them upstairs.

Outside, clear gutters, downspouts and nearby drains of leaves and debris. Blocked drainage leaves heavy rain fewer places to go, and water that cannot run off collects around the foundation. Check them again when heavy rain is in the forecast.

Sandbags are a limited measure. A row of them may help in some situations, but they do not make a house floodproof. Filling and stacking them should never take priority over leaving when officials tell residents to move to higher ground.

Never drive into a flooded road, and never steer around a barricade that blocks one. The National Weather Service sums up that rule in four words: "Turn Around, Don't Drown."

The slogan rests on how little water it takes to cause harm. The National Weather Service has said that six inches of moving water can knock an adult off their feet. The agency has also said that 12 inches of moving water can carry away a small car.

Those two figures describe two separate dangers. The first applies to anyone who leaves a stalled vehicle or tries to wade across a flooded street. The second applies to anyone who stays behind the wheel and expects the car to push through.

A foot of water is also enough to float many vehicles. A car that floats has lost its grip on the road. Its driver can no longer steer it. From that point, the current decides where the vehicle goes.

The key word in the agency's figures is "moving." A flash flood sends water across roads with force, and that force acts on anything in its path. A stretch of road that looks shallow can still push hard against a person or a car.

Barricades follow the same logic. Authorities close a flooded road because crossing it is unsafe. Driving around the barrier puts a driver into the exact conditions the closure was meant to prevent.

Walking through floodwater carries its own risk beyond the current. Floodwater can carry contaminants. That makes contact with it a health hazard as well as a drowning hazard. Anyone moving on foot should choose a path that stays out of the water entirely.

The practical step is to settle the decision before the rain starts. Agree as a household that no one drives into water covering a road, whatever its apparent depth. If a road ahead is underwater, the response is fixed in advance: stop, turn back and find another way out.

A flash flood evacuation plan must cover household members who cannot simply grab a bag and go. People who rely on medical devices, mobility aids or regular medications need their own arrangements, as do pets. Those arrangements belong in place well before a warning arrives.

Start with the people. List anyone in the home who uses equipment that runs on electricity, such as an oxygen concentrator or a powered wheelchair. Power can fail during a flood. A device that stops working turns an evacuation into a medical emergency. Ask the equipment supplier or prescribing doctor about battery backup options and how long a full charge lasts.

Mobility aids raise a different problem. A walker, cane or manual wheelchair has to travel with its owner. Someone who moves slowly also needs more lead time than the rest of the household. Decide in advance who will help that person and which vehicle has room for the equipment. Pick an exit from the home that avoids stairs or steep ground.

Regular medications call for a written record. Keep a current list of drug names, doses and prescribing doctors, along with pharmacy contact details. That list helps a shelter clinic or an unfamiliar pharmacy refill a prescription if the original bottles are lost or soaked.

Local emergency management offices are the next call. Some keep assistance registries for residents who would need help evacuating. Enrolling can alert responders in advance that a household may need help. Contact the county or city office directly to ask whether a registry exists and how to enroll.

Pets need a parallel plan. Keep a carrier for each animal that rides in one, plus leashes, several days of food and copies of vaccination records. Those records make it easier to place an animal in a shelter, kennel or boarding facility on short notice. Not every emergency shelter takes pets. Identify the ones that do ahead of time. Line up pet-friendly hotels or friends outside the flood area as backups.

The plan should also cover the trip home. Wait for local officials to give an official all-clear before bringing anyone back. Confirm that powered medical equipment will have a working outlet or a charged battery when the household returns.

#5451. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

#5450. ‘That Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago’: What Jensen Huang’s exit means for neoclouds

Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia hits the AI industry’s most indebted borrowers hardest, according to one investor who backs AI infrastructure.

Nvidia said Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. His exit follows his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, and following a board investigation into the affair. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and the board named Harvey Jones its first chair.

While Nvidia’s leadership switch-up is sending shockwaves across every industry that relies on its chips to those who simply have stock or their 401Ks resting in company, some say the companies that are most at risk are the so-called neoclouds that rely on Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia designs the chips that most AI models are trained on, and Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures them, and that’s a problem. So says Joe Kaiser, who started Switchyard Partners at the beginning of this year after serving as CEO of Mercato Partners, which managed about $1.5 billion.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius buy those chips by the hundreds of thousands, fill data centers with them and rent the computing power to AI labs and other companies, competing with Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

But Nvidia does more than sell to them. It invests in them: the company held about $329 million in Nebius shares, for example, at the end of June. Nvidia also guarantees their business. In July, Nvidia began offering to rent back unused GPU capacity from neocloud partners at a fixed rate, a floor meant to make banks more willing to lend. The company later joined a $500 billion financing platform with six institutional partners, of which Nvidia may backstop up to $125 billion. That backstop, Kaiser said, posed an issue for what lenders are pricing.

“The chip isn’t what puts them at risk, but it’s the financial backstop that allows CoreWeave or Nebius to go get those hundreds of millions of dollars of debt from Blackstone and Brookfield,” Kaiser told Fortune. “Why is Blackstone willing to back a CoreWeave project? It’s because they know that there’s an Nvidia backstop, a written backstop, behind it, and so it lowers the risk, and then obviously lowers the interest rate.”

CoreWeave carried $35 billion in debt at the end of June, and lenders had grown wary of businesses that depend wholly on AI demand, well before Huang left.

“If the capital providers now say that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Kaiser said. “At the end of the day, this is a heavy-asset, infrastructure-based industry.”

OpenAI and SoftBank’s SB Energy may be the biggest beneficiaries of Nvidia’s backstops, with CoreWeave and Nebius close behind. Kaiser referenced how Nvidia has been in talks over a reported $250 billion backstop to help OpenAI lease an Ohio data center campus that SB Energy is developing.

Following Huang’s resignation, Neocloud stocks fell Thursday: CoreWeave dropped about 9%, giving back part of a 25% rally the day before. Nebius fell 16%, though it also issued weak full-year guidance the same day. Nvidia itself lost about $450 billion in market value in the days after Huang admitted the affair, before Thursday’s drop.

Kaiser doesn’t expect Nvidia to lose its grip on AI training for at least two or three years, because customers built on its CUDA software will find it “really hard” to switch. The fight is over inference, the work of running models once they’re trained, which Kaiser said now takes up more AI compute than training. There, buyers are weighing Nvidia’s general-purpose chips against cheaper ones built for specific jobs: Qualcomm for robotics, Cerebras, Etched, Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium.

“If Nvidia no longer has Jensen as its rainmaker, did that just tip the scale towards using specialized chips?” Kaiser said.

“The bigger play is actually for the specialty chip makers,” he said, but said AMD and Broadcom will inevitably gain an opening. Google and Amazon could win twice: by pitching their own chips to labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, and by lending their balance sheets. “The Googles and others can step into that Nvidia backstop arrangement,” he said.

TSMC should come through fine, Kaiser said. He estimated about two-thirds of its capacity goes to Nvidia, but said it could shift that to other customers “in pretty short order.”

Kaiser said Huang ran Nvidia on a “hub-and-spoke” model. “The stories are true about Jensen having 60-plus direct reports,” he said, which now leaves “this leadership vacuum and vision vacuum.”

He referenced Intel after Andy Grove stepped down as CEO in 1998. “Andy Grove and Jensen both have just this iron-fist approach to management, very disciplined approach,” he said. Intel kept growing revenue after Grove left, he said, but the company lost margin and “didn’t adapt as well” as chip demand moved toward new uses.

“Intel is the roadmap here to what might be ahead for Nvidia.”

Kaiser also tied Huang’s exit to last week’s midterms, where data centers became a campaign issue. Calling Huang the industry’s “true spokesperson” for data centers, and with that spokesperson now gone, he said, the case for giant single-site data centers weakens further.

“This is just more push for distributed edge compute,” he said, “away from these mega monolithic data centers.”

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5449. Flood insurance explained: 10 things to know about the NFIP, private policies and claims

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage, and this guide explains how the NFIP, private flood policies, waiting periods, coverage limits and claims work

A burst pipe and a swollen river can leave the same water stain on a living room floor. A standard homeowners policy treats them very differently. Water that escapes suddenly from plumbing inside the house is generally covered. Water that rises from outside and pours through the front door generally is not.

That line answers a basic question: does homeowners insurance cover flood damage? For most U.S. homeowners with a standard policy, the answer is no. Flood is written into the policy as an exclusion, alongside surface water and the overflow of a body of water. Protection against rising water has to be bought separately.

Two main sources fill the gap. The National Flood Insurance Program, or NFIP, is administered by FEMA. It sells policies through participating private insurers and directly to consumers. Private insurers also write their own flood policies, with terms that differ from the federal program and from one another.

The line between a flood and other kinds of water damage has more than one edge. Water that backs up through a sewer or drain is treated as a separate risk from flood. Standard policies usually exclude it too. Covering it takes an optional endorsement.

Buying a policy is only part of the picture. Several rules shape what a flooded homeowner actually recovers. Flood insurance does not take effect the moment it is purchased. Some mortgage borrowers are required by federal law to carry it, depending on where the home sits on FEMA's flood maps. Federal flood policies cap what they pay and leave out certain parts of a home, belongings and expenses. Claims carry their own paperwork and deadlines. Federal disaster aid comes with conditions of its own and does not replace insurance.

The 10 slides that follow walk through each of these points. They start with the standard exclusion and how the federal program defines a flood. They explain which kinds of water damage a homeowners policy does pay for. They outline how the NFIP and private flood insurance work, and when sewer backup coverage applies. They close with flood zone requirements, waiting periods, coverage limits and the steps for filing a claim.

A standard homeowners insurance policy does not pay for flood damage. The HO-3 form, a widely used policy for owner-occupied single-family homes, names flood as a specific exclusion. A homeowner who wants protection from rising water has to buy a separate flood policy.

The HO-3 is often called a special form policy. It covers the house itself against any cause of loss the contract does not expressly rule out. That structure puts the weight of any water claim on the exclusions section. Flood is listed there by name.

The exclusion reaches further than the word flood alone suggests. Standard policies also rule out surface water, such as heavy rain that collects on the ground and flows into a home. They exclude the overflow of a body of water, such as a river, lake or stream that tops its banks. The standard wording used by many insurers also names waves, tides and tidal water.

That exclusion applies whether or not wind drives the water. The distinction shapes claims after hurricanes and other coastal storms. One storm can cause two kinds of damage to the same property. Wind that tears off shingles or breaks a window is generally a covered loss under the homeowners policy. Storm surge that pushes seawater into the ground floor is treated as flood and falls under the exclusion.

The standard form also contains what is known as an anti-concurrent causation clause. It says the exclusion applies regardless of any other cause that contributes to the loss at the same time or in sequence. A covered event that happens alongside flooding does not bring the flood damage itself into coverage.

The gap is not limited to the HO-3. Renters policies, known as HO-4, and condominium unit-owner policies, known as HO-6, exclude flood as well. Tenants and condo owners who want flood protection for their belongings or units need a separate policy too.

The exclusions section of an existing homeowners policy lists which kinds of water the contract leaves out. Wording can differ from one insurer to the next. The language in the policy itself decides how a water claim is handled.

The National Flood Insurance Program defines a flood as a general and temporary condition of inundation. It applies when two or more acres of normally dry land, or two or more properties, are partly or completely covered by water.

That definition is central to every flood policy the NFIP backs. It decides whether an event counts as a flood before any question of dollar amounts comes up. Water damage that falls outside it is not a flood under the program's terms.

The word "general" points to scale. A flood under this definition affects an area rather than a single room. The program sets two ways to meet that threshold. Water can cover at least two acres of land that is normally dry. Or it can reach at least two properties.

The word "temporary" matters as well. The definition describes a condition that arrives and then recedes. Land that sits underwater all the time, such as a pond, is not normally dry land. It cannot supply the acreage needed to meet the test.

Inundation can be partial or complete. A property does not need to be submerged to the roofline. Water covering part of the lot or part of the building can still count, as long as the scale test is met.

The NFIP names three causes. The first is the overflow of inland or tidal waters. Inland waters include rivers, streams and lakes that spill past their banks. Tidal waters include the ocean and connected bays. Seawater pushed ashore by a coastal storm falls into this category.

The second cause is an unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface water. This part of the definition reaches homes far from any river or coastline. A heavy downpour can qualify when it pools across a neighborhood faster than the ground and drains can absorb it.

The third cause is mudflow. The definition counts mudflow as a flood when it inundates property in the same general and temporary way.

For a homeowner with a flood policy, the definition frames the first questions in a claim. Did the water come from one of the three named causes? Did it cover at least two acres of normally dry land or reach at least two properties? A yes to both places the loss within the program's meaning of a flood.

A standard homeowners policy generally pays for water damage that is sudden and accidental and starts inside the home. A burst pipe, a leaking dishwasher and a split washing machine hose are typical examples of covered losses.

The key test is how the water arrived and how quickly. Water that escapes from a plumbing, heating or air-conditioning system usually falls within the policy. The same is generally true of water from a household appliance or a fire sprinkler system.

Coverage often extends beyond the soaked floors and drywall. Standard forms such as the HO-3 typically pay to tear out and replace part of a wall or floor to reach the source of a leak. The broken pipe or failed appliance itself is usually not covered. The policy pays for the damage the water caused, not for the part that wore out.

Frozen pipes are a winter risk with their own condition attached. Damage from a pipe that freezes and bursts is generally covered. The standard HO-3 form sets a condition for vacant, unoccupied or under-construction homes, though. In those cases, the owner must have used reasonable care to maintain heat. The alternative is to have shut off the water supply and drained the system.

Rain is treated differently depending on how it gets inside. Rain that enters through a roof or window already damaged by a covered peril, such as wind or hail, is generally covered. Rain that seeps through an aging roof or a failed window seal, with no storm damage, typically is not.

Time is the other dividing line on water claims. Policies typically exclude damage from gradual leaks and from poor maintenance. A slow drip under a sink that rots a cabinet over months usually falls outside coverage. So does damage traced to wear and tear, deterioration or a neglected repair. Mold that grows from a long-running leak is often excluded or subject to a separate limit.

The exact terms vary by insurer and by state. The policy wording decides any individual claim. Homeowners can check the declarations page and the perils section of their own policy. Those pages show which water events are listed and which are excluded.

The National Flood Insurance Program, or NFIP, is the federal program that sells flood coverage to U.S. property owners. Congress created it through the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, and FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, administers it.

Congress set up the program at a time when private flood coverage was hard to find. The NFIP gives owners in eligible areas a way to buy a separate flood policy backed by the federal government.

Most buyers never deal with FEMA directly. NFIP policies reach the public through two channels. The first is the Write Your Own program. Under it, private insurance companies sell and service flood policies under their own brand names. The federal government carries the flood risk behind those policies.

The second channel is buying a policy directly through the NFIP. FEMA sets the rates and coverage terms for program policies. The same federal rules apply whichever channel a buyer uses. Many agents who sell homeowners insurance can also write NFIP policies.

Eligibility depends on the community as well as the house. A home qualifies for an NFIP policy only if its community participates in the program. A community joins by agreeing to adopt and enforce floodplain management rules. These rules govern how and where new construction happens in high-risk areas. FEMA publishes a Community Status Book that lists participating communities.

Residents of a community that does not participate cannot buy NFIP coverage. A private flood policy is the remaining option for them.

FEMA also changed how it prices policies. Its current pricing method, called Risk Rating 2.0, took effect Oct. 1, 2021 for new policies. Existing policyholders moved to the new method at renewals starting April 1, 2022.

The older approach leaned heavily on a property's flood zone and elevation. Risk Rating 2.0 weighs more property-specific factors. These include the home's distance to a water source, the types of flooding it faces and the cost to rebuild it. Two homes in the same flood zone can receive different prices as a result.

Private insurers sell flood policies outside the National Flood Insurance Program, and some offer higher coverage limits than the federal program. Certain private policies also pay additional living expenses, a benefit the NFIP does not provide.

Additional living expenses cover applies when a flood forces a household out of its home. It is meant to pay the extra cost of living elsewhere during repairs. That can include a rental or hotel stay and meals beyond a household's normal spending. An NFIP policy pays nothing toward those costs. Not every private policy includes this benefit. Whether a given policy does is spelled out in its written terms.

Higher limits are the other main difference from the federal program. Owners of larger or more expensive homes may find that the cost to rebuild exceeds what an NFIP policy will pay. A private policy can be written for a larger amount. Some insurers also sell excess flood insurance, which sits on top of an NFIP policy and pays after the federal coverage is used up.

The tradeoff is variety. NFIP policies use standard federal wording, known as the Standard Flood Insurance Policy, whether a private company sells them or the program sells them directly. Private flood policies have no single template. Each insurer writes its own terms, exclusions and waiting periods.

As a result, two private policies with similar limits can respond differently to the same flood. One may exclude property that another covers. One may begin coverage sooner after purchase than another. A reliable comparison comes from reading the policy documents side by side, not from a marketing summary or the quoted limit alone.

Mortgage lenders add another check. A homeowner who is required to carry flood insurance can sometimes use a private policy instead of an NFIP policy. The private coverage has to meet federal standards to satisfy the lender. Confirming acceptance with the lender before buying, or before dropping an existing NFIP policy, avoids a lapse in required coverage.

Water that backs up through a sewer line or floor drain, or that collects because a sump pump fails, is usually excluded from a standard homeowners policy. Many insurers sell that protection as an optional endorsement, commonly called water backup coverage.

The exclusion applies even though the water enters from inside the house. It can surface through a basement floor drain, a toilet or a shower on the lowest level. The source is the drainage system, not a sudden break in the pipes that supply water to the home.

Backups have several common causes. A municipal sewer main can be overwhelmed during heavy rain, pushing wastewater back toward connected homes. Tree roots, grease or debris can block the private line that runs from a house to the street. A sump pump can stop working during a power outage, after a mechanical failure or in a storm that delivers more water than it can move.

An endorsement is a written change added to an existing policy. Water backup coverage attaches to the homeowners policy rather than standing alone as a separate contract. It carries an added premium.

The insurer sets the coverage limit for the endorsement. That limit is often lower than the dwelling limit on the main policy. A homeowner with a finished basement full of flooring, drywall and furniture can face a loss larger than the endorsement pays. The endorsement wording spells out which events and items it includes. Those terms differ from one insurer to the next.

Water backup coverage is not flood insurance. Flood cover addresses water that rises from outside and inundates the property, such as an overflowing river or storm surge. A backup endorsement addresses water that enters through the home's own drains and sewer connection. A house in a low-lying area can face both risks, and each requires its own coverage.

The two risks can meet in a single storm. Under a standard NFIP flood policy, sewer or drain backup is covered only when a flood in the area directly causes it. A backup without a general flood falls outside that policy. In that case, the endorsement's terms decide what gets paid.

Federal law requires flood insurance on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area when the mortgage comes from a federally regulated or insured lender. These zones carry a 1% annual chance of flooding. FEMA maps label them with codes that begin with A or V.

The requirement is tied to the loan, not only the location. A high-risk home with no mortgage falls outside the federal mandate. So does a home financed by a lender outside federal oversight. Any lender can still make flood coverage a condition of the loan.

The mandate dates to the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. That law added a mandatory purchase requirement to federal flood insurance. It applies to banks and credit unions under federal supervision. It also covers loans insured or guaranteed by government agencies such as the Federal Housing Administration and the Department of Veterans Affairs.

The zone designation comes from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Maps. A zones mark areas at risk from river, lake or shallow flooding. V zones mark coastal areas that also face wave action from storms, and they carry stricter building standards. The 1% annual chance flood is often called the 100-year flood. That label describes a yearly probability. It does not mean a flood arrives once a century, and a property can flood in back-to-back years.

Lenders check a property's designation when a loan is made, using a standard flood hazard determination form. If the borrower does not buy coverage or lets it lapse, the lender must send a notice. If the borrower still does not act, federal rules require the lender to buy a policy and charge the cost to the borrower. This is known as force-placed insurance.

Flood maps change. When FEMA issues a revised map that moves a property into a Special Flood Hazard Area, the lender can require coverage on an existing loan. Anyone can look up an address on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.

Homes outside these zones can still flood. Areas marked B, C or X $TWTR carry moderate or low mapped risk. Heavy rain, overwhelmed drainage and storm surge can still reach properties beyond mapped boundaries. Owners there are not required to carry flood insurance. They can buy it through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private insurer.

A flood insurance policy from the National Flood Insurance Program generally takes effect 30 days after purchase. A homeowner who buys cover today is not protected against a flood that arrives next week.

The rule closes off one specific approach. A homeowner cannot watch a storm forecast, buy a policy as the weather system approaches and expect the NFIP to pay for the damage. If floodwater arrives inside the 30-day window, the new policy is not yet in force.

Two dates matter on any new flood policy. One is the day the policy is bought. The other is the day cover begins. Under the standard NFIP rule, those dates sit 30 days apart. The second date decides whether a flood falls inside the policy.

The NFIP waiting period has exceptions. One applies when flood insurance is bought in connection with a loan closing. In that case, the standard 30-day wait does not hold back cover. A buyer whose lender requires flood insurance can have it in place as part of closing on the loan.

That exception is tied to the loan transaction, not to a change in the weather. A homeowner who already owns a property and decides to add flood cover ahead of a storm season generally faces the standard wait.

Private flood insurance follows different rules. Private insurers set their own waiting periods rather than using the NFIP's 30-day standard. The length can vary from one company to another. The start date appears in the policy terms, which a buyer can review before signing.

For a homeowner comparing a private policy with an NFIP policy, the waiting period belongs on the list of terms to check, next to exclusions. Both can differ by insurer. A premium quote alone does not show when protection begins.

The practical result is that flood cover has to be arranged before a threat appears, not in response to one. A policy bought during calm weather can already be in force when floodwater arrives.

A National Flood Insurance Program policy on a single-family home pays at most $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for its contents. Contents cover is a separate, optional purchase. A policy that insures only the structure pays nothing for furniture, clothing or electronics.

Building coverage applies to the house itself and the systems built into it. If rebuilding a home would cost more than $250,000, the owner carries the difference unless another policy picks it up.

Each of the two coverages carries its own limit. Owners who skip contents cover are insured for the walls and floors but not for the belongings inside them. The declarations page of a flood policy shows which coverages it carries and at what amounts.

Basements get narrower treatment than the rest of the home. The NFIP covers essential equipment there, including the furnace, the water heater and the electrical panel. Some appliances in a basement are covered as well. Most improvements that turn a basement into living space are not. Finished walls, flooring and similar upgrades below ground level generally fall outside the policy.

Several common flood losses sit outside an NFIP policy entirely. It does not pay additional living expenses. The cost of a hotel or rental while a flooded home is repaired falls to the owner. It also does not cover outdoor landscaping, such as lawns, trees and shrubs.

Vehicles are excluded too. A car damaged by floodwater falls under an auto policy instead. The comprehensive portion of that auto policy is the usual route for flood damage to a car.

One NFIP benefit reaches past repairing the damage itself. Increased Cost of Compliance coverage can pay up to $30,000 to bring a flood-damaged home in line with local building rules. Elevating the house is one use of that money. The benefit addresses a cost that can follow a major flood. Some communities require changes before a badly damaged home can be rebuilt or repaired.

A flood insurance claim starts with prompt notice to the insurer and photos of the damage taken before any cleanup begins. Under a National Flood Insurance Program policy, the policyholder generally must also submit a signed proof of loss within 60 days of the flood.

Prompt notice puts the claim on the insurer's record early. That notice goes to the insurer that issued the policy. A private flood policy follows the claim procedure written into that insurer's contract. Its deadlines and steps can differ from the federal program's.

Photographs taken before cleanup show the damage as the flood left it. Cleanup changes the scene. Waterlogged flooring gets pulled up, ruined furniture goes to the curb and walls get opened so they can dry. Once that work starts, the original condition of the home can no longer be seen directly. Pictures of each affected room and the damaged contents in it give the insurer a record to compare against the claim.

The proof of loss is a separate step from the first notice. It is a signed statement in which the policyholder sets out the amount being claimed. The NFIP clock for it runs from the date of the loss, not from the date the homeowner first contacts the insurer. FEMA has extended that deadline after some declared disasters. An extension is not automatic. A homeowner relying on one needs to confirm that it covers the specific event.

Federal disaster assistance works differently from insurance and does not replace it. FEMA aid for individuals becomes available only after a presidential disaster declaration. A flood that damages homes without prompting a declaration opens no path to that help.

Small Business Administration disaster loans are a second federal source of money after a disaster. They are loans rather than grants, and borrowers must repay them.

A flood policy is a contract the homeowner holds before the water arrives. Its payout does not depend on a declaration. FEMA individual aid does. An SBA disaster loan, by contrast, leaves the homeowner with debt.

#5447. Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

No Flock cameras in Seattle, ever. New protections against potential abuses drawn from an outside audit. A handful of cameras in new neighborhoods. Here's what the RTCC looks like from the inside. pic.twitter.com/QeYUg8ZkW3

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025, pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon said. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

“Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.
