#5446. AI industry execs brace for future without leading hype man, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Tech industry insiders awoke Thursday morning with an unfamiliar, and somewhat alarming notion to contemplate: life without Jensen Huang.

Huang’s abrupt resignation as CEO leaves one of the world’s most valuable companies without the leader who has steered it for the past 33 years; the person who almost singlehandedly transformed Nvidia from a small maker of video game graphics chips into the driving force of the AI boom.

“NVIDIA’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” Stephanie Balaouras, Forrester’s VP, group research director, told Fortune.

The importance of Nvidia, and of Huang, to the AI industry extends well beyond the company’s own P&L statement. In addition to being the leading maker of the GPU chips powering AI services like ChatGPT and Claude, Nvidia has become the AI industry’s “central bank” financing scores of other companies. And then there’s Huang’s unique standing as AI’s senior statesman and cheerleader on everything from AI regulation to industrial policy.

Whether the AI industry turns out to have lost its most famous champion with the ignominious exit of Huang and his famous black leather coat, or a more crucial, Jenga-like piece may be the most important economic question to be answered in the coming weeks and months.

“Obviously Nvidia is more than Jensen Huang, but he kind of championed a whole range of investments,” a VC investor focused on early-stage companies told Fortune.

“There is a question around whether the pace of investment in AI and the size of the amounts of capital going into companies can be continued. Because by any stretch of the imagination, it’s been quite extreme,” the investor said.

In the immediate aftermath of the news, the stock market appears to be keeping its composure. While shares of Nvidia were down 6.3% in midday trading on Thursday, and certain AI-linked stocks took a hit, the broader market reaction was relatively muted, with the Nasdaq down only 95 points.

But with spending on AI and data centers so important to the broader U.S. economy, the extent of the potential fallout from the Nvidia shakeup is difficult to overstate.

Looming largest on the horizon is Anthropic’s widely anticipated initial public offering, scheduled to occur next week. The Anthropic IPO (along with OpenAI’s IPO expected in 2027) represent make-or-break moments for the AI industry—closely watched events that will serve as proxies for the health, and momentum, of the AI business.

If nothing else, one startup founder told Fortune, the Nvidia drama raises the stakes for Anthropic’s upcoming IPO: “If the Anthropic IPO doesn’t go well and if the OpenAI IPO [down the line] doesn’t go well, there’s a question of: Is there a path to profitability for any players in the AI space?”

Antropic is seeking to raise upwards of $60 billion in the offering slated for November 18, giving the five-year old AI company a valuation that could exceed $1.4 trillion when it makes its expected Wall Street debut next week.

Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, argued that investors will recognize the strength in Anthropic’s business, regardless of the Nvidia shakeup.

“From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong and as good a position as it was before this news came out,” Alomar said.

“I’m not sure it’ll have a massive impact on them. Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need,” he said.

Anthropic’s business prospects are closely intertwined with those of the cloud providers, which provide the data centers and compute capacity to train and run AI models like Claude. (According to Anthropic’s S-1 filing, it has roughly $900 billion in compute spending commitments over the next several decades.)

While the tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have the wherewithal to ride out whatever turbulence is caused by the changes at Nvidia, the situation may be trickier for the smaller “neo-cloud” companies—many financed by Nvidia—that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the computing power.

Huang has championed these neo-cloud companies because it was good for business and the company’s influence, Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock. “He’d rather have 300 small customers who are dependent on him than three massive ones who you can’t negotiate with,” he said.

With Nvidia CFO Coleen Kress now serving as interim CEO, the company’s attitude towards neo-clouds could shift. According to a report in The Information on Thursday, Kress has occasionally pushed back against Huang’s deals in the AI ecosystem, including a deal to backstop $250 billion in credit for an OpenAI datacenter project.

The “Nvidia money train” that has kept parts of the market that propped up could come to an end, said one venture capital partner invested in numerous AI startups. “ The idea that they could count on Nvidia for future financing is unlikely.”

Shares of CoreWeave one of the leading neocloud providers were down 7.5% on Thursday, while Nebius Group, another neo-cloud company which gave a lighter-than-expected sales forecast during its quarterly earnings on Thursday, were down 18%.

Investors are likely to look harder at the numbers Huang used to justify the complex web of investments. Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, expects investors and policymakers alike may start re-examining “Jensen math.”

U.S. policy towards data centers could also come in for harsher treatment, particularly after last week’s midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly registered their opposition to having the facilities built in their communities.

Huang gave much of the industry credibility, even amid the backlash to datacenters. He was well-liked and not seen as a polarizing political figure, said Goldberg, of Seaport Research. But with Huang gone, the data center industry becomes “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” he said Goldberg.

Similarly, lawmakers advocating stricter regulation of AI technology, both the large language models as well as the chips that power the models, now have a much stronger hand. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI. But his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has destroyed his credibility on the regulatory issues.

“This guarantees new export controls,” Ed Mills, policy analyst at investment firm Raymond James, said of the spy scandal that contributed to Huang’s downfall. “It was extremely likely before the scandal and this is the accelerant to push it over the finish line.” Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are currently attached to the defense authorization bill awaiting passage on Capitol Hill.

It is also possible that Washington will enact licensing requirements or restrictions on open-source AI models. Huang had been a leading voice opposing such measures. Because the best open source models on the market have been created by Chinese AI labs, “open source equals China” in the minds of many lawmakers, particularly China hawks, Mills said. “If Washington is serious about trying to win the AI race against China we need to see regulations on open source,” he said.Brad Carson, the former Democratic Congressman who is now president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a lobby group that supports AI regulation, said he was less certain of the threat Huang’s removal as CEO poses to open source AI. Even after Huang’s downfall, such licensing requirements are unlikely given the support open-source AI has among certain factions in Congress and the technical difficulty of designing effective rules for these models, he said.

The AI policy push will happen against the backdrop of a widening investigative effort, with Nvidia’s relationship with companies such as Megaspeed and Super Micro under the microscope.

“What’s happened at Nvidia is for Nvidia to address,” said Tony Ball, CEO of Entrust, a digital security company. “But in terms of the way AI is going to continue to add value to organizations and productivity, this was an inevitable structural challenge, and governance and policy issue that the world was going to have to wrestle to the ground.”

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. #5445. Why flash floods are so deadly: 10 things to know about how fast water rises

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How fast flash floods rise and why they turn deadly so quickly, explained through 10 points on water depth, vehicles, canyons, burn scars and warnings

A flash flood can turn a dry streambed, a parking lot or a two-lane road into a fast, churning current with very little notice. That compressed timeline sits at the heart of the danger. Most river floods build over days. That gives forecasters time to issue outlooks and gives residents time to move cars, pets and belongings to higher ground. A flash flood offers no such cushion.

Understanding how fast flash floods rise and why they are so deadly comes down to several forces working at once. Intense rain can fall faster than the ground can absorb it. Steep terrain and narrow channels funnel runoff into a single path. Pavement sheds water almost immediately. Wildfire-scarred slopes can behave much the same way. Each condition shortens the gap between the first heavy rain and a fast-moving surge.

The depth of the water is only part of the threat. Moving water is heavy, and it pushes far harder than its depth suggests. A current that looks shallow from behind a windshield can knock a person down or lift a vehicle off the road. Many flood drownings involve drivers who tried to cross a flooded road that looked passable, not swimmers caught in deep water.

Geography shapes the risk as well. In arid country, a storm miles away can send a flood down a dry wash while the sky overhead stays clear. In cities, storm drains and paved surfaces can send runoff to low-lying streets faster than the drainage system can carry it away.

This slideshow walks through 10 explanations and examples of how these floods form and why they kill. It starts with the official definition and how a flash flood differs from a river flood. It then covers the depth thresholds the National Weather Service uses in its safety guidance, the physics of flowing water and the role of vehicles in flood deaths. Later slides look at canyons, cities and wildfire burn scars, along with the difference between a flash flood watch and a warning. The final slide explains how a warming atmosphere can make heavy downpours more intense.

Knowing which conditions produce a flash flood, and how little moving water it takes to become dangerous, makes it easier to recognize the moment to turn back.

A flash flood is flooding that begins quickly, generally within about six hours of heavy rain, according to the National Weather Service. The agency also counts sudden failures, such as a dam or levee giving way, as causes. That short window separates it from the slower river floods most people picture.

The defining feature is timing, not size. A flash flood can be confined to a single creek, a city street or a narrow canyon. It can also spread across a wide area. What makes it a flash flood is how little time passes between the cause and the arrival of dangerous water.

Rain is the most common trigger. A thunderstorm can stall over one spot. A line of storms can also pass repeatedly over the same ground. Either pattern can drop more water than soil and channels can absorb. The excess runs downhill and collects in streams, gullies and low-lying roads.

Structural failures work differently. When a dam or levee breaks, water that had been held back is released all at once. That can send a surge downstream even where no rain is falling. A river ice jam can do something similar when it breaks apart and releases the water pooled behind it.

A river flood follows a slower pattern. Water rises as rain from a large area, or melting snow, drains into the main channel and moves downstream. A river may crest days after the rain that caused it has stopped.

That slower pace changes how communities respond. The National Weather Service runs River Forecast Centers that model how high a river will rise. They also estimate when it will crest at specific gauges. Forecasts like these give officials time to stack sandbags, close roads and order evacuations before the water peaks.

Flash floods rarely allow that kind of preparation. The storm that creates the flood may still be overhead when the water arrives. The National Weather Service treats the two as separate hazards. It issues one set of alerts for ordinary flooding and a separate set for flash flooding.

A flash flood often gives people minutes rather than hours to get out of the way. It can turn an ordinary street or creek bed dangerous before many people recognize the threat.

The difference starts with what forecasters can see. On a large river, water from upstream rain has to travel down the channel before it reaches a town. River gauges track that rise along the way. The National Weather Service uses those readings to forecast when and how high a river will crest, often days ahead. Residents downstream get a timeline they can plan around.

A flash flood rarely offers that buffer. The rain that causes it often falls on the same small area or just upstream of it. The runoff arrives soon after. Forecasters can flag the conditions in advance. The exact creek, road or neighborhood that floods may not be clear until the water is already moving.

Timing compounds the problem. Thunderstorms that produce flash flooding can linger or repeat over one spot into the evening and overnight. A flood that arrives after dark can find people asleep, and an alert can go unheard. Darkness also makes rising water harder to notice from a house, a tent or a parked car.

Travel adds another layer of risk. A driver, camper or hiker passing through an unfamiliar area may not know which roads dip into low crossings. They may not know which creeks drain a large area upstream. They may not have heard the local forecast at all.

Rain does not have to be falling where the flood hits. Heavy rain several miles upstream can send a surge into a channel where no drops are falling. That removes the most obvious cue people rely on to judge danger.

With so short a window, the National Weather Service advises moving to higher ground as soon as flooding is threatened. Its guidance is not to wait and watch the water rise. Choosing a destination in advance, along with a route that avoids low spots, leaves less to decide once a warning arrives.

No single speed describes how fast flash flood water rises. The rate depends on rainfall intensity, the steepness and shape of the land, how wet the ground already is and the size of the area draining into a stream or channel.

For flash flooding, the pace of the rain can matter more than the storm's total. Soil can take in water only so quickly. Once rain arrives faster than that, the excess runs across the surface almost at once. A moderate rain spread across a full day may mostly soak in. The same amount falling within an hour can send much of it downhill.

The condition of the soil changes the outcome. Ground already saturated by earlier storms has little room left. Even modest rain on that ground becomes runoff. Very dry, hard-baked soil can also shed water at first. Its crusted surface resists infiltration. Bare rock, such as the sandstone common across the American Southwest, sheds most of the rain that lands on it.

Terrain controls how quickly that runoff gathers. Steep slopes move water downhill faster than gentle ones. Narrow valleys and channels squeeze the flow into a smaller space. The same volume of water then stacks up deeper than it would across an open floodplain.

The size of the drainage area — the watershed feeding a stream — sets the timing. Hydrologists use a measure called time of concentration. It describes how long runoff from the most distant point in a watershed takes to reach a given spot downstream. Small, steep watersheds have short times of concentration. Their creeks can climb sharply soon after heavy rain begins. Large river basins respond far more slowly.

Not every flash flood starts with a downpour. A dam or levee failure can push a surge downstream with almost no buildup. So can the sudden release of water held back by an ice jam or a pile of debris. In those cases the water can arrive as a moving front rather than a steady climb.

The U.S. Geological Survey runs a nationwide network of stream gauges that record water levels as they change. Those records show how a particular creek tends to behave in heavy rain. They also show that two streams hit by the same storm can respond in very different ways. One may rise gradually while the other jumps within a short window.

About six inches of moving water is enough to knock an adult off their feet, according to the National Weather Service. On most adults, that depth reaches only around the ankle or the bottom of the shin.

The danger comes from depth and motion together. Standing water at the same level mostly gets shoes wet. Flowing water pushes steadily against the feet and lower legs. A person wading through it has to lean into the current just to stay upright.

Footing is the weak point. A person stays standing because body weight presses the soles of the feet against the ground. Friction between shoe and surface keeps the feet from sliding. Moving water adds a sideways push on the legs. The submerged part of the body is also slightly buoyed. That buoyancy takes some weight off the feet. Less weight on the ground means less grip to resist the push.

The ground underneath rarely helps. Floodwater is usually brown with mud and silt. A person wading through it cannot see where they are stepping. A curb, a pothole, an open drain or a stretch of broken pavement can sit just below the surface. A single step onto an uneven or slick spot can be enough to break balance.

Once someone falls, the situation changes fast. A person lying in moving water presents far more of their body to the current than someone standing. The flow can then carry them downstream toward deeper water, storm drains, culverts or piled-up debris. Getting back up in a current is much harder than staying up in the first place.

Smaller people reach the threshold sooner. The same six inches covers a larger share of a child's leg. Children also weigh less, which leaves them less body weight holding them to the ground.

The National Weather Service builds its public safety message around this risk. Its slogan, "Turn Around, Don't Drown," applies to people on foot as much as to drivers. The guidance is to treat flowing water across a path, trail, street or low-water crossing as impassable instead of testing it.

The same logic covers everyday situations. Walking along the edge of a flooded street, fording a creek on a hiking trail and stepping off a curb into fast runoff all carry the same basic risk. Moving to higher ground and waiting removes the need to judge the water at all.

About 12 inches of moving water can float many vehicles, according to the National Weather Service. The agency's guidance adds that about two feet of rushing water can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and pickups.

Buoyancy explains why. Archimedes' principle holds that an object in water is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. A car is a large, mostly hollow shape. Its cabin, trunk and engine bay hold air, and its tires are filled with air as well. As water climbs the sides of the body, the vehicle displaces more of it, and the upward push grows.

A car does not need to float completely free to be in trouble. As buoyancy takes on part of the vehicle's weight, the tires press less firmly on the pavement. Less pressure means less grip. Steering and braking depend on that grip. A driver can lose control well before the tires leave the pavement.

Once traction is gone, the current can shove the vehicle sideways. It can slide off the roadway, drift into a ditch or a deeper channel, or tip onto its side. At that point the people inside have no way to steer out of the water.

Bigger vehicles are not exempt. A tall SUV or a full-size pickup weighs more than a compact sedan. It is also larger, so it displaces more water as the level rises. The Weather Service's two-foot guidance names SUVs and pickups explicitly. Higher ground clearance can keep the cabin dry a little longer. It does not anchor the vehicle to the road.

Water can also cause mechanical trouble. If it reaches an engine's air intake, the engine can stall. That leaves a car stranded in a rising current with no power to back out. Electrical systems that run power windows and door locks can also be affected once water gets inside.

These depths are guidance, not fixed limits. The point at which a particular vehicle floats depends on its weight, its shape and how fast the water is moving. A lighter car or a faster current can reach that point at a shallower depth.

Fast-moving floodwater hits hard because water is heavy and its push grows much faster than its speed. Fresh water weighs about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot. The force a current exerts on an object rises with the square of how fast that current is moving.

The weight is the starting point. A cubic yard holds 27 cubic feet, which puts a cubic yard of fresh water at roughly 1,685 pounds. In metric terms, one cubic meter of fresh water has a mass of about 1,000 kilograms, or one metric ton.

That mass does not sit still in a flash flood. It moves downhill through channels, streets and low-lying roads. Anything in its path has to absorb the momentum the water carries.

Speed is the larger factor. In fluid dynamics, the drag a current places on an object depends mainly on three things. They are the water's density, the area of the object facing the flow and the square of the current's velocity. The squared term is what makes speed the dominant variable.

Doubling a current's speed roughly quadruples the force it applies. Tripling the speed raises the force about ninefold. A modest rise in speed therefore produces a much larger rise in push.

Area matters as well. A narrow post in the water presents little surface to the flow. A car door or the side of a house presents a great deal. The same current delivers far more total force against a wide, flat surface than against a slim one.

Floodwater is also rarely clean water. Flash floods pick up silt, sand and gravel. That sediment makes the water denser than the 62.4-pound figure for fresh water, and denser water pushes harder at the same speed.

Debris turns the current into a battering ram. Fast flows can carry tree limbs, logs, fencing, trash bins and even vehicles. Each object strikes whatever lies downstream with the speed of the water behind it. Floodwater is usually brown and opaque. People in or near it often cannot see what is coming.

The force acts on the ground, too. Fast water scours soil and gravel from beneath pavement, bridge supports and embankments. That erosion can undermine a structure that still looks intact from above.

These relationships describe how force scales, not a fixed number for any single flood. The actual force in a given flood depends on its depth, its speed, the shape of the object in its path and the material the water is carrying. All of those vary from one channel to the next.

Vehicles sit at the center of flood fatalities. About half of flood-related drownings happen when someone drives a vehicle into hazardous floodwater, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The choice to drive in can feel routine. A flooded road often looks like a broad, shallow puddle stretched across the pavement. A driver who has crossed the same dip or low-water crossing many times may assume it is safe to cross again. In a flash flood, conditions at that crossing can change from one storm to the next, and from one minute to the next.

Depth is hard to judge from the driver's seat. Floodwater is usually brown with mud and sediment. The road surface disappears beneath it. Nothing on the surface reliably shows how deep the water is in the middle of the crossing, where the road often dips lowest. At night, headlights glare off the water and reveal even less.

The road itself may no longer be there. Fast-moving water can scour away pavement and the soil beneath it. That can leave a collapsed section or a deep hole hidden under the surface. A car that rolls onto a washed-out stretch can drop suddenly into water far deeper than the edge of the flood suggested.

Control can disappear quickly. Once the tires lose firm contact with the road, the driver can no longer steer or brake. The vehicle then goes wherever the current carries it.

The engine is another weak point. Water drawn into the air intake can stall it. The occupants are then stuck in the flow, unable to reverse out.

Escape becomes difficult once a car is in the water. Pressure from the water against the doors can make them hard to push open, and occupants may have very little time to act. Rescue crews trying to reach a stranded car must contend with the same current.

The safest decision comes before the tires touch the water. Choosing another route, or waiting for the water to recede, removes the risk behind the CDC figure.

A dry canyon or desert wash can flood under a clear sky. Rain that falls miles upstream collects in the channel and moves downstream as a surge. It can reach people who never saw a storm cloud overhead.

That disconnect makes desert drainages especially hazardous. Across the southwestern U.S., an arroyo is a creek bed that carries water only after storms. It can sit empty for months. Hard, thin desert ground absorbs little of a sudden downpour. The runoff gathers in the lowest channel available.

Slot canyons narrow the problem further. These are deep, tight passages carved into rock, sometimes only a few feet wide, with walls that rise far above a visitor's head. Water entering a slot has no floodplain to spread across. It climbs the walls instead. Smooth sandstone sides offer few ledges to scramble onto. Exits can be far apart.

Antelope Canyon in Arizona shows how that plays out. On August 12, 1997, a flash flood swept through Lower Antelope Canyon, a slot canyon on Navajo Nation land near Page, and killed 11 tourists. The rain that fed it fell upstream, away from where the group was walking.

Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon is a different landscape. It is a steep mountain river canyon rather than a desert slot, but the same mechanics applied. On July 31, 1976, a thunderstorm stalled over the upper part of the canyon and dropped roughly 12 inches of rain in about four hours. The Big Thompson River turned into a flood that killed 144 people.

U.S. Highway 34 follows the river through that canyon. Residents, campers and travelers were spread along the road and the riverbanks when the water came down. The flood struck on the eve of Colorado's centennial, during a holiday weekend.

These settings share two traits: a limited view of the sky and limited ways out. Someone standing in a narrow channel can see only a strip of sky. The storm cell feeding the drainage may sit beyond the rim, out of sight. Warning signs on the ground tend to arrive late. They include water turning muddy, floating debris or a roar from up-canyon.

The practical response follows from the terrain. Check the forecast for the whole watershed rather than only the trailhead. Inside a canyon or wash, the safer move is to climb to higher ground rather than try to outrun the water along the channel floor.

Cities and freshly burned hillsides both turn rainfall into runoff faster than natural ground does. Pavement and storm drains rush water to low points, while wildfire-scarred slopes shed rain and can unleash debris flows of mud, rock and trees.

On undeveloped land, soil and vegetation soak up part of a storm before water reaches a stream. Roofs, roads and parking lots absorb almost none of it. Nearly all the rain that lands on them flows off the surface.

Storm drains are built to move that water away quickly. That speed is the purpose of the system, but it also concentrates runoff in channels, culverts and the lowest streets. When a downpour exceeds what the pipes can carry, the excess runs across the surface instead. Underpasses, basements, sunken roads and older districts built along creeks tend to fill first.

Ellicott City, Maryland, shows how the pattern can repeat in the same place. The historic town's Main Street flooded on July 30, 2016. It flooded again on May 27, 2018, less than two years later. The downtown sits in a narrow valley where small streams run down to the Patapsco River. Water from the surrounding hills drains toward that low ground.

Burned ground behaves differently but produces a similar result. A wildfire strips away the plants, roots and leaf litter that slow water and hold soil in place. Intense heat can also leave a water-repellent layer in the soil. Rain then runs off the surface instead of sinking in.

On steep slopes, that runoff can pick up ash, loose soil, boulders and fallen trees. The resulting mixture is called a debris flow. It is far denser than floodwater alone, and it can destroy buildings in its path.

Montecito, California, experienced this in January 2018. The Thomas Fire had burned the mountains above the community the previous month. When heavy rain fell on the bare slopes, debris flows surged down creek channels and into neighborhoods. The flows killed 23 people.

The danger does not end with the first storm after a fire. Burned slopes can remain prone to fast runoff and debris flows for several years, until vegetation returns and the soil recovers. In cities, the hazard is more lasting. As more ground is paved, less of each storm can soak in, and more of it reaches the low points at the same time.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding, according to the National Weather Service. A flash flood warning means flooding is happening or about to happen. The agency also issues a third, higher alert, the flash flood emergency. It is the Weather Service's most severe flash flood alert.

The watch and the warning call for different responses. A watch is a signal to prepare. It is the time to check the forecast, learn the route to higher ground and decide where to go if conditions worsen. No flooding has to be under way for a watch to be issued.

A warning removes that margin. It tells people in the affected area that water is rising now or will be shortly. Under a warning, the Weather Service's guidance is to move to higher ground right away. Waiting to see the water before leaving can use up the time needed to get out.

The flash flood emergency is reserved for rare situations. The Weather Service uses it when a flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage is happening or expected. It is not a different kind of flood. It marks an existing warning that has reached its gravest level.

These alerts reach the public through several channels. Flash flood warnings can trigger Wireless Emergency Alerts on mobile phones inside the warned area. NOAA Weather Radio also broadcasts them around the clock.

The flash flood alerts are separate from the Weather Service's flood watches and flood warnings. Those cover flooding that develops more gradually.

Temperature affects how much rain a storm can deliver. Warmer air can hold about seven percent more water vapor for each one degree Celsius of warming. This is known as the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship.

More moisture in the atmosphere gives storms more water to release. That can raise the intensity of heavy downpours, the short, hard bursts of rain that drive flash flooding. The relationship describes the atmosphere's capacity to hold water, not the outcome of any single storm. Whether a given downpour becomes a flood still depends on where the rain falls, how long it lasts and how much the ground below can absorb.

#5444. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”

That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5443. Nvidia’s next CEO: The outside contenders to succeed Jensen Huang

The biggest guessing game in business has begun: Who can fill Jensen Huang’s shoes?

Colette Kress, chief financial officer at Nvidia since 2013, was appointed interim CEO of the company on Thursday. Kress will also continue in her CFO role as the board conducts its search for Jensen Huang’s permanent successor.

“Colette is very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told Fortune. But Simmons, who has worked in executive recruiting for almost 30 years, thinks Nvidia’s board will seek a technologist as Huang’s permanent successor, potentially from outside the company.

If Nvidia goes with an external candidate for the CEO job, Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at The Futurum Group, is putting his money on Arm CEO Rene Haas.

“He spent seven years at Nvidia and understands Jensen’s culture; and what makes him interesting is that Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs run on Arm architecture,” Boloor wrote in an X post. “So while he missed [the] rise of NVLink, Mellanox and rack-scale AI he understands [the] CPU side of Nvidia’s platform better than almost anyone else on the outside.”

Sam Sugarman, a venture capital and private equity investor who co-founded and leads the VC/PE Secondaries practice at Concordia Capital, also placed Haas on his list of external candidates.

Haas would bring a combination of Nvidia experience and public-company leadership, having steered Arm through its 2023 IPO and expanded its business beyond processor licensing. His background spans engineering, product strategy and sales. But his familiarity with Nvidia dates to an earlier era: he left in 2013. The board will have to assess whether running Arm has prepared him for Nvidia’s much larger, more complex business.

Sugarman also pointed to AMD CEO Lisa Su as a potential successor to Huang. Su (who ironically happens to be a distant cousin of Huang’s) would bring a combination of semiconductor engineering credentials and a proven record of running a major chipmaker. She has led AMD since 2014, overseeing a turnaround that made it a formidable competitor in processors and a challenger to Nvidia in AI chips. That experience could appeal to a board. But recruiting her would mean persuading a sitting CEO to leave the company she rebuilt.

Meanwhile, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told Fortune that he sees Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple; Tom Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud; and Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, “as the top three external candidates for Nvidia’s CEO role.”

Cook would bring experience with a challenge few executives have faced: succeeding a technology company’s defining leader. Cook took over from Steve Jobs and spent 15 years running Apple before becoming executive chairman in September. Cook’s mastery of supply chains and logistics would be a good fit at Nvidia, and the fact that Apple has developed its own processors in-house over the past decade means Cook has some direct experience in the chips business. His continuing work on Apple’s international relationships would also be relevant to a company navigating geopolitical pressures.

But his continuing responsibilities at Apple as chairman could complicate the prospect of recruiting him. That said, Cook has the support of one high-profile observer: President Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday that Cook should replace Huang.

Kurian would offer a connection to Nvidia’s AI infrastructure business. Before taking over Google Cloud in 2019, Kurian spent 22 years at Oracle, ultimately becoming president of product development. At Google Cloud, he has also worked closely with Nvidia through the companies’ AI infrastructure partnership. The question is how readily that experience would translate to leading the chipmaker itself.

Arora would bring the experience of a sitting public-company chief executive with a career spanning enterprise technology, global sales and investment. Before joining the cybersecurity company in 2018, Arora was president and COO of SoftBank and held senior commercial roles at Google, including chief business officer. His appeal as a candidate could depend on whether Nvidia wants a strategist who can build around its technical leaders.

There may be pros and cons for each potential candidate, but the board’s choice will ultimately determine Nvidia’s fate. “There’s such a small pool to fish in when you think about people capable of stepping into this,” Simmons said.

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.

#5442. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5441. Jensen Huang's exit has investors asking if Nvidia will keep bankrolling the AI boom

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Investors are concerned that Nvidia could scale back its financing of data centers under new leadership, which would slow the AI boom

David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Nvidia $NVDA named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO on Thursday after founder Jensen Huang resigned, and the board has begun a search for a permanent successor.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 14% in Thursday trading before paring losses and closing down about 4%. The stock is still en route to a sixth consecutive week of losses, the longest run of that kind since 2012, according to CNBC. The company will post its next earnings figures on Tuesday.

Kress will keep her CFO role while she serves as interim CEO. The board is looking at both insiders and outsiders for the permanent job. Kress said in a statement that she plans to expand on the base Huang spent 33 years laying.

Kress joined Nvidia as CFO in 2013, after finance roles at Cisco $CSCO, Microsoft $MSFT and Texas Instruments $TXN, according to CNBC. Kress has held the post for more than double the typical length of service among CFOs at S&P 500 and Fortune 500 companies, according to Bloomberg.

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC before the announcement that Huang "didn't do anything without her." Ives called Kress "a Swiss Army knife for Nvidia."

Boards frequently look to their finance chief to lead temporarily when trouble hits, according to Bloomberg. "In a time of crisis, you want to convey the message of stability and confidence, even though there's tremendous instability right now," said Cathy Logue, a managing director at executive search firm Stanton Chase, according to Bloomberg.

Huang resigned after reports of two extramarital affairs, one of which involved a businesswoman that American spy officials suspect works for China's intelligence services. Huang admitted infidelity in a note to employees on Sunday, and the board opened an independent investigation the same day. He also left the board, effective immediately.

The board named Harvey C. Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys $SNPS, as its first chair. "We expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said in a statement.

Investors are concerned that Nvidia could scale back its financing of data centers under new leadership, which would slow the AI boom, according to Reuters. In its latest earnings report, Nvidia disclosed $164.5 billion in financial commitments.

Shares of CoreWeave and Naver, both Nvidia customers, fell 6% or more, while shares of Broadcom $AVGO and AMD $AMD rose.

#5440. Tech Moves: Wizards of the Coasts names president; new execs at Skydance, Pulumi, Marchex and Syndio

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:24 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:04 am

— Dan Ayoub, the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games. Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said. “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”

Earlier in his career, Ayoub spent more than a decade at Microsoft, primarily with its 343 Industries video game studio, now called Halo Studios.

— Farah Ali has joined the media company Skydance as vice president of engineering, based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. She previously spent a decade at Electronic Arts over two stints, most recently as vice president of AI transformation and technology.

Ali has also served as an affiliate professor at the University of Washington, teaching courses in software entrepreneurship, and as a technical advisor for Madrona Venture Labs. She was co-founder and chief technology officer of FreightWeb, a Seattle-based logistics technology startup.

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth.

— Irene Chang has joined Pulumi as chief revenue officer. The Seattle startup automates cloud infrastructure tasks such as managing networks and databases, optimizing costs and ensuring compliance.

Chang said Pulumi’s culture and product won her over. “We automate deployments so teams can provision resources in seconds and scale from simple apps to enterprise architectures without losing control or compliance,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

Kroll joined the company in 2015 as CTO, chief operating officer and chief information officer. She took over as CEO in 2022 after founder Dan Price resigned while facing assault and reckless driving charges. That case and a second were dropped, and Price maintained his innocence.

#5439. Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune. His father was a U.S. Army Colonel and church-goer, who then became a vice president at the Walt Disney World Company. Jones himself is a billionaire, which Forbes says is “almost entirely due to his Nvidia director’s compensation” and the fact that he owns 0.03% of the company.

“Harvey has a deep sense of history,” Chris Rowen, who cofounded the semiconductor processor company Tensilica with Jones in 1997, tells Fortune. He has a house on Nantucket and enjoys sailing classic yachts and fine art. “He has a smooth polish,” Rowen said. But Rowen also said that, despite outward appearances, there’s nothing effete about Jones. “He is such a gentleman, so articulate, and so well-sanded on the outside that you might worry there isn’t a deep fierceness and technical insight inside, but beneath that smooth exterior is a really bright, insightful, aggressive guy.”

At a time of great turbulence, Jones can offer Nvidia a “steady pair of hands” to “sort out” its next chapter, Herscher said. She described him as a “charming elder statesman” who at this point in his career is likely “very hard to ruffle.”

Jones and Rowen played distinct roles while leading the team at Tensilica. While Rowen played the role of technical leader and mentor, Jones was a skilled manager who helped keep the team on track. “His experience was such that he exuded this confidence and experience,” Rowan said. “If he thought we were on the right track, people were instantly comforted. He really communicated a sense of the larger picture and gave people a great deal of confidence that the wider world needed and approved of what we were doing.”

“He’s very strategic,” Herscher said. “I’m sure he’s right now figuring out the right strategy and steps going forward. He’s always looking around corners.”

Jones’ experience and board tenure also begs the question of how he failed to identify the enormous reputational risk of Huang’s affairs, three of which are known as of this writing. Huang also notoriously had many reports, up to 60 at one point, and no clear successor or succession planning.

“Jones may be the right person to steady the ship, but his longevity is both his greatest qualification and the strongest reason to scrutinize his leadership,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult tells Fortune. “The board cannot simply present itself as the solution without examining its role in creating the problem.”

Case in point: Huang’s affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was known inside the company, and appears to violate its code of conduct, The New York Times reported. The code of conduct instructs all employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.” The board promises to promptly investigate all reports of misconduct. What happened?

Jones will likely lead the process to select Nvidia’s next CEO, Herscher said, though she had not spoken to him about it directly, and Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. But that’s typically how the process would work in a situation like this, Herscher said, drawing on her knowledge from sitting on three public boards, and being the co-founder of The Chairs Circle, which runs educational programs for board chairs.  The fact that Jones also sits on Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee makes it even more likely that he will lead this process, she said, as usually that committee is involved in the process.

The search will likely take at least a few months, Herscher said. The board will likely hire a recruiter to identify candidates—something Bloomberg reported this week that Nvidia has already done. That firm will likely do the first outreach, Herscher said, and then Jones will speak to the most promising candidates, along with the rest of the internal search committee.

All signs point to Jones being an effective recruiter, with a wide net of contacts in the industry, Herscher said.

Longtime technology executive Chi-Foo Chan described Jones as “a very persuasive guy” in a 2019 oral history interview with the Computer History Museum, referring to the conversations the two had when Jones convinced Chan to join Synopsys, the electronics company Jones led from 1987 to 1998.

Nvidia shareholders are hoping those skills can wrangle a big fish to come in as Nvidia’s next CEO. Potential successors may include Rene Hass, who is currently the CEO of the chipmaker Arm.  President Trump, who allegedly did not act on reports of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook might be a good pick.

Whoever it is, they’ll need the right operational and product development chops to keep the GPUs flowing.

#5438. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5437. ‘A dark day’: Jensen Huang’s sex drive threatens to pop the AI bubble, and the industry isn’t sure what’s next

Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Beatrice Nolan. In today’s issue:

Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco.

We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase, and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research.

Plus, we’ve got Nick Fox from Google. We’ve got Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao. We’ve got Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, Vanta’s Christina Cacioppo, Unconventional AI’s Naveen Rao, Brex’s Pedro Franceschi, Maven Clinic’s Kate Ryder, Box’s Aaron Levie, Atlassian’s Mike Cannon-Brookes, New Work Foundation’s Clara Shih, Twilio’s Khozema Shipchandler, Rubrik’s Bipul Sinha, Harvey’s Winston Weinberg, Dynamic Creatures’ Marc Theermann, SendCutSend’s Jim Belosic, Apptronik’s Jeff Cardenas, Accenture Song’s Ndidiamaka Oteh, and Senra Systems’ Jordan Black. It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on December 7th and 8th. You can apply to attend here.

Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO may be the biggest story in AI we’ve seen since the launch of ChatGPT almost exactly four years ago. Not only because it’s a stunning, swift downfall, but also because it’s the end of the first major phase of AI development as we’ve known it. At Fortune, we’ve been following the story closely over the past two days. You can check out our coverage by following the links in the “Fortune on AI” section of this newsletter.

It turns out, one man might just be able to single-handedly pop the AI bubble by not keeping it in his pants, with not one but three affairs—at least that we know about so far. But in all seriousness, this is a sad story. It’s a visceral betrayal for Huang’s family, his wife of 41 years, Lori, and their two children, both of whom work at Nvidia.

Huang has disappointed just about everybody in his orbit, from shareholders to customers, to people who held him up as a role model. Martin Casado, an investor at the prominent firm a16z called today a “dark, dark day,” and a “horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world.”

“It’s very sad by every dimension,” Penny Herscher, a longtime executive in the semiconductor industry, told me today. “It’s sad for his family, for the employees, for the customers. Jensen’s a remarkable person, and it’s sad to see such a remarkable person in this horrible situation—self-inflicted, but horrible.”

“I am extremely sad today as I see Nvidia without Jensen Huang,” one Nvidia employee posted. Several others have made similar public remarks.

My hunch is Nvidia will prevail, given the immense amount of money and geopolitical stability hanging on the health of its GPU business. But there will likely be a period of uncertainty, both in the boardroom and in Washington. America’s position at the top of the AI industry hangs in the balance, and stricter regulation may be more likely, especially given the Democratic Party’s sweeping midterms wins. As Jeremy Kahn wrote in Tuesday’s edition of Eye on AI, Huang had been a leading voice opposing both U.S. export controls on AI technology and government regulations on open models, and now that community has lost their main champion.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!” posted Clement Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, the open source repository Nvidia acquired for nearly $13 billion in September. “But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!”

There is much more to the story yet to unfold. Huang has agreed to appear before Congress. More investigations are likely to ensue. Meanwhile, rumors are swirling that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei may have orchestrated Huang’s downfall. Amodei has warned that open models can serve as uncontrolled weapons that bad actors can harness to incur serious societal harm, and is in favor of industry-wide slowdowns. I’m not quick to believe that theory, mostly because there is not yet any proof, but also Anthropic had every incentive to wait until after its IPO if it was going to take down Huang. The dark cloud his ousting has cast over the AI industry threatens Anthropic’s valuation as investors enter arguably the greatest period of instability we’ve seen yet in AI.

“My expectation is a 10–15% valuation haircut, potentially approaching 20% if Nvidia’s leadership crisis raises doubts about its $10 billion anchor commitment,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult, tells Fortune. “Anthropic’s underlying business hasn’t changed overnight, but investor confidence has. I expect the anchor to hold, but investors will demand a greater margin of safety. The larger question is whether this marks the beginning of a broader repricing of AI risk.”

The big unknown is how the stock market will react. Nvidia shares are trading down 4% at the bell today, a modest dip.

As far as silver linings go, there will be a few winners to come out of Huang’s downfall. Nervous Nvidia customers could place bigger orders with other chipmakers, such as Google, Amazon, AMD, and Broadcom. Another winner could be Nvidia’s next CEO, who stands to score the role of a lifetime, and perhaps propel the company into a new and even more successful era. That search is already underway. But given the allegations against Huang at this time, particularly that he may be complicit in funneling chips to China via Megaspeed, the shell company helmed by his paramour Alice Huang—there could always be more executives involved.

The biggest story in AI since ChatGPT is far from over.

Emily Forliniemily.forlini@fortune.com@emilyforlini

#5436. ‘I Just Cannot Get Ahead’: Why Americans Are Under Extreme Financial Pressure, According to a New Report

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

One 73-year-old borrower described owing nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards.

Why does getting ahead feel so out of reach? A new analysis from the Urban Institute offers a look at the financial strain Americans are facing.

The report, which drew from U.S. Census Bureau data, revealed that 23.5% of Americans with a credit history have debt in collections. They owe a median amount of $2,913.

As grocery bills and other essentials take a bigger toll on household budgets, some Americans are relying on credit cards to bridge the gap. However, steep interest charges can turn that short-term relief into debt that is difficult to pay off, even for borrowers who are making payments.

Susan Cannon described that cycle to Business Insider earlier this year. The 73-year-old owes nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards, with interest rates ranging from roughly 12% to 35%. She lives in a mobile home in rural Texas. Despite paying more than the minimum balance on her credit cards, she struggles to reduce her balances while continuing to charge necessities such as groceries and gas to her credit cards.

“I can’t get the balance down because I am still having to use credit cards at the end of the month to get groceries and gas,” Cannon told the publication. “I pay my bills, but because of the interest rates, it keeps going up — I feel like I’m being gouged.”

Despite Cannon’s best attempts to build a savings account, her monthly payments are all going towards interest payments on her credit cards.

“I just cannot get ahead,” Cannon told Business Insider.

Where Americans live can make a noticeable difference in how heavily overdue their bills are. For example, in rural Jim Hogg County in South Texas, more than half of residents with a credit history have debt in collections, according to the report. Nationwide, the share is 23.5%, making the county’s rate more than twice the national figure.

How quickly an unpaid bill reaches collections depends on the type of debt. Credit card accounts typically enter collections four to six months after a missed payment, while unpaid medical bills generally take three to six months. The balances also differ: The analysis put the median delinquent credit card debt at $680, compared with $1,492 for medical debt.

Student loans follow a different path, with the rules varying between federal and private lenders. Federal loans generally fall into default after 270 days without payment. Borrowers can then pursue options such as loan rehabilitation to resolve the default and restore their loans to good standing.

The New York Federal Reserve determined that Americans collectively owe $18.8 trillion in debt as of the second quarter of the year.
