#5420. From Working the Drive-Thru at Wendy’s to Becoming the CEO of EBONY — Eden Bridgeman Shares the Lessons That Built Her Leadership Style

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

EBONY CEO Eden Bridgeman explains how her franchise background and her father’s leadership lessons are helping her take an 80-year-old cultural institution into the future of media.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

Following the event, Bridgeman shared her thoughts on leadership that serves your team, finding success in the attention economy and defining power that truly makes an impact.

As a teenager, you worked at Wendy’s and Chili’s. What is one specific habit or rule from those shifts that you still use as a CEO? One thing I learned very early is that the customer experiences the whole business, not your department. If something was wrong with an order, the customer did not care whether the mistake happened at the register, in the kitchen, or somewhere else. They simply knew the experience did not meet their expectations. Working in restaurants teaches you very quickly that everyone has some responsibility for the final outcome. Restaurants also taught me the importance of staying close to the business. You learn things from the front line that you cannot always see in a report.

You were CMO of a restaurant franchise operator, and then took over an 80-year old media brand. What surprised you most about the media business? Honestly, how many businesses exist inside of the media business. Coming from restaurants, there were certainly complexities, but the economic model was relatively clear. Media has a very different ecosystem. You have the audience consuming the product, advertisers funding parts of the business, platforms influencing distribution, creators and talent shaping relevance, technology affecting discovery, and increasingly commerce and experiences creating additional revenue opportunities. All of those constituencies matter, but they do not always want the same thing.

That requires a different kind of discipline. One of the biggest lessons for me has been that attention and revenue are not the same thing. A piece of content can perform extremely well culturally and still not create meaningful business value unless you have built the right infrastructure around that attention.

What practices from the restaurant world do you think can apply to success in media? There are actually quite a few. The first is frequency. Restaurants understand that growth is not just about convincing somebody to visit once. The second is consistency. In restaurants, brand standards exist because people expect a certain experience every time they walk through the door. Media brands need that same clarity. And then there is measurement. Restaurant businesses are incredibly disciplined about understanding performance at a granular level. You know what is selling, when it is selling and where there are operational problems. I bring that mindset to EBONY because I believe creativity becomes more powerful when you understand its impact.

Your father bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020. When you took over in 2021, what were the first things you fixed or rebuilt? I tend to be careful with the word “fixed,” because it can suggest that everything before you was wrong. That is not how I view EBONY. We inherited an extraordinary brand with generations of cultural equity, but the business around that brand had to operate in a fundamentally different media environment. So much of my focus has been on rebuilding the infrastructure necessary for EBONY to compete as a modern media company. That means strengthening how we operate, how we sell, how we develop partnerships, how we think about content and distribution, and how we measure whether the work is producing the outcomes we intended.

But there was also a more philosophical question that had to be answered: What does it mean to modernize EBONY without disconnecting it from what made it important in the first place? There are generations of people who have a personal relationship with this brand. Then there is a younger generation whose relationship with media, culture and identity is completely different. My responsibility is not to choose between those audiences. It is to understand the fundamental truth that made EBONY matter historically and translate that truth into products, experiences and storytelling that feel relevant now. Legacy gives you permission to enter the conversation. Relevance determines whether people continue listening.

Are there any leadership lessons or words of encouragement from your father that you think about regularly? I would describe it less as one particular quote and more as a leadership philosophy I learned from my father: the inverted pyramid.

The idea is that leadership is not about positioning yourself at the top with everyone working up toward you. You turn the pyramid upside down. As a leader, your responsibility is to support the people doing the work and make sure they have what they need to be successful.

That has stayed with me because it changes the way you think about leadership. A title may give you authority, but leadership is really about service, accountability and creating the conditions for other people to succeed.

As CEO, I try to remember that my role is not to have every answer or to be the center of every decision. My responsibility is to provide clarity around where we are going, remove obstacles where I can, make the difficult decisions when necessary, and give the team the support and accountability they need to do their best work.

I think that philosophy takes on another layer at EBONY. There is a responsibility to the people working to move the business forward, but also to the audience and community that have trusted this brand for generations.

The higher you move in an organization, the more people you are responsible for serving, not the more people who are responsible for serving you.

My father led humbly, as a servant leader, and that is the lesson from him I carry most directly into how I try to lead today.

Where do you think are the biggest opportunities for EBONY and other legacy media brands in today’s media landscape? I think the biggest opportunity is to stop defining a media company primarily by the content it publishes. Content will always be essential, but it can extend into original intellectual property, experiences, commerce, recommendations, partnerships and new forms of distribution. It can create opportunities for brands that want genuine cultural credibility. And it gives us the ability to convene communities both digitally and physically.

I also believe there is significant opportunity in understanding audiences more deeply. Our history is an enormous competitive advantage, but history cannot become an excuse for standing still. Younger consumers are not obligated to love EBONY because their parents or grandparents did. We have to earn their relationship with the brand on their terms.

If we can combine the trust and cultural authority built over generations with the technology, formats, distribution and business models available today, I think the opportunity is much larger than traditional publishing.

The Power 100 honorees range from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator. How do you define “power”?

I think power has become much more distributed. Traditionally, we tended to associate power with institutions: the person running the company, controlling capital, holding political office or deciding who gained access. Those forms of power still matter enormously. But technology and social platforms have created entirely different ways for people to build influence.

A young person can create something from their bedroom and develop an audience larger than many traditional media outlets. A creator can introduce millions of people to an idea, product or cause almost instantly. An entrepreneur can build a community without first receiving permission from a traditional gatekeeper.

That changes the way we should think about power. For EBONY, I think power is ultimately about the ability to create meaningful impact. Can you shift a conversation? Can you open a door that was previously closed? Can you build something that creates opportunity for other people? Can you influence how people see themselves or what they believe is possible? When I think about power today, I am interested not only in who has it, but what they are doing with it.

Eden Bridgeman began her working life with shifts at Wendy’s and Chili’s—jobs that taught her key lessons on a career path that put her in the driver’s seat of one of the most iconic brands in media history.

Bridgeman went on from working behind the counter to becoming the CMO of Manna, Inc., a restaurant franchise operator. And in 2021, after her father, the late Ulysses “Junior” Bridgeman, bought EBONY and JET at a bankruptcy auction in 2020, she took the reins of EBONY.

This fall, EBONY unveiled its 2026 Power 100 list, a class that stretches from Jay-Z and Byron Allen to iShowSpeed and a STEM kid creator, all celebrated at a gala at the Hollywood Palladium under the theme “The Stories We Shape.” One of the categories, the Junior Bridgeman Business Vanguard, is named in her father’s honor.

#5419. ‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am

Editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter. The company was not involved in this story.

Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

“So you want an internship this summer?” he asked Miya McClain, as she remembers it.

She was Miya Sneed then, 18 and homesick at Mills College in Oakland, Calif. She had come home to speak for Technology Access Foundation, the Seattle nonprofit where she had gone from knowing nothing about computers to building software and leading a team of student interns. Earlier in the luncheon program, she had shown the crowd a scheduling system she built for TAF.

Microsoft had planned the offer in advance and already had her resume, but she had no idea what was coming. A Seattle Times photographer caught the look of shock on her face, and the photo ran the next day on the front of the newspaper’s business section.

That internship, the first of two, led to a full-time job at Microsoft after college. She spent eight years there before moving into product leadership roles at Nordstrom, Cisco and Smartsheet. Today McClain is senior vice president of product management at SumerSports, a sports analytics company.

“Most of my jobs came through connections with TAF,” she said, crediting the organization for repeatedly “opening doors I didn’t even know could be opened.”

That’s the path Trish Millines Dziko had in mind when she left Microsoft 30 years ago to start TAF with her partner, Jill Hull Dziko: teach kids of color to work with technology, and get them hired by tech companies.

But about eight years in, she saw a problem. TAF’s interns were thriving, she said, but many couldn’t get into college computer science or engineering courses because their high schools had already steered them into lower-level math and science.

To change that, TAF would need to reach students by sixth grade, inside the schools.

So TAF went into public education. The organization, which marked its 30th anniversary Oct. 1, now co-manages a public middle and high school in Federal Way, Wash., and coaches teachers in other public schools.

“No matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills. They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

Executive director, Technology Access Foundation

Working with entire schools, rather than kids who signed up for a tech program, changed the goal, too. The focus now is on skills students can use in any field, whether or not it’s tech.

Students learn science, technology, engineering and math through projects that combine subjects and put classroom lessons to use. In 2020, for example, two students at TAF’s Federal Way school turned a gardening robot into a model 3D printer using a cake-frosting syringe, a threaded rod and a motor, as GeekWire reported at the time.

“What we want to make sure is, no matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills,” Millines Dziko said. “They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

The shift has cost TAF money. The organization has missed out on larger funding opportunities, Millines Dziko said, because it isn’t focused solely on tech and isn’t growing as fast as some funders would like. In the early 2010s, as education philanthropy flowed to charter schools, TAF couldn’t raise enough to open the additional schools it had planned.

“But we stuck with what was true, and what works for our kids,” she said, “and we’re still here.”

Millines Dziko grew up in New Jersey, raised by a single mother who cleaned floors for a living. She told the Seattle P-I in 1995 that she believed she’d been placed in a lower-level math class because of her race. She took summer-school classes to work her way into honors.

She studied computer science at Monmouth College on a basketball scholarship and began working at Microsoft in 1988 as the first tester on SQL Server. “She was always a force to be reckoned with,” said Bob Muglia, the longtime Microsoft executive who hired her, speaking with GeekWire at the organization’s 30th anniversary party in October. His foundation now supports TAF.

She later moved into a diversity role and took over Microsoft’s high school internship program, making it technical and filling it almost entirely with Seattle kids of color. When she pushed the company to reach students earlier, she said, “the attitude was, it’s not broken, so let’s not fix it.”

Then her partner, Jill Hull Dziko, a social worker in Seattle Public Schools’ behavior-disorder classrooms, brought seven or eight middle schoolers to campus. They were rowdy on the shuttle ride over and went silent when they walked into a room of high school interns testing a new handheld computer.

On the way back, Millines Dziko recalled, they were saying, “I want to be an engineer. I want to do what they did.”

She left Microsoft in August 1996 and put $150,000 of her own money into TAF. If she didn’t help others, she told the P-I the next year, her late mother “would want me to have my butt kicked.”

TAF set up in a Columbia City storefront next to a Taco del Mar. When they first opened the door, she said, they could see the basement through the subfloor, and the staff wired the network themselves. The first students started after-school classes in 1997, training for paid summer internships.

McClain joined the second class as she entered ninth grade, along with her older sister. Millines Dziko taught them to take apart a computer and write their first programs. “She’s encouraging, but she’s also very strict,” McClain said. “We all got jobs that summer, so obviously she taught us something.”

In 2000, TAF started a program for younger students called TechStart. At the anniversary party in October, Sherry Williams, TAF’s executive director of operations, who joined in 1997 as its fourth employee, told the crowd about a young girl who was afraid of math. The girl’s mother brought her every afternoon, and the girl kept working at it.

One day she walked in wearing a T-shirt that said “I love math.”

“Although her school wasn’t serving her, in our after-school program, she was being served,” Williams said. “And she knew she could do anything after that.”

TAF opened a public school, TAF Academy, with Federal Way Public Schools in 2008. Mike Miles, one of its first ninth-graders, went reluctantly. The school looked way too small, he told the Federal Way Mirror the following year. “I didn’t want to have six kids in my class, but my parents made me go anyway.”

He was ahead in math, and the new school couldn’t offer the class he needed, so he spent his first year in the back of the room teaching himself from a textbook.

The next year, TAF arranged for him to take math at another public school down the street. Looking back as a parent, he said in a recent interview, he appreciates that the school was willing to “swallow your pride a little” and acknowledge that it couldn’t give him what he needed. He got the math education there, and where he is today, he said, is “better than what I ever could have expected.”

Miles, now 32, graduated in 2012 with TAF Academy’s first class, earned a business degree at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and leads data teams at a cybersecurity startup in the Washington, D.C., area.

He remembers sitting in a circle in social studies, discussing the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed Black teenager in Florida, and learning to keep disagreements from turning into “a shouting match,” a skill he relies on in his work now.

Federal Way wasn’t the original plan. TAF spent two years designing a school for Seattle Public Schools, and in 2006 it proposed one for Rainier Beach High School, first as a replacement for the school and then as an academy inside the building.

Many students and teachers saw it as a takeover. Teachers worried the academy would drain resources from the existing school, and families objected that the district had discussed the proposal for a year without telling them. At a packed community meeting that November, there was shouting, and the PTSA president walked out with dozens of students, The Seattle Times reported.

“It was just the dumbest and the most frustrating thing I had ever been through,” Millines Dziko said in a recent interview. “I said we’re done, no more.”

Federal Way Superintendent Tom Murphy read about it, called her and came up to Seattle to meet. After a couple of hours, she said, he told her, “You belong in Federal Way.” TAF is now working with its fifth superintendent there, she said.

The lowest point, she said, came around 2012, when TAF had to lay off staff for the second time. Education philanthropy was pouring into charter schools, a planned expansion into Renton had stalled for lack of money, she said, and TAF had just moved into a new building.

She recalled seeing reports that only a small share of major philanthropic funding went to nonprofits led by people of color, and she started asking herself a question. “Is me being a leader of this organization gonna hold us back from getting funding? Would it be better if we had someone who was white to lead the organization?”

She talked it over with Williams and Zithri Saleem, two of her top leaders, and “we almost went down that road,” she said. But she reconsidered. “That’s not the answer either,” she said. Instead, TAF had to “get out there and show them,” and find other people interested in its work.

Seattle came back around after Denise Juneau became superintendent. In 2020, the school board approved a TAF partnership at Washington Middle School in the Central District. Three years later, facing a budget shortfall, the district cut it, as GeekWire reported at the time. “It’s solely about money,” Millines Dziko told The Seattle Times then.

Asked whether she could see herself working with Seattle Public Schools again, she said, “No.” The district has “way too many problems,” she said, and dealing with them “takes our energy away from places where we could be having impact.”

In 2024, TAF was among the nonprofits chosen in MacKenzie Scott’s open call, after a process that included peer review. TAF expected $1 million and got $2 million. “It wasn’t the money; it was the belief in our work,” Millines Dziko said.

TAF used $500,000 for operating needs it had been saving for and put the rest in a certificate of deposit, she said.

TAF reported about $4 million in revenue and $5 million in expenses in its Form 990 for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025, and ended the year with about $11.4 million in net assets. Millines Dziko said the organization’s annual budget is now close to $7 million, and its fundraising team raises about 93% of it, mostly through grants.

TAF Academy had been recognized for test-score gains. It was named a School of Distinction in 2012 for improvement in middle-school reading and math. In 2016, the district cited three consecutive years of recognition as one reason for merging it with Saghalie Middle School. The combined school, TAF@Saghalie, opened in 2017, and TAF co-manages it with the district.

TAF@Saghalie’s four-year graduation rate for the class of 2025 was above 88.5%, compared with 82.6% statewide, according to state data. On state tests in 2024-25, 17% of the school’s low-income students who took the tests in grades 6–8 and 10 met the English language arts standard and 11% met the math standard, compared with 30% and 15% for low-income students in the same grades across Federal Way Public Schools.

Millines Dziko argues that standardized tests don’t measure what matters. They assume every student had a teacher who covered everything on the exam, she said, and “they demean kids,” charting their academic course as early as third grade.

TAF trains teachers to track each student’s growth and is building its own way to document it. Teachers score students from 1 to 4 against standards, backed by photos of projects and samples of student work. The data lives in the modern version of SQL Server, the Microsoft database Millines Dziko was hired to test in 1988.

The system is in the third year of a pilot. Only selected teachers are participating, and TAF is still working out how much time teachers can spend documenting students’ work while teaching, she said. TAF is bringing in an evaluator from the University of Washington Bothell to review the pilot, she said.

Millines Dziko’s goal is for every district in the country to use it, and for standardized tests to “go out the window,” with the money states spend on them going to teacher training instead. “I believe it will,” she said.

Miles liked the project-based learning but said he found gaps in his preparation when he got to college. “I took physics at TAF Academy, took physics in college, and I was not prepared,” he said. What he got in return, he said, was “a different way of thinking.”

TAF looked like a program for teaching technical skills, he said, but “they taught kids how to be people.” He tries to pass that on to his son, he said, including putting others first and using his gifts to help others.

TransformED, TAF’s teacher-coaching program, places a full-time coach in a partner school for five years. It works with five schools now and plans to add 10 more over five years, at about $200,000 per school per year, Millines Dziko said. In September, TAF hired a former Atlanta principal, Donya Loyd Kemp, to lead it, as GeekWire reported.

Millines Dziko is wary of the rush to bring AI into classrooms. Students can use it to find sources, she said, but then they have to investigate those sources themselves. “It should be used as a tool to gather quickly, so I can now use most of my time doing the thinking.”

Millines Dziko said the region’s tech companies should invest in public schools as a way to attract and keep families here, not just with donated products and the occasional volunteer day. “That’s performative,” she said.

What she wants are lasting relationships, like the ones TAF has with smaller companies that come back to its schools every year to give students real problems to solve. As for the big tech companies, “I need them to be more about pouring into instead of extracting out of,” she said.

Millines Dziko turns 70 in July. For the past year and a half, she said, Williams and Joshua Halsey, TAF’s executive director of education, have taken on more of the leadership, freeing her to spend more time raising money and building relationships.

She doesn’t expect to stop working, she said, predicting that she’ll never retire.

At the 30th anniversary party, she hugged about three-quarters of the room, by her count. Looking around at her former students, many with kids of their own, it hit her.

“This is 30 years, man, and look at y’all,” she said, recalling the moment later. “Y’all are good.”

#5418. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5417. Crypto Slump Could Be Far From Over, Barclays Analyst Warns

Another sell-off could be on the way for crypto after a leading strategist at Barclays warned that the recent U.S. stock market rally may not last.

There are more signs of trouble in the cryptocurrency market, with a leading strategist at Barclays warning that the recent rebound in U.S. stocks may not last.

Alexander Altmann, the global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, is now somewhat skeptical of the strength of the stock market rebound after the brutal sell-off that has also dragged cryptocurrencies lower.

He lists factors such as negative market breadth, mediocre growth stock performance, a modest rebound in neocloud stocks, the ongoing crypto slump, and a flat quality factor.

The concerns from Altmann come amid increasing worries that the AI investment frenzy that has been a key driver of U.S. equity market performance may not be sustainable.

Barclays strategist was one of the few Wall Street experts who questioned whether the U.S. midterm elections would bring lasting benefits to stocks.

Barclays has flagged the risk that investment strategies sensitive to volatility could help worsen the market decline.

According to Barclays models cited in Bloomberg’s report, volatility-control funds may be at risk of dumping as much as $135 billion of U.S. equity futures in the 24 to 48 hours following Thursday’s market mayhem.

On the Oct. 29 episode of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast, Altmann also argued that investors are in a “denial phase” concerning the risks to the AI sector.

He pointed to growing financing pressure on neocloud companies that host computing resources for AI applications as a sign of early stress in the industry.

#5416. 3 Ways Businesses Can Create Lasting Value Across Borders

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From building relationships to adapting to local markets, lasting growth depends on more than simply expanding a company’s reach.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.

Yet Asia is not a single market. Doing business in Singapore is very different from doing business in Vietnam, Indonesia or Japan. Each has its own expectations, regulations and ways of building relationships.

I believe this diversity is precisely what makes Asia such an interesting place from which to learn. For entrepreneurs looking to expand internationally, three lessons stand out.

In many parts of Asia, business relationships are built gradually. People want to understand who they are dealing with, whether they can rely on them and whether there is a genuine commitment to working together.

This is not unique to Asia, of course, but it is particularly relevant in a region where business practices and cultural expectations can vary considerably between countries.

When entering a new market, entrepreneurs naturally focus on commercial opportunities. They study demand, calculate potential returns and consider how quickly they can establish operations. These are important questions, but they should not come at the expense of understanding people.

The Asian Development Bank’s Asian Economic Integration Report 2025 examines how regional cooperation, investment and participation in global value chains have helped shape Asia’s economic development.

Behind these economic relationships are businesses that must learn to work together across borders. Reliable partnerships, mutual understanding and the ability to resolve differences are essential to making that cooperation successful.

I have always believed that trust is built through consistency. People remember whether we honor our commitments, communicate honestly and treat them fairly when difficulties arise.

A partnership may begin with a commercial agreement, but its strength is often tested when circumstances change. Markets can become uncertain, costs can rise, and plans do not always unfold as expected.

For entrepreneurs, the lesson is to resist the temptation to treat relationships simply as a means of entering a market. Take time to understand local expectations, listen carefully and choose partners whose values are compatible with your own.

The strongest relationships are often those that continue long after the first transaction has been completed.

One of the most valuable lessons from Asia is that geographical proximity does not necessarily mean cultural or commercial similarity.

A business that succeeds in Singapore cannot assume that the same approach will work in Thailand or Indonesia. Consumer preferences, purchasing habits, regulations and expectations of service can differ significantly. This makes Asia an excellent reminder that international expansion requires flexibility.

The OECD’s 2026 Digital Trade Review of ASEAN highlights both the region’s growing digital opportunities and the regulatory differences that continue to complicate cross-border business.

The report estimates that ASEAN’s digital trade exports have reached $387 billion, representing nearly 20% of the region’s total exports. At the same time, differences in national regulations and cross-border data requirements remain obstacles to deeper integration.

For businesses, the implications are clear. Technology may make it easier to reach customers in another country, but it does not eliminate the need to understand how that market operates.

I believe successful international businesses distinguish between the principles they should preserve and the practices they should be willing to change.

A company’s commitment to quality, integrity and customer service should remain consistent wherever it operates. But how those commitments are delivered may need to be adapted to local circumstances.

This requires listening to local employees and customers rather than assuming that decisions made at headquarters will always be appropriate. It also requires humility. Entrepreneurs need confidence in their ideas, but they must remain willing to acknowledge when something is not working.

Sometimes the wisest decision is to test a smaller opportunity, learn from the response and adjust before committing substantial resources.

Asia’s diversity reminds us that successful expansion is not about imposing the same formula everywhere. It is about understanding what people value and finding a way to meet their needs without compromising what the business stands for.

Perhaps the most important lesson from Asia’s economic development is the value of investing in people, skills and long-term capabilities.

Many of the region’s economies have developed through participation in international production networks. Businesses do not necessarily manufacture an entire product in one country. Instead, different stages of production take place across several markets, drawing on specialized skills and resources.

The ASEAN Investment Report 2025 highlights how investment has supported the development of regional supply chains in industries including semiconductors, automotive manufacturing and apparel.

This is significant because international investment can contribute more than capital. When supported by training, knowledge-sharing and strong local partnerships, it can help businesses and workers develop capabilities that remain valuable over time.

For entrepreneurs, I believe there is an important distinction between establishing operations in another country and becoming a meaningful part of its economy.

A business may open an office, hire employees and begin generating revenue. But if every important decision is made elsewhere and local people have few opportunities to develop, its long-term contribution may be limited.

By contrast, businesses that invest in training, develop local leaders and encourage the exchange of knowledge can create stronger foundations for growth.

This does not require a large organization or an elaborate program. Smaller businesses can provide mentoring, professional development and opportunities for employees to take on greater responsibility.

These investments may not deliver immediate financial returns, but they help build the experience and confidence that organizations need as they grow.

I also believe there is something important about creating opportunities that extend beyond the business itself. When people acquire new skills, they carry that knowledge throughout their careers. Their development can benefit other organizations, industries and communities.

Asia’s experience demonstrates the potential of economies working together while developing their own capabilities. Entrepreneurs everywhere can learn from that approach.

Asia’s economic success has not followed a single model. Different countries have developed their own strengths, and the region continues to face challenges involving trade, regulation and economic uncertainty. Nevertheless, its experience offers useful lessons for businesses seeking opportunities beyond their home markets.

Relationships require patience. Local differences deserve respect. And lasting growth depends on developing people and capabilities, not simply increasing sales.

There will always be pressure to expand quickly, particularly when competitors appear to be moving ahead. But entering more markets is not necessarily the same as building a stronger business.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to consider not only where their next opportunity might be, but also what they can contribute when they get there. Can they become trusted partners? Can they serve customers in ways that reflect local needs? Can they create opportunities for people to learn and grow?

These questions may not produce the fastest route to expansion, but they encourage a more sustainable approach to international business.

To me, the greatest lesson from Asia is that creating value across borders requires more than the movement of goods, services and capital. It requires an understanding of people and a willingness to build relationships that endure.

Businesses that recognize this have an opportunity to achieve something more meaningful than international reach. They can create lasting value wherever they operate.

Asia has undergone an extraordinary economic transformation over the past several decades. Countries that once played relatively modest roles in international commerce have become important centers of manufacturing, technology, finance and innovation.

What interests me most about this transformation is not simply the speed of growth, but the way businesses across the region have learned to operate in markets with very different cultures, languages and economic conditions.

Consider Southeast Asia. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment into the region reached $226 billion in 2024, an increase of 8% even as global investment flows declined. The region has become an important part of international supply chains, connecting businesses and customers across Asia and beyond.

#5415. Constellation Space launches its platform for managing fleets of satellites with AI tools

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Alan Boyle on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:10 amNovember 12, 2026 at 9:11 am

Seattle-based Constellation Space is rolling out its flagship software platform, which uses machine learning to streamline operations for fleets of satellites and the ground networks that serve them.

“We build models in-house for things like weather, attenuation, signal jamming, demand … and synthesize all of that to help operators understand what their ground contact plan looks like in the future, and how to optimize their fleets,” CEO Kamran Majid told GeekWire.

The Constellation Platform is tailor-made for a growing number of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit. Keeping track of thousands of satellites — and the best opportunities for downlinking data from each of those satellites — is becoming an increasingly complicated task.

Constellation Space, which was founded last year, draws upon Majid’s experience as a NASA engineering intern and as a software engineer working on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.

“At Starlink, I saw firsthand how manual mission-control processes break down as constellations scale,” he said. “I started Constellation to help smaller teams get ahead of link failures instead of spending their time rebuilding pass plans and recovering from outages.”

Majid’s fellow co-founders include chief technology officer Raaid Kabir, a veteran of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, and Omeed Tehrani and Laith Altarabishi, who were previously software engineers at Capital One. “We’re a team of six people right now,” Majid said.

One year into its existence, Constellation Space has already gained traction. Several months ago, the startup said it raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Y Combinator, Nvidia, OpenAI, Samsung Next and other investors.

Majid said an early version of the Constellation Platform has attracted more than 10 customers, including Amazon Web Services. It’s also used by more than 20 academic institutions. “Our annual contract value this year is $2.25 million,” he said.

The platform combines forecasts for factors affecting satellite transmissions — including space situational awareness, weather conditions, signal-to-noise ratios, signal jamming and bandwidth demand — to predict how many gigabytes of data can be transmitted during a given pass. Operators can then use that data to optimize transmission settings and schedules.

Its machine-learning model is pre-trained on data from a global network of sensors. Once it’s deployed, the model adapts to each fleet’s specific hardware and ground stations. Constellation Space says satellite operators can boost downlinked data per pass by as much as 36%.

Majid said the journey from SpaceX to startup has been “really interesting.”

“The mindset is very similar,” he said. “I was previously an engineer. Now I’m finding myself in more of a business role. The mindset is just ‘first-principles thinking’ about everything. Eliminate all the requirements that don’t make sense before you even start to think about solving the problem. Those core tenets have stayed as we’ve progressed as a venture, and I think that’s been really important to our success so far.”

Setting up the startup in the Seattle area, where more than half of the world’s satellites are built, has also been interesting.

“We are a Y Combinator company, so we were in San Francisco for a couple of months, and there was a lot of pressure from the community in SF to have everyone be in San Francisco. We definitely felt that a little bit,” Majid said.

“But operating in the satellite sector of the space industry, Seattle is becoming more and more of a hub for the space industry in general,” he said. “Space companies are either completely moving here, opening up headquarters here, or just branching out here. It’s that, mixed in with Seattle just being known as a tech hub — and also, we all love Seattle.”

#5414. Binance's CZ Debunks False Elon Musk Banter With AI

Just about a week after Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao's brief banter with Elon Musk over his unsettling humor about Binance's recent $6 billion attack, another rumor about Musk's comment on the exchange surfaced again.

While the claims had come amid growing speculation about Elon Musk making peace with CZ, the post had immediately gone viral, receiving mixed reactions from the crypto community.

While the post claimed that billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk criticized Binance for its dominance in the crypto market, CZ dismissed the claims, calling out the poster for spreading misleading information.

Notably, the post claimed that Musk had questioned Binance's alleged 80% market share, arguing that its dominance was limiting competition within the crypto industry.

Moreover, the poster added that Musk had advised crypto users to move their funds to alternative exchanges to encourage competition, suggesting that such a move could potentially create the opportunity for another bull run.

Nonetheless, CZ debunked the information, declaring it false while issuing a subtle warning to the poster about spreading information that is not true.

After CZ declared the information to be false, he further backed his response with proof from an AI search, which clearly showed the falseness of the claims.

Notably, CZ shared a screenshot of the AI search result that disputed the alleged comments, stating that no original post from Musk could be found supporting the claims about Binance's 80% market share.

It also mentioned that Elon Musk did not encourage users to move their funds to competing exchanges either.

A few hours after CZ dismissed the false claims, Elon Musk also joined in, testifying that he never said any of the things mentioned in the post.

As proven by CZ's AI search, Musk acknowledged that the post was fabricated, backing CZ's response.

#5413. Small Business Owners Have More AI Insight Than Ever — But It’s Stuck in Dashboards. Here’s How to Put It to Work.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Small business owners today have access to a significant volume of data when it comes to managing their business, and their employee data may reveal insights that are hiding in plain sight.  Most business leaders have access to workforce dashboards to track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire in real time, and more. What they truly need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Small business owners have access to more workforce data than ever, and that data may hold insights hiding in plain sight. Most business leaders can track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire and more on real-time dashboards. What they really need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

That gap was highlighted in Paychex’s 2026 Business Leaders Priorities Report, which found that AI adoption and usage rank among the top challenges keeping businesses tied to slower, costlier processes. Many people assume the barrier is a lack of information. In reality, most small businesses already have plenty of workforce data and plenty of tools telling them what it means. The real barrier is speed and, increasingly, proof.

HR leaders are now expected to justify workforce decisions to the C-suite as they happen, not just at the end of a quarter. Decisions are often made before a meeting ends. Leaders need a clear view of their workforce, including why a staffing or scheduling decision was made, before the change shows up on a P&L.

This is becoming a major pressure point for many small businesses, and it’s exposing a design flaw that has existed in workforce technology for years: Insight and action live in different places.

A dashboard can tell a business leader that something needs attention, but acting on it often means switching to another system. Every extra step gives the moment a chance to pass. By the time a decision is made, it’s reactive instead of strategic, and the leader defending it has to reconstruct the reasoning after the fact instead of pointing to it in the moment.

Consider a restaurant owner whose overtime costs are trending above budget. A dashboard might flag the issue, but if that insight only appears in a report reviewed days later, the costs may already be locked in. When the same insight surfaces in the scheduling system the owner or manager uses every day, they can review staffing levels and adjust sooner, before the trend becomes a bigger problem that takes longer to fix.

When workforce insight sits in a separate report or standalone dashboard, it competes with everything else on a leader’s plate that day. It’s one more tab, one more login, one more thing to remember to check. If a busy owner or manager doesn’t have time to act on an insight, it might as well not exist, and decisions that affect business outcomes get delayed or missed.

The businesses making faster, more defensible workforce decisions aren’t necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated analytics. They’re the ones that understand insight only matters if it shows up inside the systems people already use, like payroll, scheduling and time tracking.

When a scheduling conflict or compliance risk appears in a tool a manager uses every day, they can act on it immediately. When it appears somewhere else, they have to go looking for it, and most small business leaders don’t have that time.

This is where AI has the potential to change the equation. The most effective AI tools do more than generate reports or highlight trends. They proactively surface relevant insights, offer recommendations and deliver guidance within the workflows where managers already spend their time. AI is most valuable when it shortens the distance between knowing and doing, while giving people the context they need to apply their own judgment.

Small business leaders aren’t struggling because they lack workforce data. They’re struggling because valuable insights are often separated from the systems where workforce decisions actually happen. Closing that gap means being more deliberate about which data matters, where it needs to appear and who has the authority to act on it. It doesn’t mean simply adding another AI tool to the tech stack.

Start by auditing where your team’s data lives compared with where decisions actually get made. If those are two different places, that’s the first gap to close. Then look at how much of your workforce data requires a separate login or report to access. Every extra step is another chance for useful information to lose its relevance before it can inform a good decision.

Next, decide where AI can provide meaningful support without removing human judgment from the process. The goal isn’t to automate every workforce decision. It’s to give the right person the right information, in the right context, at the moment it’s most useful.

What separates the businesses that get this right has less to do with how much they invest in AI and more to do with whether workforce insight is built into the flow of daily work. As small business leaders face growing pressure to explain decisions in real time, speed, context and accountability are becoming real competitive advantages.

The next chapter of AI won’t be defined by how much information it can generate. It will be defined by how well it helps leaders make smarter, more timely decisions. Businesses that can move from insight to action faster, without sacrificing human judgment, will be better positioned to adapt to change, support their workforce and compete in an increasingly complex environment.

Small business owners have access to more workforce data than ever, and that data may hold insights hiding in plain sight. Most business leaders can track turnover, overtime, engagement, cost per hire and more on real-time dashboards. What they really need is the ability to turn that data into a decision before the moment that matters has passed.

That gap was highlighted in Paychex’s 2026 Business Leaders Priorities Report, which found that AI adoption and usage rank among the top challenges keeping businesses tied to slower, costlier processes. Many people assume the barrier is a lack of information. In reality, most small businesses already have plenty of workforce data and plenty of tools telling them what it means. The real barrier is speed and, increasingly, proof.

HR leaders are now expected to justify workforce decisions to the C-suite as they happen, not just at the end of a quarter. Decisions are often made before a meeting ends. Leaders need a clear view of their workforce, including why a staffing or scheduling decision was made, before the change shows up on a P&L.

#5411. ‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center plan draws Eastern Washington protests

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon’s plans to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.

Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Big tech is shady. No more data centers” and “Water for life, not data,” according to the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin and its photos of the event.

The majority of the roughly 56 public comments were opposed to or had concerns about data center development, including worries about groundwater supplies, effects on agriculture and wildlife, and a lack of transparency, the Union-Bulletin reported. Supporters pointed to potential benefits from job creation and economic development.

The meeting highlighted continued resistance to data centers from communities concerned about higher electricity bills, depleted freshwater supplies and other environmental and social repercussions. Over the past year, tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft have pledged to limit those impacts and invest in host communities, but those commitments have not ended the opposition.

Elected officials are increasingly considering legislation and local ordinances to set standards and require greater transparency — an approach some tech leaders say could help address public concerns.

“There is a role for good laws, and if laws emerge that require that everybody do this work in a responsible way, I think that might be part of the solution,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, recently told reporters at a company event.

Commissioners in Western Washington’s Skagit County last month adopted significant restrictions on data center development. The facilities are prohibited in unincorporated areas, with some exceptions, and new caps on size and electricity usage will limit the technology to small-scale operations.

The planned Walla Walla County campus is one of two projects that would mark Amazon’s first large-scale data center developments in its home state. The second is in West Richland, part of the Tri-Cities. Amazon already operates smaller data centers in Washington.

The Walla Walla County campus would occupy roughly 134 acres at Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. Its three proposed single-story data center buildings would create about 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

According to a company fact sheet, the campus would use roughly 14 million gallons of water from the public utility to cool its equipment during its first year of operation. Amazon says it is working with the port to build a system that would replace the utility-supplied cooling water with nonpotable water drawn from the Columbia River. Wastewater from the campus “will meet industrial reuse standards,” the company said.

The campus would also use about 6 million gallons of utility-supplied water annually for employee needs.

Amazon’s fact sheet says the company will cover the electricity costs associated with the data center and that the “expenses aren’t added to the bills of local residents or businesses.”

The company is also working with partners to develop a nuclear power plant using small modular nuclear reactors near the Tri-Cities. The proposed plant could begin operating in the 2030s and “will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said.

Despite Amazon’s assurances, many attendees at Monday’s meeting called for a one-year, countywide moratorium on new data center development, the Union-Bulletin reported. Commissioner Bertha Clayton said she would consider a pause on new applications to give officials time to draft an ordinance to better regulate the developments.

Clayton said zoning changes adopted now would be unlikely to affect the current phase of Amazon’s project. The other two commissioners have previously said they do not support a moratorium, according to the Union-Bulletin.

The proposal is undergoing an environmental review under Washington’s State Environmental Policy Act, or SEPA. The review will assess potential environmental impacts and identify measures to address them. It will also determine whether the project requires a more detailed environmental impact statement.

#5410. Your Customers Are Asking AI About Your Company. Here’s How to Audit What It Says.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is changing how customers research businesses. CEOs need this eight-step, modern reputation audit to figure out what customers are seeing.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

Google reported this year that AI Overviews had more than 2.5 billion monthly active users and AI Mode had surpassed 1 billion monthly users. CEOs should account for this behavior in the same way they learned to pay attention to Google results and online reviews.

I work in online reputation management, and at my company Reputation Pros, we recommend treating a reputation audit as a recurring business process. You do not need sophisticated software to start. You just need the right questions and a system for recording what you find. Here is an audit I recommend.

Typing your company name into an AI platform will not tell you enough. Instead, put yourself in the position of a prospective customer conducting due diligence. Ask questions that require the platform to explain what it knows about your company.

Start by copying and customizing this prompt: “I’m considering doing business with [COMPANY NAME]. Research its online reputation as a prospective customer would. Summarize what the company is known for, common positive themes, recurring complaints or criticisms, significant controversies and information that could reasonably affect a customer’s decision. Separate verified facts from allegations or opinions. Where possible, identify the sources supporting each important claim and flag information that may be outdated or uncertain.”

Run the same prompt through several major AI platforms. Do not focus solely on whether the answers sound positive or negative. Look for patterns.

Does the same complaint appear several times? Does one platform emphasize an old controversy? Does another describe your company incorrectly? Which publications, review sites or other sources appear repeatedly?

Record the results. One response does not define your reputation. Differences between platforms can show you where additional investigation is necessary.

CEOs naturally focus on branded searches, but customers do not always begin there. Someone looking for a financial adviser, attorney, software company or home services provider may start by asking for reputable companies in a particular market. The customer may then compare two or three businesses before searching any company individually.

Test that part of the journey too. Use questions such as:

Pay attention to how your company appears in those answers. Do not assume that an omission means something is wrong. Instead, investigate whether credible online sources clearly establish the expertise, history and services your company claims.

This exercise can reveal a problem that a branded Google search will miss: The information people find about your company may look fine, while the broader information environment barely associates your company with the category you want to lead.

Customers are not the only people conducting online research. Potential employees, investors, vendors and business partners can investigate company leadership before making decisions. A CEO’s online reputation deserves its own audit.

Try this: “Research [CEO’S NAME] as if you were a potential business partner conducting due diligence. Summarize their professional background, current business affiliations, documented accomplishments, controversies, lawsuits or regulatory matters and recurring criticism. Distinguish verified facts from allegations and opinions. Identify the sources supporting significant claims and flag information that appears outdated, conflicting or uncertain.”

Check the basic facts first. Is the current position correct? Are former positions described as current? Are business affiliations accurate? Does the answer confuse the CEO with someone who has a similar name?

Do not ignore an error because it happens to make the CEO look good. An inaccurate award, inflated job title or incorrect company affiliation can create credibility problems just as easily as negative misinformation.

Executives sometimes see an unfavorable result and immediately ask how to remove it. Ask whether it is accurate first.

I use five simple classifications when examining reputation issues:

Those categories force you to distinguish between information that damages your reputation and information that you simply dislike.

A legitimate negative customer review requires a different response from a false claim about your company. An accurate article from six years ago requires a different approach from a biography that incorrectly lists an executive’s former employer.

AI can help organize this part of the audit. Copy a concerning response and ask: “Extract every factual claim in the following response that can be independently verified. Organize the claims by Claim, Source Cited, Verification Needed and Potential Business Impact. Do not assume a claim is accurate because it appears in the response.”

Then verify the important claims yourself using reliable sources. Do not use one AI system to declare another AI system correct. Use AI to identify what needs checking. Use primary and authoritative sources to determine what is true.

An unfavorable AI answer is often the symptom rather than the underlying problem. Investigate the sources behind it.

You may discover an outdated executive biography, an old news article, incorrect directory information, inconsistent company descriptions or customer complaints appearing across multiple sites. Ask the AI platform to show its work when the product supports citations. You can also use this prompt: “Based only on the sources available in your answer, identify the sources that support the major claims about [COMPANY]. For each source, list the claim it supports, its publication date if available and whether newer authoritative information appears to conflict with it. Do not infer a source if you cannot identify one.”

Then open the sources. I consider this one of the most important steps in a modern reputation audit. Asking “How do we change this AI answer?” too early can send a company in the wrong direction.

Ask a better question: “Why does this information exist?” A factual problem at the source gives you something concrete to investigate.

AI has expanded reputation management, but it has not completely replaced traditional search yet.

Search your company name, executive names and relevant combinations such as your company plus “reviews,” “complaints,” “lawsuit” and other terms a prospective customer might reasonably use.

Look beyond position. A negative article does not become significant simply because it ranks highly. Determine its date, source, context and accuracy. Find out whether multiple independent sources support the underlying claim or whether dozens of pages repeat information originating from a single source.

The same principle applies to positive coverage. Ten websites repeating the same press release do not provide the same independent validation as 10 separate authoritative sources.

Your audit should measure the quality of the information surrounding your company, not simply count positive and negative links.

Review management creates another risk CEOs should examine. The Federal Trade Commission’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It addresses practices including fake or false reviews and incentives conditioned on a review expressing a particular positive or negative sentiment.

The FTC sent warning letters to 10 companies in December 2025 over potential violations of the rule and noted that violations can result in substantial civil penalties. Ask your marketing and customer service teams how they request reviews.

Are incentives involved? Does anyone ask specifically for a five-star review? Do employees write reviews? Does an outside vendor manage the process? Does anyone discourage dissatisfied customers from leaving legitimate feedback?

CEOs should understand the answers. I recommend one simple test: Could you comfortably explain your review-generation process to a regulator? If you hesitate, investigate it.

Finish the audit by creating a basic spreadsheet. You only need seven columns:

Run the same core questions every quarter and compare the findings.

Label accurate information and isolated criticism as issues to monitor. Investigate recurring inconsistencies, outdated information and unsupported claims. Prioritize consequential factual errors, impersonation and rapidly spreading false information for action.

Consistency matters more than complexity. The first audit tells you what your reputation looks like today. Repeating the process shows you where it is moving.

A company preparing for an acquisition, leadership change, product launch or other major event may need to run the audit more frequently. Most CEOs can start with a quarterly review and adjust based on the risks they uncover.

Your goal is not to make every search result positive or force every AI platform to praise your company. Neither goal is realistic. Your goal is to know what customers can discover about you, understand where that information comes from and correct factual problems where you legitimately can.

In 2026, people increasingly ask machines to help them evaluate businesses and the people running them. CEOs should know what those machines are finding before an important customer, employee or business partner asks.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

#5409. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.
